Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended King's His Majesty in the House of Peers; where His Majesty Speech was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the ''P011*1, Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr.

Speaker said be had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

When 1 last met you in Parliament, I renewed to you the Assurances which I had before given you. That it was My fixed Purpose to preserve the general Tranquillity, maintaining, at the same Time, the Honour of My Crown, together with the just Rights and Interests of My People; and it was with much Satisfaction that I indulged the Hope of being still able to continue to My Subjects the Enjoyment of Peace with Honour and Security. Since that Time, those very Considerations which I then promised you that I would never sacrifice, even to the Desire of Peace, have laid me under an indispensable Necessity of preparing for a different Situation.

By the Act of the Governor of Buenos , in seizing by Force one of My Possessions, the Honour of My Crown, and the Security of My People’s Rights, were become deeply affected. Under there Circumstances I did not fail to make an immediate Demand, from the Court of Spain, of such Satisfaction as I had a Right to expect for the Injury I had received. 1 directed also the necessary Preparations to be made, without Loss of Time, for enabling Me to do Myself Justice, in case My Requisition to the Court of Spain should fail of procuring it for Me: And these Preparations, you may be assured, I shall not think it expedient to discontinue, until I shall have received proper Reparation for the Injury, as well as satisfaClory Pqoof that other Powers are equally sincere with Myself in the Resolution to preserve the general Tranquillity of Europe. In the mean time, I have called you together thus early, in order that I may be able to receive from you such Advice and Assistance, as, in the farther Progress of this very important Business, may happen to become re-quisite.

With respect to the State of My Colonies in North America, although I have the Satisfaction to acquaint you, that the People in most of them have begun to

depart

Resolution for Address*

4 13 0 Novembris. . 1770.

depart from those Combinations, which were calculated to distrefjs the Commerce of this Kingdom; yet, in feme Parts of the Colony of the very un-

warrantable Practices are still carried on, and My good Subjects oppressed by the same lawless Violence which has too long prevailed in that Province.

I hope and trust, that the Precautions which have already been used for securing this Country again (I the Visitation of that fatal Calamity, which has of late appeared in some of the distant Parts of Europe, will, with the Blessing of God, prove successful. But if, from any Alteration of Circumstances, it should at any Time be found that farther Provisions will be wanted, I cannot doubt of your ready Concurrence for so lalutary a Purpose.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I will order the proper Efti mates, for the Service of the ensuing Year, to be laid before you. They must unavoidably, in Our present Situation, exceed the usual Amount. Every unnecessary Expence My Concern for the Ease of My good Subjects will ever make Me careful to avoid. But I should neither consult their Interest nor their Inclination, if I were to decline any Expence which the Public Security, or the Maintenance of the National Honour, does at any Time require.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I am sensible how little I need say to you, at this Time, to prevail upon you to unite in whatever may belt promote the true Interest of your Country. In all your Deliberations upon Points of a domestic Nature, let the Extension of our Commerce, the Improvement of the Revenue, and the Maintenance of Order and good Government, be always in your View. With respect to Foreign' Measures, there will, I am persuaded, be no other Contest among you, than who shall appear most forward in the Support of the common Cause, in upholding the Reputation, and promoting the Prosperity, of the Kingdom. For the Attainment of these Ends, you shall ever find Me ready to exert Myself to the utmost. I have no Interest, I can have none, distinct from that of My People.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, To return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His most gracious Speech from the Throne: To offer to His Majesty our Congratulations on the happy Delivery of Her Majesty, and on the Birth of another Princess; together with our Assurances, that we esteem every Increase of His Majesty’s Royal Family an additional Security for the Continuance of that Happiness which we have already experienced under its au-lpicious Government:

To assure His Majesty, that, among the many Proofs we have received of His Majesty’s constant Attention to the Welfare and Prosperity of His People, His Majesty’s earnest Desire to continue to us the Blessings of Peace, could not fail to inspirq us with Sentiments of Gratitude and Affection; but that we could have reaped little real Satisfaction from the Enjoyment of those Blessings, had we not at the same Time been able to place the justest Confidence in His Majesty, that His Majesty would never be induced, by a mistaken Ten-derness for the present Ease of His People, to sacrifice their more essential and more lading Interests;

That we cannot but consider these as having been dangerously struck at^by the Violence lately committed by a Spanish Governor upon one of His Majesty’s Pof-

lessions: That, under these Circumstances, His Majesty’s Determination so make an immediate Demand from the Court of Spain, of such Satisfaction as His Majesty had a Right toexpedt, and at the same Time to direct the necessary Preparations to be made, without Delay, for enabling His Majesty to do Himself Justice, in case His Majesty’s Requisition from the Court of Spain should fail to procure it, demands our most hearty Acknowledgments: And that we rejoice to find, that His Ma-8

jesty will not discontinue these Preparations, until His Majesty shall have received a proper Reparation for the Injury, as well as satisfactory Proof that other Powers are equally sincere with His Majesty, in the Resolution topreserve the general Tranquillity To assure His Majesty, that, in the Prosecution of this His Majesty’s Purpose, His Majesty will not be disappointed in His Expectation of receiving from His faithful Commons every Degree of Support, which, in the Progress of this very important Business, shall become requisite: That, with this View', we will enter without Delay into the Confederation of the Supplies for the ensuing Year; and whatever extraordinary Expences the Public Service ft]all require, we will chearfully provide for, in such Manner as maybe least burthensome to His Majesty’s Subjects:

To declare, that, in considering the State of His Majesty’s Colonies in North America, we will neglect no Means of securing the commercial Interests of this Kingdom, or of providing for the Protection of His Majesty’s good Subjects there from every Degree of Violence and Oppression:

'To return His Majesty our unfeigned Thanks, for the timely Precautions His Majesty has used for guarding against the Introduction of that fatal Contagion, which has of late appeared ifl fbme of the distant Parts of Europe; and to declare, that while, with His Majesty, we place our ultimate Reliance upon the Divine Providence for our Preservation from lo great a Calamity, we shall consider it as our indispensable Doty to make use of every reasonable Precaution which human Forefight can suggest to us:

To assure His Majesty, that we will apply ourselves with all due Diligence to the Dispatch of the Public Business; in which we will not fail steadily to pursue those great Ends recommended to us by His Majesty in His Speech from the Throne, as well as by His Royal Example; and that, if any Hopes should have been conceived, or it may have been any where surmised, that among His Majesty’s People there were any such Differences subsisting, as could in the least Degree abate the Ardour of their affectionate Attachment to His Majesty, or prevent their joining, as One Man, in seconding His Majesty’s View's, for maintaining unfuliied the Lustre of His Crown, and preserving undiminithed the Rights of His People, we doubt not, by our Proceedings, to convince the World how false and injurious arc all such Surmises; and to make it manifest, that, whenever we are called upon in the Cause of our King and Country, there will be but One Heart and One Voice among His faithful Commons.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed, to draw up an Address, to be presented to His Majesty, upon the said Resolution:

A Petition of the principal Inhabitants of such Part of the High Street, in the Parish of Mary Ma/felon, otherwise Whitechapelas lies in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House;

And a Member who had not been sworn at the Table coming into the House; and the said Member having taken the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration; and having delivered in to the Clerk of the House an Account of his Qualification, and taken and lubscribed the Oath of Qualification, according to the Laws made for those Purposes;

The said Petition was read; Setting forth, That the said Street is a great Thoroughfare, being the principal Avenue to the City of London, and greatly frequented by Travellers; and that such Part of the said Street as lies within the City of London is already properly paved; but such Part of the said Street as lies within the County of Midd/eJ'exis ill paved, and the Passage through the fame greatly obstructed by Ports and Projections, and annoyed' by Signs, Spouts, and Gutters, projecting into and over the lame, whereby, and by the deep Channels across many Parts of the said Street, the same is rendered incommodious and dangerous; and that the Petitioners are willing, for the public Accommodation, to contribute to the utmost of their Abilities, and submit to an additional Tax, towards paving the said Street in a proper Manner, and rendering the same commodious; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that unless they are aided by a small daily Toil (except on Sundays) on all Coaches, Landaus, Chariots, Benins, Charles, Chairs, and Calalhes, and upon Saddle Hones, parting through the Turnpike at Mile End, in the same County, and also upon Carriages loaded with Play and Straw, which shall be brought, pitched, or fold, on Market Days, in any Part of the said Parish, the utmost that their Circumstances will admit them to pay, will not be adequate to the proposed Expence: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations and RestriClions as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Serjeant Glynn, Mr. Alderman Townsend, See.: And they are to meet Tomorrow

Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Person;, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the Mayor, Magistrates, Common Council, Guardians of the Poor, Merchants, Manufacturers, and principal Inhabitants, of the City of Norwich, was presented to the House, and read; Expressing the Apprehensions of the Petitioners, that, if the Exportation of Corn, Malt, or Grain, should be permitted for the ensuing Year, a very great Dearness and Scarcity of those Necessaries of Life will inevitably ensue; which, joined to the advanced Rates at which all other Provisions now fell, will produce the most ruinous Consequences to the industrious Poor, and greatly dirtrefs (in different Degrees) all Ranks of People in this trading and populous City: And therefore prayir.g, That the Exportation of Corn, Grain, and Malt, may be prohibited for a limited Time; or that such other Relief may be given in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That all Persons who will question any Re- ufoal turns of Members to serve in Parliament do question Order*, the same within Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in; and that all Members who are returned for Two or more Places do make their Election by this Day Three Weeks for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place; and if any Thing shall come in Question touching the Return or Election of any'Member, he is to withdraw during the Time the Matter is in Debate; and that all Members returned upon Double Returns do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned*against.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given falle Evidence, in any Ca(e, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That, in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient Time, to be appointed by the House, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members; giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners, or their Agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from Time to Time, take into his Custody any Stranger, or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committeie of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

The Lord Greville reported from the Committee ap- Addreli on pointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be pre- King’s footed to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn Speec ' up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, return Your Majesty our humble Thanks, for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne:

We beg Leave to offer to Your Majesty our Congratulations on the happy Delivery of Her Majesty, and on the Birth of another Princess; esteeming every Increase of Your Majesty’s Royal Family, an additional Security for the Continuance of that Happiness which we have already experienced under its auspicious Government:

Among the many Proofs we have received of Your Majesty’s constant Attention to the Welfare and Prospe-riiy of Your People, Your Majesty’s earned Deftre to continue to us the Blessings of Peace, could not fail to inspire us with Sentiments of Gratitude and Affection:

But we could have reaped little real Satisfaction from the Enjoyment of those Blessings, had we not at the same Time been able to place the justest Confidence in Your Majesty, that You would never be induced, by a mif-taken Tenderness for the present Ease of Your People, to sacrifice their more essential And more lading Intends.

These

Mcflape t# ihc Queen.

8 i4° — »5‘

These we cannot but consider as having been dangerously struck at, by the Violence lately committed by a Governor upop One of Your Majesty’s Possessions.-Under these Circumstances, Your Majesty’s Determination to make an immediate Demand from the Court of Spain of such Satisfaction as you had a Right to expect, and at the same Time to direct the necessary Preparations to be made, without Delay, for enabling Your Majesty to do Yourself Justice, in case Your Requisition to the Court of Spain should fail to procure it, demands our most hearty Acknowledgments; and we rejoice to find that Your Majesty will not discontinue these Preparations until You shall have received a proper Reparation for1 ihe Injury, as well as satisfactory Proof that other Powers are equally sincere with Your Majesty in the Resolution to preserve the general Tranquillity. In the Pro- fecution of this Your Majesty’s Purpose, Your Majesty will not be disappointed in Your Expectation of receiving from Your faithful Commons every Degree of Support which, in the Progress of this very important Business, shall become requisite: With this View, we will enter without Delay into the Consideration of the Supplies for the ensuing Year; and whatever extraordinary Expences the public Service shall require, we will chear-.fully provide for, in such Manner as may be least burthensome to Your Majesty’s Subjects.

In considering the State of Your Majesty’s Colonies in North America, we will neglect no Means of securing

the commercial Interests of this Kingdom, or of providing for the Protection of Your Majesty’s good Subjects there from every Degree of Violence and Oppression.

We return Your Majesty our unfeigned Thanks, for the timely Precautions You have uled, for guarding against the Introduction of that fatal Contagion which has of late appeared in some of the distant Parts of Europe: And while, with Your Majesty, we place our ultimate Reliance upon the Divine Providence for our Preservation from so great a Calamity, we shall consider it as our indispensable Duty to make use of every reasonable Precaution which human Forefight can suggest to us.

We assure Your Majesty, that we will apply ourselves with all due Diligence to the Dispatch of the public Business; in which we will not fail steadily to pursue those great Ends recommended to us by Your Majesty in Your Speech from the Throne, as well as by Your Royal Example. And if any Hopes should have been conceived, or it may have been any where surmised, that among Your Majesty’s People there were any such Differences subsisting, as could in the least Degree abate the Ardour of their affectionate Attachment for Your Majesty, or prevent their joining, as One Man, in seconding Your Majesty’s Views, for maintaining unsullied the Lustre of Your Crown, and preserving undiminished the Rights of Your People, we doubt not, by our Proceedings, to convince the World how false and injurious are all such Surmises; and to make it manifest, that, whenever we are called upon in the Cause of our King and Country, there will be but One Heart and One Voice among Your faithful Commons.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to His Majesty.

Rejuived. That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are ' of H is Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know His Majesty’s Pleasure, when He will be attended by this House.

Ordered, That His Majesty’s most gracious Speech to both Floufes of Parliament be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

A Petition of the Merchants and Tradesmen of the Port of Live:pool, on Behalf of themselves, and more particularly of those concerned in the Whale Fishery to Greenland, Davis's Straits, and the Seas adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, since the passing of the Act for the Encouragement of the Greenland Fishery, that Trade has greatly increased; but, as the same will expire at the End of the present Session of Parliament, the Trade can only enjoy the Benefit of the next Season under the present Act; and that the Greenland Trade cannot be carried on, unless a Bounty

be continued; and that the Extension of the said Bounty to a longer Term than has been lately granted would encourage many more Vessels to be employed in the Trade, and would enable the Adventurers to export a considerable Part of the Produce of their Fishery to Foreign Markets: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief as shall seem meet.

Sir James Pennyman, Baronet, having this Day presented his Petition, complaining. That at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Scarborough, in the County of York, which began on d'dvtbe Eleventh Day of last, the Petitioner and Ralph Bell, Esquire, were Candidates, and that the said Ralph Bell was then incapable of being elected to serve in Parliament; and that the Petitioner was at the said Election duly chosen by a Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been solely returned by Francis Coulson and John Esquire?,

the then Bailiffs,-and returning Officers of the said Borough; nevertheless the said Bailiffs having illegally received divers Votes for the said Ralph Bell, from Persons who had no Right to vote in the said Election, returned the said Ralph Bell, and also the Petitioner, as duly defied for the said Borough, contrary to the Law requiring fair and free Elections, in Violation of the Rights of the Electors, and to the great Injury of the Petitioner; and the House having appointed this Day Fortnight, at Two of the Clock, to take the said Petition into Consideration, you are therefore to take Notice, That the House will, at that Time, take the same Petition into Consideration.

Given under my Hand, this 15th Day of November, 1770.

Ft. Norton, Speaker.

To Sir James Pennyman, BarOnet.

The like Notice to Ralph Bell, Esquire.

Gentlemen,

I thank you for this very dutiful and affectionate Address; and for the ffefh Mark you give of your Attachment to Me and My Family, in your Congratulations on the happy Delivery of the Queen, and the Birth of another Princess.

? Your ready Concurrence in My Sentiments, and your chearful Assurances of Support, afford Me the highest Satisfaction. Whiteebapef Mr. Serjeant Glynn reported from the Committee, to Paying, whom the Petition of the principaf'fnhabitants of such Part of the High Street, in the Parish of Saint Mary Matfelon* otherwise Whitechapel, as lies in the County of Middlesex, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition j and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards dilivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition;

Mr. George Wyatt, Surveyor, being examined, laid. That the said Street is a great Thoroughfare, and such Part thereof as lies within the County of Middlesex is extremely ill paved, and the Passage through the same greatly obstructed by Posts and Projections, and annoyed by Signs, Spouts, and Gutters, by Reason whereof the said Street is not only incommodious, but dangerous to Persons passing through the fame.

8

That he had made an Estimate of the Expence of paving the said Street, amounting to £. 6,216. 2 s.; and that the annual Expence of keeping the same in Repair, will be about £. 113.

Mr. John Coverly, being examined, said. That the

Number of Houses are 146, and the annual Rents amount to £.4,822; that they pay at present about Four Shillings in the Pound on Rack Rent for Parochial Taxes — That an Increase of 12 din the Pound, will amount to no more than £. 240 per Annum; and that the proposed Tax upon Hay and Straw, will be about £. 200 per Annum — That to the Annual Expence Hated, by Mr. Wyatt should be added for Collectors, Clerks, and other incidental Expences, near £. 100 more; and that in Mr. Wyatt's Estimate no Allowance is made for the Expence of passing the Act — That the Expence at present of Paving does not amount to more then Ten Shillings per Annum for each House; and that the Inhabitants are unable to pave the said Street, and keep the same in proper Repair, without the Aid of a Toll upon Pleasure Carriages and Saddle Horses passing through the said Street, and on Carriages loaded with Hay and Straw, which shall be fold there.

Serjeant Glyttn, and Sir Charles Whitworth, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

to whom the Petition of the Commissioners for putting in Execution the several Acts of Parliament, for paving, cleansing, and lighting, the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and other Places, within the City and Liberty of West min fter, and other Parts therein mentioned, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Tabic. Where the same was read; and is as followeth -, viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. George Marquand, Surveyor to the said Commissioners, being examined, said, That great Progress has been made in the Works directed to be done by the said Acts; but, by Reason of the Insufficiency of the Funds, and Want of some further Powers, ‘the Commissioners are unable to complete the same:

That he is of Opinion, that if a Committee was appointed in every Parish, for the Purpose of making Rates, and otherwise assisting in the Execution of the said Acts; and Commissioners were to be appointed by each Parish, to be added to the present Commissioners; the Purposes of the said Acts might be more effectually carried into Execution.

Mr. Christopher Fowler, Treasurer to the said Commissioners, being examined, confirmed the above Evidence.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report*the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Merchant, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth* That the Course of the Thames forms a large Bend* or Angle, round the Surrey Shore, between Westminster bridge and the New Bridge at Black; in

the Middle of which Bend, the said River is so much wider than at either of the said Bridges, as tends to weaken v the Rapidity of the Stream, and thereby contributes to that Accumulation of Mud and Silth on the Side, and that very extensive Sand Bank on the other, so long and so generally complained of; and that the Navigation of the said River is greatly impeded by the said Sand Bank, especially at Low Water, whilst the Mud and Silth, so collected on the North Shore, renders the Access to the Wharfs and Grouti|ds on that Side very difficult, and in some Parts of the Tide impassable, to the manifest Iryury of the Public, as well as private Detriment of the Proprietors of the said Wharfs and Grounds; and that the Petitioners conceive the said Navigation might be greatly improved, and the said Nuisances and Inconveniences considerably diminished, by an Embankment of the North Part of the River, within the Bay or Hollow of the said Bend, which, by advancing the unequal and irregular Fronts of the said Wharfs and Grounds into an uniform Curve, would give a proper Direction to the Stream, and, by narrowing the unnecessary Width of its Bed in this Part, would considerably deepen the Channel of the River; and that the Petitioners, having very valuable Freehold and Leasehold Interests in the Houses, Wharfs, and Grounds, in Durham Yard, Salisbury SCecil and Beaufort Buildings, next adjoining to the said River, are willing to execute such Embankment, in the Front of their re-fpcftive Properties, at their own Expence: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for authorizing them to take in, indole, and embank, so 'much and such Part of the said River, in such Manner, upon such Terms and Conditions, and under such Restrictions and Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

1A Petition of Thomas Rumbo/d,of Hill Street, Berkley New Square, in the* County of Middlesex, Esquire, was pre- Shoreham fented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, at the ®e on* last Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of New Shoreham, in the County of Sussex, John Purling, Esquire, William James, Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and that the Petitioner was then duly elected, by a very great Majority of the legal Voters of the said Borough; the Number of Persons who had Right to vote, that polled at the Election, being in the Whole 128, of which 87 gave their Voices for . the Petitioner, 37 for the said John Purling, and for the said William James; and that, notwithstanding this Majority in the Petitioner’s Favour, which gave him a Right to be returned as duly elected for the said Borough, Hugh Roberts, the Constable and Returning Officer, who presided at the said Election, after having entered upon the Poll the Names of all the Persons who gave their Voices for the Petitioner, and after having administered to them the Bribery Oath (which they fe- . verally took) in Contempt of the Duty of his Office, did, arbitrarily and illegally, and without any Cause, but the wicked Partiality of his own Mind, declare the Votes given in Favour of the Petitioner to be illegal, and returned the said John Purling as the Person duly elected to serve as a Burgess for the said Borough, in manifest Defiance of the Statutes requiring fair and free Election, and to the grievous Injury of the Petitioner: And therefore praying the House, to give him such Relief as the Nature of his same requires, and to inflict such Pu-nifoment upon the said Hugh Roberts, the Returning Officer, as the Enormiry of his Guilt requires.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tomorrow Seven night, the 1 ith Day of this Instant December, at Two of the Clock, in the Afternoon.

Thomas Rumbold, Esquire, having this Day presented his Petition, complaining. That at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of New Shoreham, in the County of which came on the 26th

Day of November la Purling, Esquire,

William James, Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and that the Petitioner was then duly elected by a great Majority of the legal Voters of the said Borough j the Number of Persons who had a Right to vote, that polled at the Election, being in the Whole 128, of which 87 gave their Voices for the Petitioner, 37 for the said John , and for the said William James; and that, notwithstanding this Majority in the Petitioner’s Favour, which gave him a Right to be returned as duly elected for the said Borough, Hugh Roberts, the Constable and Returning Officer, who prdided at the said Election, after having entered upon the Poll, the Names df all the Persons who gave their Voices for the Petitioner, and after having administered to them the Bribery Oath, which they severally took, in Contempt of the Duty of his Office, did, arbitrarily and illegally, and without any Cause, but the wicked Partiality of his own Mind, declare the Votes given in Favour of the Petitioner to be illegal, and returned the said John Purling as the Person duly elected to serve as a Burgess for the said Borough, in manifest Defiance of the Statutes requiring fair and free Election, and to the grievous Injury of the Petitioner; and the House having appointed Tomorrow Seven-night, the 1 ith Day of this Instant at Two of the Clock in the Afternoon, to take the said Petition into Consideration, You are therefore to take Notice, That the House will, at that Time, take the same Petition into Consideration.

Given under my Hand, this 3d Day of December 1770.

Flr Norton, Speaker.

A Petition of John March, Richard William

Clarke, William Cooper, Samuel Smith, William Ewer, and James Lee, Esquires, the Trustees of a Charity founded by Sir John Morden, Baronet, deceased, for the Benefit and Support of decayed Merchants, commonly called Morden College, situate near Blackheath, in the Parish of Charlton, and County of Kent, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, gives His Consent, as far as His Majesty’s Interest is concerned, that the House may do therein as they shall think fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That his late Majesty King William the Third, by his Letters Patent under the Great Seal of England, bearing Date the 4th Day of November, in the nth Year of his Reign, for the Consideration therein mentioned, did grant to, or in Trust for, the said Sir John Morden, his Heirs and Assigns for ever, the Manor or Lord ship of Old Court, with the Lands thereto belonging, in the Parish of East Greenwich, and County of Kent; and that the said Sir John Morden, intending to make some Provision for the Comfort and Support of aged and decayed Merchants, erected, at his own Expence, a House, or College, near Blackheath, for their Reception; and, by his last Will and Testament, bearing Date the 9th Day of March 1702, he gave and deviled all his Real Estates to certain Trustees, and their Heirs and Assigns, for ever, in Trust for the Use of the said College, and for the Maintenance and Support of poor aged and decayed Merchants of England, whose Fortunes had been ruined by the Perils of the Sea, and other unavoidable Accidents; and that the Petitioners, by virtue of divers Mesne Assignments and Conveyances in the Law, are now seised of the said Manor or Lordship of Old Court, and of the other Real Estates of the said Sir John Morden, in Trust, for the Benefit of the Charity so founded by him; and that the Trustees of the Charity for the Time being have, at various Times, possessed divers Parts of a certain Parcel of Land, in the Parish of East Greenwich, called Hill, on

an jApprchension that the same was Part of the Lord ship or Manor of Old Court, and have, at various Times, granted Leases of several Parts of the feme to fuodry

Persons, who have erfcfted Houses thereon; but the said Hill having been claimed, on Behalf of His Majesty, as being Part of His Royal Manor of East Greenwich, Informations of Intrusion have been exhibited, by His Majesty’s Attorney General, in the Court of Exchequer, against several of those Lessees; and that, in order to comprotnife the said Matter, and to feve Expence to the Charity, it has been agreed, between the Surveyor General of His Majesty’s Lands, on Behalf of His Majesty of the one Part, and the Petitioners on the other, to the following Effect; that the Petitioners do admit the Right of the Crown to the said Hill, and to all other the Wastes of the said Manor of East Greenwich; and that they be acquitted and discharged of all Accounts, Claims, and Demands whatever, for or in respect of any Rent, Profit, or Advantage, which have been heretofore received or made by them, or any of their Predecessors in the said Trust; and that they have a proper Consent for their applying for, and obtaining, an Act of Parliament, to indemnify the Petitioners against all Suits, Afticms, Cods, Charges, Damages, and Expences, for and on account of their or any of their Predecessors, in the said Trust, having, without any legal Title, entered into Possession of the said Hill, and exercised Acts of Otfner-ship therein and also to indemnify the Petitioners, their Officers, and Servants, touching any Matter or Thing relative to the entering into the said Agreement; ana to enable his Majesty to grant to them a Lease of the said Hill, and of the Houses and Buildings erected thereon, for the Term of 50 Years, without paying any Fine for the fame, referring therein One Third Part of the neat Income which they now receive from the said Premises, as a Yearly Rent; and also to enable His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, from Time to Time, to grant, unto the Trustees of the said Charity for the Time being, a Lease or Leases of the said Premises, for any further Term or Terms rtot exceeding 50 Years, each referring therein Qne Third Part of the neat Income, which, at the respective Times of granting fucU subsequent Lease or Leases, they shall receive from the same, as a Yearly Rent; and they declare their Willing-ness to be restrained from taking any Fine for Building Leases or for Renewals of Leases of any Houses already built,- or to be built on the said Hill; and that the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury have approved of the said Agreement, with these Restrictions; that, in such Lease or Leases, there shall be contained proper Covenants torestrain the Petitioners, and their Successors, from erecting any Buildings whatever on any Part of the Top or Plain of the Hill, or inclosing any Part thereof, without the Consent and Approbation of the Crown; and also to restrain the Trustees of the Charity for the Time being from digging, and carrying away from off the said Premises, any of the Soil, Chalk, Lime, -Stone, or Gravd, of the said Hill, or any Part thereof; and from taking any Fine or Ernes for Building Leases, or for Renewals of Leases of Houses thereon; and tljat the said Sir John Morden, by his Will, di-rested that there should be placed in his feid College so many poor Merchants as the clear Yearly Rents and Revenue of his Estates would maintain, allowing to each Merchant £. 20 a Year, to be laid out in Provisions and Necessaries, as is particularly prescribed in the Will; and by a Codicil thereto he declared, that the said Pension should be reduced to /.15 a Year; and that the Sum of £. 15 a Year is at this Time too small and inadequate an Allowance for Provisions and Necessaries for the Persons intended by the Founder of the Charity to be benefited thereby, the feme being but little more than what is generally allowed to Persons of very low Education and Condition of Life, inso much that many Merchants, who, through Casualties and Age, are reduced to Want, are hindered from applying to partake of lb scanty an Allowance; and that, if the Petitioners were enabled to increase the said Pension to

a Sum

That Leave may be* given to bring in a Bill to confirm the said Agreement, and to enable His Majesty to grant to them a Lease, without Fine, of the said Hill, called Maidinstone and of the Houses and Buildings erected or to be erected thereon, for the Terrh of 50 Years, according to the beforementioned Terms of the said Agreement; and also to enable His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, from Time to Time, to grant unto the Trustees of the said Charity for the Time being, a Lease or Leases thereof, for such further Term or Terms, not exceeding 50 Years each, as to His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, shall feetn proper, under ldch Regulations and Restrictions as are before mentioned; and to release, exonerate, and discharge, the Petitioners and their Successors, of and from all Accounts, Claims, and Demands, for or in respect of any Rent, or Arrears of Rent, or other Profit or Advantage heretofore made by the Trustees of the said Charity for the Time being, for, or in respect of the said Hill, whilst they, have been in Possession thereof; and ailo to indemnify the Petitioners, their Officers and Servants, for what they have done, or shall do, in and about the compromising the Matters in Dispute between the Crown and them, relating to the said Hill; and to authorize and impower the Petitioners, and the Trustees of the said Charity for the Time being, to increase the Pensions paid to each poor Merchant, to such Yearly Sum or Sums as they shall think proper, not exceeding £. 40 to any one Person in any one Year; or to grant to the Petitioners such other Relief and Assistance in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Merchants and Tradesmen of the Port of Kingston upon Hull, on Behalf of themselves, and more particularly of those concerned in the Whale Fishery to Greenland, Davis’s Straits, and the Seas adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That since passing the Act for the Encouragement of the Greenland Fishery, that Trade has been carried on at the said Port with only indifferent Success; and, as the said Act will expire at tire end of the present Session of Parliament, the Trade can only, enjoy the Benefit of the next Season under the present Act; therefore it is by Experience found, that the Greenland Trade cannot be continued, except a Bounty be allowed, which, if continued for a longer Term than has been lately granted, it would encourage many more Vessels to be employed in the Trade, and would enable the Adventurers to export a considerable Part of the Produce to foreign Markets: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises under Consideration, and grant them such Relief as shall seem most meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Merchants arid Tradesmen of the Port of Live)pool, on Behalf of themselves, and more particularly of those concerned in the Whale Fishery to Greenland, s

Straits, and the Seas adjacent, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Westminster A Petition of the Governors and Directors of the Paving. Poor, in Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of that Part of the Parish of Saint Andrew born, which lies above the Bars, in the County of

dlesex, and the Parish of Saint George the Martyr, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read Reciting Part of an Act of the 6th Year of His present Majesty, for the better regulating and employing the Poor; and for cleanGng, lighting, and watching, the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and other Places, within the Parishes aforesaid; and Setting forth. That, in consequence of the said Act, the Governors and Directors elected, pursuant thereto, have proceeded to put the same in Execution; and that the said Act has been found fully and effectually to answer every salutary Purpose intended thereby, within the said Parishes; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill has been brought in, to amend, and render more effectual, several Acts made, relating to paving, cleansing, and lighting, the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and other Places, within the City and Liberty o and Parts adjacent;

and that the Petitioners find, that the said Parishes are intended to be included in the said Bill, for all the Purposes of paving, cleansing, and lighting; and, if the same should pafsintoa Law, in the Manner thereby proposed, it must, in Effect, amount to a Repeal of the said Act of the 6th of His present Majesty, and thereby defeat the said Parishes of the principal Benefits by the said Act intended; and that, if the Powers granted by the said Act of the 6th of His present Majesty’s Reign to the said Governors and Directors were extended, and proper Powers given to pave the said Parishes, as well as to light and cleanse the fame, it would effectually answer every salutary End, within those Parishes, which can be possibly effected by the Bill now proposed by the Westminster Commissioners, and in a more easy

and commodious, and, as the Petitioners conceive, in a much let's expensive, Manner: And therefore praying. That the said Bill, so far as it relates to the lighting, cleansing, and paving, the said Parishes of Andrew Holborn, above the Bars, and Saint George the,

may not pal's into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against being included in the said Bill, and also against such Parts thereof as the Petitioners conceive may affect the Rights, Privileges, and Interests of the said Parishes.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

Mr. Alderman Townsend accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition; Mr.

James Clare, being examined, said, That the Streets,

Lanes, and other Places within the said Precinct (except such Part as is paved by virtue of an Act of the Seventh Year of His present Majesty) are become dangerous, and that several Nuisances and Incroachments have been made therein; and that if the said Precinct was properly paved, cleansed, and lighted, and a regular Watch established, and also Power granted to remove the present Nuisancesand Incroachments, and to prevent the like for the future, it would be a great Benefit to the Inhabitants of the said Precinct.

Mr. JoJ'eph Harrison, being examined, confirmed the above Evidence.

Herring A Petition of the several Inhabitants of the Burghs >i(bcry. of Campbeltown, Ayr, Irvine, Roth say, and Dumbarton,

and of the Town of Greenock, thereunto subscribing, on Behalf of themselves and others in Scotland, concerned in the White Herring Fishery, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That in the 23d Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, a Bounty of Thirty Shillings per Ton, was given to all Vessels employed in the White Herring Fishery, fitted out in the Manner prescribed by the said Act; which Bounty, in the 30th Year of the said Reign, was increased to Fifty Shillings per Ton, payable out of the Customs i and that the Petitioners, under the Faith of h.wing the said Bounty regularly paid, have, at a great Expence, carried on the said Fishery, to a considerable Extent j but are in such Difficulties, from the Deficiency of the Fund allotted for the Payment of this Bounty, that they will be obliged to give up this valuable Branch of Trade, unless the Payment of the said Bounty shall be put on l'ome better Footing: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and give the Petitioners such Redress therein as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to _ whom it is referred to consider of the several Laws now in being, for the Encouragement of the British White Herring Fishery.

A Petition of several Trustees appointed to put m Execution an Act of Parliament, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing several Roads leading through the County of Selkirk, whefe Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act, and have borrowed £.3,000 Sterling on the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted, which Sum hath been duly applied, and now remains due; and that, in order effectually to amend the said Roads, and to keep the feme in good Repair, they find it necessary to borrow a further Sum of Money, which, by the said Act, they are not authorized to do; and that, by reason of some Exemptions from Payment of Toll, and from some other De-fefts in the said Act, the Money already due, and which is necessary to be borrowed for repairing the said Roads, cannot be paid off, and the said Roads amended, and kept in good Repair, unless those Exemptions are re pealed, and some other Amendments made in the said Act, and the present Term thereof further continued: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers of the said Act, in such Manner as the House shall think fit.

A Petition of the several Commissioners of the Navigation of the Rivers Thames and Ijis, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, and of the several Gentlemen, Land Owners, Tradesmen, Manufacturers, and others, of the Counties of Middlesex, Surrey, Berks, Bucks, Oxford, Gloucester, and Wilts, whole Names are thereunto

subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Navigation of the Rivers Thames and Ijis, from the City of London, Westward, to the Town of Crick/ade, in the County of Wilts, is at divers Times of the Year rendered impassable, by the bad State, Condition* and Construction, of the Locks and Weirs upon the said Rivers, and for Want of a proper Depth of Water in many Places; and that, by improving the Channel of the said Rivers, and making the same navigable at all Seasons of the Year, the Intercourses of Trade and Commerce will be very much extended, and the Charge of Water Carriage considerably lefl'ened, and many local Benefits produced to the several Towns and Places lying near the Course of the said Rivers; and that, by several Acts of Parliament, made in the Reigns of King William and Queen Mary, and of his late and present Majesty, a Duty of Six Pence per Chaldron is laid upon all Coals and Culm imported into the Port of London, to the Payment of which, the Petitioners and their Ancestors, Conlumers of Sea Coal, in the Counties West of London, have contributed, without any Advantage to themselves from the Application of its Produce, the same being appropriated intirely to the Ornament, Convenience, and Benefit, of the City of London and its Environs: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given lo bring in a Bill for improving and completing the Navigation of the said Rivers of Thames and Ijis, from the City of London Westward, to the Town of Cricklade, in the County of and for

defraying the Expences thereof, by laying an additional Duty of One Penny per Ton, or Chaldron, on all Coals and Culm imported into the Port of London, for a certain Term, or by any other Mode of Taxation, as to the House shall leem meet.

And being returned;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said A cl of the 23d of Henry the 8 th. Cap. v; and also,

An Act passed in the S xth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act for paving the Streets " and Lanes within the Town and Borough of Southwork, and certain Parts adjacent in the County of " Surrey, and for cleansing, lighting, and watching, the 11 fame, and also the Courts, Yards, Alleys, and Pafsages adjoining thereto, and for preventing Annoyances therein ;" — were severally read.

By which last mentioned Act it is Enacted, That, in case of the repairing, altering, cleansing, or emptying, any Sewer, Vault, or Drain, within the Limits described in the said Act, Notice is to be given to the Commissioners for putting the said Act in Execution, or to their Surveyor or Clerk, who are to cause the same to be repaired, and the Expences thereof are to be paid by the said Commissioners, who are to bereimbursed by the Commissioners of Sewers; and the Commissioners for putting in Execution the said Act of the 6th of His present Majesty, are further impowered to turn the Course of Gutters, to alter or repair Grates, to make new ones, to make new Sewers, or to repair, alter, cleanse, or empty, the old Sewers at their Discretion; the Expences of all which Works are directed to be defrayed by the Commissioners of Sewers; and in case of Non-payment the said Commissioners are empowered to bring an Action or Actions at Law, against the Petitioners Clerk or Treasurer, for recovering such Sums as shall have been expended for the Purposes aforei'aid. Then

Mr. Thomas Lintall, Clerk to the Commissioners of Sewers, produced a Bill of Expences, as delivered to him, amounting to £. 705. 155. 9; and said, That Seven

other Bills had been afterwards delivered to him, amounting to £. 548, on which they have brought an Action against him — That he pleaded he did not owe the Money; upon which, Issue was joined, and the Cause came on to be tried the last Summer Assizes for the County of Surrey. — The Plaintiff having declared in an Action of Debt — The Counsel for the Defendant made a Question, Whether it should not have been an Action upon the same ? Lord Mansfield, the Judge, who tried the Cause, directed the Jury to find a conditional Verdict on the Fourth Count of the Plaintiff’s Declaration for £. 22, which Verdict was to be subject to the Opinion of the Court of King’s Bench, upon a same to be stated as to the Propriety of the said Action being brought as an Action of Debt; and if the Court of King’s Bench should be of Opinion with the Plaintiff, the Verdict was to (land, and the Plainriff was to be at Liberty to bring a future Action for the Residue of his Demand; but if the Court should be of Opinion with the Defendant, the Verdict was not to (land, but the Defendant was to be at Liberty to enter up a Judgment of Nonsuit against the Plaintiff: So the Cause stands at present, it not having been yet argued.

Then the Commission of Sewers was produced, and read; and,

Mr. Thomas Lintall, being again examined, said. That the Commissioners have no Authority to raise Money for Work they do not perform; that their Commission extends far into the County of , and even into

Kent; and that it would be very hard had they a Power to r.iife Money upon the rest of the County, who receive no Benefit from the Sewers in the Borough: — That the whole Extent of the Commission is divided intofeparate Districts, and that Money is raised upon the several Districts in Rotation, as it is wanted for the Execution of the Commission, and, as it is collected, is paid into the Hands of the general Expenditor, and by him paid out by Order of the Commissioners of Sewers for necessary Repairs; nor are the Commissioners of Sewers impowered by their Commission to expend any of the Money by them raised, except upon Works which shall appear either by View of the Commissioners, or the Presentment of a Jury, to require Reparation or Amendment; neither of which

Vol. 33.

previous necessary Measures have been taken in the Works done by the Commissioners of the Pavements: That there are Seventeen public Sluices under the Commission, which are repaired, or made new, as the Cale requires; and the Rates are made on the Owners and Occupiers of Messuages, Lands, and Tenements, drained or benefited thereby That there are Twenty-two or Twenty-three Districts; and that the Rates are always made by Juries:

That the last Rate made for the'District which contains the Limits under the Direction of the Commissioners of Pavements, was on the 6th of February 1766, and amounted to £.944. 171. which was paid into the general Fund, and from thence issued as Occasion required.

And the Bailiff to the Commissioners of Sewers informed your Committee, that the next District in Rotation to be taxed was the aforesaid District: Then Mr. Gunter, Solicitor to the Commissioners for Pavements, said, That he was directed to bring an Action against the Commissioners of Sewers for £.705, on Two several Claul'es relating to the Grates and Sewers; that £.548, Part of that Sum, was for repairing and cleansing Sewers, and the Remainder for fixing Grates; that the Reason for bringing the Action for the Sum of £.548 only, was, because "the Paving Act authorizes the Com-’missioners to bring an Action against the Clerk for the Expence of repairing Sewers only, and the Commissioners of Sewers are by the Act directed to pay the Expences of the Grates'; the Commissioners of Pavements are not authorized to recover the same from their Clerk, but from the Commissioners.

Mr. John Fellowes, Surveyor to the Commissioners of Pavements for the Eastern Division of , pro-

duced to your Committee an Account of the Expenditure of the said Sum of £.705. 15*. 9 whereby it appeared, that Part of the Expence was incurred for covering. Part for turning, extending, enlarging, and cleansing, the Sewers, and Part for carting away the Soil.

John Middlmarsh, Esquire, one of the Commissioners of Sewers, and Expenditor, informed your Committee, That the Commissioners are not impowered to raise any Money for calling and cleansing Sewers; and that the Commissioners always call a Jury to make the Rates.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

2id January 1771.

SIR,

I am commanded by the House of Commons to acquaint you, That you are, immediately upon the Receipt of this, to summon the Representatives of your County, and Boroughs within the same, to attend their Service in Parliament on this Day Fortnight, the 5th Day of February next; the House of Commons intending to proceed with the utmost Severity against such of their Members as shall then neglect to attend the Service of the House: And you are to give me an Account of the Receipt of this, and".vhat you have done thereupon* upon Pain of incurring the Displeasure of the said J^ouse.

I am.

Sir,

Your humble Servant,

Flr Norton, Speaker.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth. That, by several Acts, of the 22d and 23d of King Charles the Second, the Second of King William and Queen the Seventh of Queen Anne, and the Tenth of King George the Second, Powers are granted to the Petitioners, to appoint Commissioners for making, enlarging, amending, and cleansing, the Vaults, Drains, and Sewers, within the said City and Liberties thereof; and that, by another Act, made in the Eighth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, the foie Power and Authority of paving, cleansing, and enlightening, the Streets, Lanes, Squares, Yards, Courts, Alleys, Passages, and Places, within the said City and Liberties, are vested in the Petitioners; and that the said Powers relative to the Vaults, Drains, and Sewers, and the said Powers relative to the Pavements, although vested in the same Persons, are exercised separately and dillindlly, under different Authorities, whereby, the Petitioners conceive, several of the good Intentions of the said Act cannot be so effectually answered as they might be if the said several Powers were con-lolidated, and the Persons intruded therewith appointed m and by one and the same Commission; and that several of the Streets and Places within the said City and Liberties, for Want of proper Drains or Sewers, are frequently annoyed, the Houses and Buildings therein weakened and rendered of less Use, and the Healths of His Majesty’s Subjects greatly affected; and that the whole Expe.nce of making, altering, repairing, and cleansing, the said Sewers and Drains, is at present defrayed by Assessments upon the Inhabitants, contrary to the Practice in the City, of Westminster, and moll other Towns and Places, a Mode of Taxation attended with many Hard ships and Injullice; and that the Petitioners have Reason to think that the present Fund for paving, cleansing, and lighting, the said City and Liberties, might be sufficient to answer, by Degrees, the Expence of making new Sewers and Drains where wanted, and of enlarging old ones where necessary; and that such Application would be readily submitted to by the Inhabitants, if the Expence of altering, repairing, and cleansing, all the Sewers and Drains made, or to be made, was to be defrayed by Assessments upon the Landlords or Proprietors of Houses and Lands within the said City and Liberties: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for consolidating, extending, and rendering more effectual, the Powers granted by several Acts of Parliament for making, enlarging, amending, and cleansing, the Vaults, Drains, and Sewers, within the City of London and Liberties thereof, and for paving, cleansing, and enlightening, the Streets, Lanes, Squares, Yards, Courts, Alleys,

A. 1771*

Passages, and Places, arid prevertting and removing Ob-drudlions and Annoyances within the same.

Translation of the Declaration signed and delivered by Prince De Majferano, Ambassador Extraor-

dinary from his Catholic Majesty, the 22d of January 1771.

His Britannic Majesty, having complained of the Violence which was committed on the 10th of June 1770, at the IYland commonly called the Great Malouine, and by the English, Falkland's in obliging, by

Force, the Commander and Subjects of His Britannic Majesty, to evacuate the Port by them called,

a Step offensive to the Honour of His Crown; the Prince De Majfareno, Ambassador Extraordinary of his

Catholic Majesty, has received Orders to declare, and declares. That his Catholic Majesty considering the Desire with which he is animated foe Peace, and for the Maintenance of good Harmony with His Britannic Majesty, and reflecting that this Event might interrupt it, has seen with Displeasure this Expedition tending to disturb it, and in the Persuasion, in which he is of the Reciprocity of Sentiments of His Britannic Majesty, and of its being far from his Intention to authorize any Thing that might disturb the good Understanding between the Two Courts.; His Catholic Majesty does

9

disavow the said violent Enterprize; and in Confluence, the Prince De Majferano declares. That his Catholic Majesty engages to give immediate Orders, that Things shall be restored in the Great Malouine, at the Port called Egmont, precisely to the State in which they were before the Tenth of June 17.70; for which Purpose, his Catholic Majesty will give Orders to One of his Officers, to deliver up to the Officer authorized by His Britannic Majesty, the Port and Fort called Egmont, with all the Artillery, Stores, and Effects, of His Majesty, and His Subjects, which were at that Place the Day above named, agreeable to the Inventory which has been made of them.

The Prince De Majferano declares at the same Time, in the Name of the King his Matter, that the Engagement of his said Catholic Majesty, to restore to His Britannic Majesty, the Possession of the Port and Fort called Egmont, cannot nor ought any wife to affect the Question of the prior.Right of Sovereignty of the otherwise called Falkland's Iflan — In Witness whereof, I the underwritten Ambassador Extraordinary have signed the present Declaration with my usual Signature, and caused it to be sealed with our Arms. ,the

Twenty-second Day of January One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-one.

'(L. SJ Signed

Le Prince De.

Translation of the Acceptance by the Earl of / Rochford, in His Majesty’s Name, the 22d January 177x, of the Spanish Ambassador’s Declaration of the same Date.

His Catholic Majesty, having authorized the Prince of Majferano, his Ambassador Extraordinary, to offer

in his Royal Name, to the King of a

Satisfaction for the Injury done to His Britannic Majesty, by dispossessing Him of the Port and Fort of Port Egmont; and the said Ambassador having this Day signed a Declaration, which he has just; delivered to me, expressing the rein, that his Catholic Majesty, being desirous to restore the good Harmony and Friendship which before subsisted between the Two Crowns, does disavow the Expedition against Port Egmont, in which, Force has been used against His Britannic Majesty’s Possessions, Commander, and Subjects; and does also engage, that all Things shall be immediately restored to the precise Situation in which they flood before the 10th of June 1770; and that his Catholic Majesty shall give Orders, in Consequence, to One of his Officers, to deliver up to the Officer authorized by His Britannic Majesty, the Port and Fort of Port Egmont, as also all His Britannic Majesty’s Artillery, Stores, and Effects, as well as those of His Subjects, according to the Inventory which has been made of them; and the said Ambassador having moreover engaged, in his Catholic Majesty’s Name, that what is contained in the said Declaration, shall be carried into Effect by his said Catholic Majesty, and that Duplicates of his Catholic Majesty’s Orders to his Officers shall be delivered into the Hands of One of His Britannic Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, within Six Weeks; His said Britannic Majesty, in Order to shew the same friendly Dispositions on his Part, has authorized me to declare, that He will look upon the said Declaration of Prince De Majferano, together with the full Performance of the said Engagement on the Part of his Catholic Majesty, as a Satisfaction for the Injury done to the Crown of Great Britain. — In Witness whereof, I underwritten, One of His Britannic Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, have signed these Presents with my usual Signature, and caused them to be sealed with our Arms. London, the Twenty-second Day of January One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-one.

(L, S.) Signed

Rochford.

Brrmondsey A Petition of the Churchwardens of the Parish of

Assessment. Saint Mary Magdalen, , in the County of

Surrey, whose Name? are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act passed in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for paving the Streets and Lanes within the Town and Borough of Southwark, and certain Parts adjacent, in the County of Surrey; and for cleaning, lighting, and watching, the fame, and also the Courts, Yards, Alleys, and Passages, adjoining thereto; and for preventing Annoyances therein, all Parish Churches, Church Yards, Chapels, Meeting Houses, Schools, Warehouses, Hospitals, Prisons, and all other public Buildings whatsoever, and all dead Walls and void Spaces of Ground, situate within the said Streets and Places, are directed to be rated at a Rate not exceeding Sixpence for every Square Yard belonging to every such Parish Church, Church Yard, and other public Building, dead Wall, and void Space of Ground; and that the Commissioners by the said Act appointed, have for Four Years pad rated and assessed the Parish Church and Church Yard of Bermondsey aforesaid, at the Rate of Fifty Pounds per Annum, although they have not hitherto paved or repaired any Part of the Street or Ground lying before the said Church or Church Yard; and that the said Commissioners have, from Time to Time, rated and assessed some Churches, Church Yards, public Buildings, dead Walls, and void Spaces of Ground, within the said Streets and Places, by the Square Yard, for the Content thereof, and others only for the Content of the Street or Ground lying before the fame: which latter Mode of Assessment, the Pe-tioners apprehend, ought in Justice to be extended in an equal Degree to all Churches, Church Yards, public Buildings, dead Walls, and void Spaces, lying or being within the Limits of the said Act; and that the Petitioners find, by the Votes, a Bill hath been brought in, to explain and amend Part of the said Act: And therefore praying the House, That Provision may be made in the said Bill, directing the said Commissioners to make, for the future, their Rates or Assessments, from Time to Time, in an equal Manner, on all Churches, Church Yards, public Buildings, dead Walls, and void Spaces of Ground, comprised within the Limits of the said Act; or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of certain Manufacturing Mills, in the Neighbourhood'of mingham, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners Mills are dependent, for a Supply of Water, upon certain Streams or Rivulets, which have, by the Proprietors of the Birmingham Canal Navigation, been occasionally in the last Summer turned into the said Canal, for the Supply of Water loft thereout by Leakage or otherwise; and the Petitioners believe, that although, pursuant to the Act for the establishing the said Canal, as great a Part as possible of the said Water had been returned, by the Weirs and other Conveniences on the said Canal, into the original Channel-or Course for supplying the Petitioners said Mills, and notwithstanding the last Summer proved in general very wet, yet the Petitioners found themselves occasionally under great Difficulties, in the short Periods in which they were deprived of the said Streams and Rivulets; and, as a very considerable and constant Leakage hath aril'en upon the present Termination of the said Canal, the Petitioners are greatly alarmed at the Petition of Charles Colmore, Esquire, for continuing the said Canal from its present Termination up to Ring, through Ground (as the Petitioners are informed) equally hazardous in Point of Leakage to that last passed in the present Termination, and which may greatly affest the Property of the Petitioners in their said Mills, for Want of a regular Supply of Water; and that the present Termination of the said Canal appears sufficient for most of the Purposes of immediate Utility and Convenience to the Town of Birmingham and the adjacent Country: And therefore hope the Proprietors of the said Canal will be reftiained by Law from extending the said Canal any further in its present Line of Direction, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, in Opposition to the Bill of the said Charles , now

London The Lord Mayor of London reported from the Com-Vaolti, mittee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Alder-^Sewer* men> ant* Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, several Acts of Parliament of the 22d and 23d Years of King Charles the Second, the Second Year of King William and Queen Mary, the Seventh of Queen Anne, and the Tenth of King George the Second, were read; whereby divers Powers are granted to the Petitioners, to appoint Commissioners for making, enlarging, amending, and cleansing, the Vaults, Drains, and Sewers, within the said City and the Liberties thereof.

Another Act, made in the Eighth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for the better paving, cleansing, and enlightening, the said City and Liberties, and for preventing Obstructions and Annoyances within the same, was also read; whereby the foie Power and Authority of paving, cleansing, and enlightening, the Streets, Lanes, and other Public Passages, within the said City and Liberties, are vested in the Petitioners, to be executed by such Persons as (by virtue of the said Act of the Z2d and 23d of King Charles the Second) were, or thereafter from Time to Time should be, authorized or appointed by the Petitioners, to be Commissioners of the Sewers for the said City and Liberties, or by any Seven or more of them.

Mr. George Wyatt, Surveyor to the said Commissioners, being examined, said, That, notwithstanding the Powers relative to the Sewers and Pavements are vested in the same Persons, yet they are exercised separately under different Authorities, by which Means the Commissioners are disabled from Arrying the good Purposes, intended by the said Acts, so conveniently into Execution as they would be, if the said Powers were consolidated; which would prevent many Difficulties and Delays which

Vol. 33.

now frequently happen in the Execution of the said Acts.

That several Streets and Places within the said City and Liberties are frequently annoyed, and the Buildings much injured, for want of sufficient Drains and Sewers.

That many of the Streets have no Sewers at all; and in such Streets the Inhabitants are obliged to have their Kitchens above Ground, or to make Cess Pools, which are a great Nuisance.

That the whole Expence of making, altering, repairing, and cleansing, the said Sewers and Drains, is at present paid by an Assessment upon the Inhabitants, which' is not only contrary to the Practice in the City of

mirfler, but a manifest Injustice; as a Person may be put to the Expence of removing Filth, which other Persons have suffered to accumulate for a great Number of.

Years. , '

That he is of Opinion (as the Annuitants die off) the present Fund for paving, cleansing, and lighting the said City, will be sufficient, by Degrees, to answer the Expence of making new Sewers where wanting, and of enlarging the old ones where necessary; which Expence, he thinks, would be chearfully submitted toby the Inhabitants, if the Expence of altering, repairing, and cleansing them, were to be defrayed by the Proprietors of Houses and Lands; and that he is of Opinion, that an Assessment. upon the Landlords for this Purpose would not amount to more than Four Pence in the Pound once in Five Years.

Upon the Whole, your Committee came to the following Resolutionsf Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petititioners have proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for consolidating, extending, and rendering more effectual, the Powers granted by several Acts of Parliament, for making, enlarging, amending, and cleansing, the Vaults, Drains, and Sewers, within the City of London and Liberties thereof, and for paving, cleansing, and enlightening, the Streets, Lanes, Squares, Yards, Courts,

Alleys, Passages, and Places,'and preventing and removing Obstructions, and Annoyances, within the same.

The First Resolution of the Committee, being read a-Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The subsequent Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for consolidating, extending, and rendering more effectual, the Powers granted by several Acts of Parliament, for making, enlarging, amending, and cleansing, the'Vaults,

Drains, and Sewers, within the City of London and Liberties thereof, and for paving, cleansing, and enlightening, the Streets, Lanes, Squares, Yards, Courts, Alleys,

'Passages, and Places, and preventing and removing Obstrudions and Annoyances within the same: And that the Lord Mayor of London, Sir Robert Ladbroke, Mr. Alderman Harley, Mr. Alderman Trecothick, and Mr. Alderman Oliver, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, gives His Consent, as far as His Majesty’s Interest is concerned, that the House may do therein as they shall think fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That, by Indenture, bearing Date the 24th oi October 1741, and Fines and Recoveries duly levied and suffered in pursuance thereof, several Manors, Lands, and Hereditaments, in the Counties of Leicester, Derby, Nottingham, and Stafford, the ancient Inheritance of the Petitioner’s Family, were settled and assured to several Uses, whereby the Petitioner (subject to the Payment of several Sums of Money, and to a Rent Charge in Nature of a Jointure to the honourable Atut Widow, the Petitioner’s Mother; and to another Rent Charge also in Nature of a Jointure to the Right honourable Mary Countess Dowager Ferrers, now Wife of Lord Frederick Campbell) is become entitled, in Possession, to the said Premises for his Life, with several Remainders over; and as to the Reversion in Fee of the said Manors and Hereditaments, in the County of Stafford, the same was limited, by the said Settlement, to Lawrence Shirley, the Petitioner’s Father; and as to a Moiety of the Manors and Hereditaments, in the Counties of -cester, Derby, and Nottingham, the same were limited, after the precedent Limitations, to the Use of the honourable Lady Ann Compton, deceased, for her Life, and, after her Decease, to the Use of her First and other Sons successively, in Tail Mail, Remainder to the honourable Lady Charlotte Compton, deceased, for Life, and, after her Decease, to the Use of her First and other -Sons fuc-celfively, in Tail Male, with Reversion in Fee to the Petitioner’s said Father; Great A Petition of the Inhabitants of Great , in the
