Mr. Barrow reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and others, residing near, or frequently travelling, the Roads therein after mentioned, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had dire died him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.. William Sabine, being examined, laid. He is a Surveyor, and has been used to take Levels and the Elevations of Hills: — That he knoWs the present Turnpike Road from Melksham to Bath; — that the Elevation of Hill is 7 Degrees, and of Hill 6 Degrees,

which Hills being so steep, make the Road very inconvenient: — That a new Road, from Melksham, to go hear Broughton, Wraxhall, and to the Bot-

tom of the Hill near Batbford, would remedy the above Inconveniences, and reduce the utmost Elevation of any Part of the Road to 3 Degrees: — That the Course of it will be upon a Rock, from which Materials may be got: — That it may easily be made, and will be nearer by One Mile than the present Road.

Being aiked, what will be the Length of the Hill in the proposed Road ? he said. One Mile and a Quarter; — dnd being aiked, what is the Length of Bathford Hill ? he said. One Furlong; — That the present Road from Bath to Kingsdown has many small Hills in it; and that Kingsdown Hill is steep for the Space of Two FurlongsBeing aiked, whether Bathford Hill can be reduced to 3 Degrees by winding up it ? he said, It cannot, because the Road cannot wind up it without sinking: — And being aiked, whether Kingsdown Hill can be reduced ? he laid, it may be made easier, but hot so ealy as the proposed Road; and that the Hill would be a Mile in Length -. — Being aiked, How much longer the Hill would be, if reduced to Degrees of Elevation-? he said. Not much, because the Road mull turn short at the Top of the Hill.

Being further examined, he said. The Road from Bathford to Bath follows the Course of the River Avon, and enters Bath through Walcot Street, which is very narrow; in feme Places not above Ten Feet wide; particularly opposite Walcot Church, where Two Carriages cannot pass each other: — That the Breadth necessary for 3 Carriages to go a-breast, is 30 Feet: — That this Inconvenience would be obviated by making a Road from Bathford to Bathwick, and from thence to the Bridge now building over the Avon at Bath, which will be Half a Mile nearer: That there will not- be any Ascent in it, and the Entrance to the interior Parts of Bath from it will be very convenient.

That there are many Hills in the Road from Bath to Bradford, which might be avoided, if a new Road was made from Bradford to Farlywick, there to join the new-intended Road between Melksham and; the

Whole of which new Road would be level, and nearer than the present Road by i of a Mile.

Being aiked. How far it is from Bradford to wick ?he said, Two Miles and 6 Furlongs.

And being further examined, he said. The Road from Froom and other Places, to Bath, by Entry Hill and Holloway, is in many Places very steep and narrow: — that the Elevation of Entry JHill is Nine Degrees — of Holloway, Six Degrees: — That those Hills may be avoided, by making a new Road by Odd Down, near the Old Glass House, to Barracks, and from the Red *9

Lyon in Wells Road to Barracks, and from thence to Lyncome and the said new Bridge: — That it will be about Half a Mile round, and mud cut through some Gardens and Orchards, to the Owners of which he does not know that any Application has been made: That in the above proposed Road, the Rile will not be above Three or Four Degrees.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to make a Road from Melksham, by or near Broughton, Wraxhall, and Farlywick, in the County of Wilts, to the Bottom of the Hill near Bathford, in the County of SometJet, over the River Avonto Bathwick, and from thence to the Bridge how building near the Old Ferry, opposite the City of Bath; and also a Road from Bradford, to join the abovementioned Road, near Farlywick and also a Road from the Turnpike Road oa

Lord George Cavendish reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, Land Owners, Merchants, Traders, Manufacturers, and others, residing in and near the several Market Towns of terfield, Worksop, and Retford, in the several Counties of Derby, York, and Nottingham, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; And had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Brindley, an Engineer, being examined, said. That he has surveyed the Country through which the intended Canal, from Chesterfield, to join the River Trent, at Stockzvith, is to pass; that it is practicable, and will be a general Benefit to the Country, and of public Utility; and that so far from being an Injury to Individuals, he. apprehends it will be as great a Benefit as any Navigation the Witness was ever concerned in; and that there will will be Water sufficient: And,

Mr. Bn ight, also an Engineer, being examined, as to the Expence of making the said Canal, said. He apprehended, it would amount to £. 97,000 or thereabouts, and that the Traffick thereon will very amply answer the Expence.

Mr. Anthony Lax, being examined, said, that £.55,000 and upwards, hath been already subscribed, and that there is not the least Doubt but a Sufficiency will be subscribed in due Time; that it is not a nominal Subscription, but a real one, and that the Subscribers have paid Two Calls already: And being asked, as to the Commodities likely to be carried on the Canal, he mentioned Coal, Lime, Lead, Timber, Corn, and all other Sorts of Goods and Merchandize, and particularly Lime for Manure, which is now carried at a great Expence by Land Carriage, and therefore not near the Quantity used that will be when it can be conveyed by Water.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making a Navigable Cut, or Canal, from Chesterfield, in the County of Derby, through or near Worksop and Retford, to join the River Trent, at or near in the County of Nottingham: And that Lord George dish, Mr. Clarke, Sir Cecil IVray, and Mr. Offley, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

and that, by virtue, and under the Powers and Authorities of the said Act and Agreement, the said Samuel Cox did purchase divers Estates, within the Limits described by the said Act; and built, or caused to be built, many substantial Dwelling Houses on the Ground fopurchased, and on Ground held of the said Dean and Chapter for very short Terms of Years; and hath borrowed divers large Sums of Money, on the Security of the said Estates, Houses, and Ground; but, by reason of the Scarcity of Money, and other unforeseen Causes, the said Samuel Cox was not able, within the Term of Five Years limited by the said Act, nor hath hitherto been able, to finish all the Houses so built, nor to make all the Purchases requisite for carrying the Purposes of the said Act into Execution; and therefore hath not, nor could obtain, from the said Dean and Chapter, any Leases, or make any Exchanges with them; and that divers Builders are now willing to finish the Houses already built, and to proceed in completing the said Square and Streets, or the greatest Part thereof, pursuant to the Intentions of the said Act, provided the Powers given by such Act, for making proper Purchases, and for granting Leases for Ninety-nine Years, and the other Powers in the said Act mentioned, are revived, and veiled in proper Persons, to be named for that Purpose; and without which, the Petitioners and the said other Mortgagees are likely to be very considerable Sufferers: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for granting to such Person or Persons as the House shall think fit to

sfppoint, and also to the said Dean and Chapter, and to all other Bodies Corporate or Collegiate, such further Time, for making such other Purchases, granting such Leases, and making such Exchanges, and for carrying the Scheme or Intention and Purposes of the said Act into Execution, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Charles Whitworth, Mr.

Mr. James Morrell, an Attorney at Oxford, and Steward to several of the Colleges there, laid, That the contingent Tenure of the College Estates is productive of many Inconveniences: — That it would be a very great Advantage to all Bodies Corporate within the said Uni-yerlity and City, if they were im powered to alienate their Estates, as it would encourage Persons to rebuild or repair their Houses.

A Copy of which Letter is as follows viz.

SIR,

From the House of Commons, 5th February 1771.

By the Command of the House of Commons, 1 wrote to you on the 22d of last Month, acquainting you, that immediately upon the Receipt thereof, you was to.sum-ruon the Representatives of your County, and Boroughs within the same, to attend their Service in Parliament, on Tuesday the 5th of this Instant February, and to fend me an Account of the Receipt of my Letter, and your Proceedings thereon: But having received no Answer from you, the House has commanded me to write to you again. I am, therefore, in obedience to the Order of the House, to require you to fend me such Account; and I hope you will be able to give some Reason for this seeming Neglect.

I am,

Sir,

Your, humble Servant,

And the Witness further said, That if the Owners or Lessees of Collieries, or Coal Works, adjacent to the said Roads, from whence through these Roads, the Country and neighbouring Towns are supplied, were obliged to give Tickets, denoting the Quantity of Coal, to the Carters, to whom the same shall be delivered* and the Carters to deliver such Tickets to the Buyers thereof, many Frauds and Abuses, now practised, would be prevented.

And the Agent for the Petition of the several Commissioners of the Navigation of the Rivers Thames and Isis, having informed your Committee, That the Petitioners desired Leave to waive so much of their Petition, as relates to the laying an additional Duty of One Penny per Chaldron on Coals, your Committee proceeded to inquire into the other Matters contained in the said Petition: And called

Mr. Robert Bunker, a Bargeman, who being examined, said. That he knows the River Thames from London to Reading-, that in feme Places there is always want of Water, and in dry Seasons impafiable — That feme of the Locks are blown up, and others so constructed, that Vessels are obliged to be drawn up with a Cable — That the Witness has gone from Quto Reading, in Three

Days, and has femetimes been a Fortnight or Three Weeks for Want of Water, and that he has lain a Month at Sunbury, for Want of Water to carry him up — That if there were Twenty Locks upon the River, it would render it navigable for Barges to go at all Times. — That a Barge of 150 Ton, which will take 50 or 55 Men to navigate, may be done by 12 or 13 Horses, and that the Witness has lccn 65 Men in a Line.

The Reverend Mr. John Spicer, being examined, said. That he is One of the Commissioners of the Navigation of the Thames and Isis, and has-attended for Twelve

Years

ii Geo. III. li ° Febructrii* 151

Years past — That several Complaints have been made of the present State of the Navigation, and of the extravagant Demands of Bargemasters for Carriage of Goods, which has been a growing Evil for Forty Years, which, he said, was owing to the enormous Size of the Barges, the extravagant Wages given to the Bargemasters Servants, the great Advance of the Price of Hirelings (or Persons who hale the Barges) and of the Tonnage on Locks (which within these Forty Years has increased near double) and the Combinations of the Reading Bargemasters; and that the Locks and Gulls in the River being very difficult to pass, renders it dangerous for Barges passing, by reason of the great Fall, which Fall increases in proportion to the Height of the Weir; but the Witness apprehends, the Occasion of the principal Obstructions to the Navigation of Barges upwards, is from the Locks and Gulls; for that he computes upon an Average, that Three Hours are taken up in dragging a Barge through each of the Eight Locks, between Reading and Monkey; but

that if Turnpike Pounds wereere&ed, and short Canals cut for the Barges to pals by the Side of the Lock or Gull, they might pal's by the Eight Turnpikes in I’wo Hours, which would be a Saving of Twenty-two Hours in the Twenty-four — That by the present Mode of Navigation, every Barge is obliged to wait at the lower End of the Gull, till the Lock is opened, and a sufficient Quantity of Water let down to carry the Barge up to the Lock; that the Witness has seen the largest Barges to the Westward of , waiting a

Day, sometimes Two Days, for Water to carry them up, and when a Flalh of Water comes, the Whole of it is wasted, the Bed of the River above, drained, and no Water left for the Miller to work with; but that if Turnpikes were used, no more Water would be wasted than the Turnpike Pound holds, and in this Instance, the Miller would be remarkably benefitted b^ the proposed Plan. — That he is persuaded, if the Barges were reduced to One hundred Tons, , and Horse Towing Paths made use of, the Freight of Goods from London to Reading would be much the same as it was Forty Years ago, and would save Two or Three Miles in an Hour.

Mr. William Grover, being examined, was asked, What the Expence was of navigating a Barge from Windforto Hedfor Wharf? He said, that a Barge of Two hundred Tons with Men and Horses would cost Twelve Pounds; but if it was to be performed all by Horses, it would not be more than 4. 6 j. or 4. 1 os.; that upon an Average the Year round, there is about Seventy Men to tow a Barge, which might be done by Nine or Ten Horses, which would be a Saving of 13J. in the Thirty Miles; and that if the River was to be put into proper Order, and Pounds used instead of Locks, the Navigation of the River would be more safe and constant.

Mr. Joseph Nico/s, an Engineer, being examined, informed your Committee, That the present Mode of navigating the Thames was by drawing Flashes from Letchlade and higher, by which Means the River becomes nearly exhausted in every Reach, which frequently prevents the navigating up or down in the Summer Sealon for many Days together between Letchlade and London; which, the Witness said, might be remedied by the Addition of Pound Locks from Letchlade to Boulter's Lock, which would render the River navigable at all Times, (extreme Floods and Frosts excepted, and in those Two States much longer navigable than now) by short Cuts below and above Boulters Lock, and fomo Erections and Horse Towing Paths, the Navigation would be rendered both certain, and much more constant, than now, and at half the Expence.

Mr. Thomas Newell, being examined, confirmed (the Evidence of the foregoing Witaefles, with respect to the Utility of Pound Locks; and added. That there are frequent Stoppages of Barges, by reason of Shoals and Vox.. 33.

other Impediments, which might be removed, and the Navigation otherwisej improved, at the Expence, in his Opinion, of 40 or £. 50,000.

The Counsel for the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, offering to go into an Examination, to shew, that a Canal Navigation might be made from Reading to Monkey Island, which would be preferable to the River in its proposed improved State, were restrained from proceeding thereupon by your Committee, who thought that Enquiry more proper for the Committee, to whom the Petition for the said Canal is referred.

The Counsel for the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, afterwards infilling upon being heard in Regard to the Right of the City of London, to the Conlervancy of the River Thames, and your Committee being informed by several Members present, that their Rights would be preserved in the proposed Bill, thought it unnecessary to hear them any further.

Resolved, That Hugh Roberts, the late Returning Officer for the Borough of New Shoreham, in the County of Sussex, having, at the last Election for the said Borough; received upon the Poll 87 Persons who voted for Mr.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for the Communication which His Majesty has been graciously pleated to make, of the Declaration signed and delivered by the Prince of on the

Part of his Catholic Majesty, the 22d of January last, and of His Majesty’s Acceptance thereof.

To testify to His Majesty our sincere Satisfaction, at finding that the King of Spain has, in Compliance with His Majesty’s just Demand, disavowed the violent En-terprize against Port Egmont, in Falkland's Island, and.

engaged to give immediate Orders for restoring all Things to the Situation in which they stood before the Time of the said Enterprize.

To express our Hope, that the Spirit of Moderation, as well as the Firmness, which His Majesty has manifested in His Conduct upon this Occasion, will, by inclining the other Powers of Europe to concur with His Majesty in His Views of preserving the general Tranquillity, prove the Means of securing to His Majesty and His People the permanent Enjoyment of honourable Peace.

And to assure His Majesty, that, in every Situation, His faithful Commons will steadily persevere in giving His Majesty their most affcftionate and zealous -Support.

Election*1" Hugh Roberts was, according to Order, brought to the Bar; where he, upon his Knees, received a Reprimand from Mr. Speaker; and was ordered to be discharged out of Custody, paying his Fees.

The Reprimand was as followeth;

Hugh Roberts,

You have been convicted, upon the cleared and most satisfactory Proof, of returning a Member so this House, against a very great Majority of Votes admitted by yourself, and which now stand upon the PoU.

This Offence, considered in the Abstract, and without the accompanying Circumstances, is a Crime of an atrocious Nature; it strikes at the very Being of this House: for, if Practices of this Sort were to obtain, the Commons of Great Britain, who are now the Represen-tatives of the Free People of this Kingdom, would be merely the Delegates of corrupt Returning Officers.

In vain have our Ancestors been anxiously careful to secure the Freedom of Elections, by all the Means Human Wisdom and Forefight could fugged; in vain have they particularly guarded against the Partiality of , the Returning Officer, and obliged him, by every Tie, to a faithful Discharge of that Trust, which the Constitution hath repoled in his Hands, if Men are to be

found daring enough to fend Members to this House, who were never chosen by the legal Electors.

You have said, that you did not receive tire Votes absolutely, but only admitted them to poll conditionally, and subject to future Rcvision, as appears by the Queries set against their Names.

I think this Circumstance alone, was it true, would not much avail you; for I have always been of Opinion (although 1 do not know that the Resolutions of the House have gone so far) that the Practice of receiving Votes with Queries by the mere Authority of the Returning Officer, and without the Consent of the Parties, is illegal; I am sure it is dangerous; for, if once it be admitted by this House, that the Returning Officer has a Right to receive Votes upon Terms which are to subject them to his future Decision, after the Poll is doled, and the Numbers known, it will always be in the Power of that Officer, so to manage the queried Votes, as to return which of the Candidates he pleases; and; if he is either an artful Man himself, or artfully assisted by others, he will also be able so to do the Business, as to make it difficult to set afide what he hath done, and more difficult to punish him for doing it.

But your same does not afford you even this Exj cufe; for it has been proved, that, although you reserved the queried Votes for future Discussion and Rc-consideration, you made your Return without either, as soon as the Poll was over; rejecting, as you declared, all those who had voted for One of the Candidates (which amounted to a great Majority of the Whole) on account, as you alledged, of Corruption; notwithstanding you had administered the Oath against Bribery to all, except One, of those you thought proper to reject.

There are, however, Circumstances in your same which greatly extenuate your Offence, and which the House hath, with Pleasure, laid hold of, to mitigate the Severity of your Punishment; and this they have done at the Recomendation of those very respectable Gentlemen who composed that Committee, which, by its Conduct upon this Occasion, hath merited, not only the Thanks of this House, but the general Applause of the Public. — By a steady Attention to Justice, and a firm Perseverance in obtaining it, they have surmounted a Variety of Difficulties, in carrying into Execution a new Law, which has founded a new Court of Judicature, for the Trial of Parliamentary Elections; a Law which, if it continues to be executed for the future, with equal Abilities and Integrity, as it has been in this Instance, will be a Blessing to this Country, and do Honour to the Memory of the Person who planned, and to the Parliament which adopted and passed it.

You have proved, that you were formerly a Member of a Club, in the Borough over which you presided, which hath profanely assumed the Name of The Christian Club-, a Club, instituted for the most infamous Purpose, that of felling the Borough to the highest Bidder; that this Club consists of a great Majority of the Electors; and that the Members of it bind themselves, to one another, and to Secrecy, by Oaths, in Writing, and Bonds with large Penalties; that they carry on this scandalous Traffick by a select Committee, who never appear or vote at any Election, on account of their Scruples of Confidence, having actually received the stipulated Price of the Borough; but that the rest of the Members of this Club vote as they are directed by their Committee, and, without Hesitation, take the Oath against Bribery (as they did in the present Instance) and, when the Election is over, receive their Share of the Price which has been paid to their Factors.

You proved likewise, that you voluntarily quitted this Club, in February last, when there was no Vacancy, and when you could have no Expectation of being the

Returning

ii Geo. III. i4° — 18'

Returning Officer, in case a Vacancy should happen It has likewise appeared in Evidence that you acted by the Advice of Counsel.

And you have insisted, that though you may have acted illegally, you have not acted intentionally wrong; and that you should not have rejected the queried Votes, if you had not been convinced in your Conscience that they were all corrupted.

These are the favourable Circumstances under which the House have considered your Cafe; and, on Account of them, have inflicted upon you the mildefl Punish-nient that the Nature of their Proceedings will permit.

And I am, in Obedience to their Commands, to REPRIMAND you for this Offence; which I now do: And I am, by their Order, to acquaint you, which I also do, that you are discharged, paying your Fees.

An ESTIMATE of the Expence of Maintaining of the Children, received into the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of exposed and deserted Young Children On or before the 25th Day of March 1760, from the 31st Day of Decemberi770,excluGve, to the 31st Day of December 1771, inclusive.

The Number of the said Children living, under the Care of the Governors and Guardians of the said Hospital, on the 31st Day of December 1770, was Three hundred and Ninety-six - -

The Expence of maintaining whom, at the usual Calculation of Seven Pounds Ten Shillings each, amounts to Two tlmifand Nine hutidred and Seventy Pounds only; which is no more than the Expence of Cloathing them at One Pound each, and Two Shillings and Six-pence a Week for Nursing: but a greater Expence mull accrue this Year, by reason of those Children who are diseased and infirm, and consequently cannot be placed out Apprentice,

Beside the above 396 Children, there have been taken into this Hospital since the 25th of March 1760, 338 Children, most: of whom were under the moll distressed Circumstances, or Orphans of Soldiers and Sailors, whereof 34 have beeen Apprenticed, 9 claimed, and x 16 dead, so that there are 199 Children now alive, which are wholly maintained and provided for out of the Income arising from private Donations, and are not, or ever have been, estimated to Parliament.

Signed by Order of the Committee,

396

Tho' Collingwood, Secretary.

Mr. Robert Whitworth, Surveyor, being examined, said, That he had surveyed the Lands, and drawn a Plan, which he produced, for a Navigable Canal from Reading to Monkey Island; that he has been employed in Works of this Nature, and has been employed in most of the Navigable Cuts in this Country: That the proposed Cut will be as little injurious to Land Owners as any he has ever been employed in; and if carried into Execution, the Navigation thereof will be greatly preferable to, and more expeditious than, any Navigation which can be made through the old Course of the River Thames: That a Barge of 120 Tons, by the Canal, may go from Reading to Monkey Island in about 6 Hours, the Expence of which, at One Halfpenny a Ton per Mile, would be about £. 4. 7 s. — That he had not measured the Length, but has taken the Falls of the River, from Reading to Monkey IJian, which is 49 Feet 1 i Inches from the highest Head that can be penned; and the Fall from the Mouth of the River Kenneth to Monkey Island, is 48 Feet, and there are 9 Locks, including the Rennet Lock; and believes they were erected for the Use of the Mills only, there being no Lock between Monkey Island and Isleworth; and he knows no Realbn why the Navigation from Reading to Monkey , might not be as good without Locks, as that from Monkey Island to Isleworth, the Fall being no greater in proportion to the Length; the Fall from Monkey Island to Isleworth being 62 Feet and an Half.

Being asked his Opinion, as to the Practicability of making'a convenient and permanent Navigation by the

Course of the RiveV; he said. It is impossible to make it permanent, except it is constant: He gave an Instance in the present Winter, when it was stopt, first by Floods for about Two Months, and then by a Frost for near Three Weeks; and added, that these are Obstructions above the Power of Art to remove: That the Navigation on the Canal may be as liable to Obstructions by Frosts as the Course of the River, but not more so, as Locks are in the first Instance ‘affected by Frosts in all Navigations, but that Floods cannot obstruct the Navigation of the Canal, since it will be made altogether out of the Reach of them.

Being cross-examined, he said, He surveyed the Land ' through which the Canal is to pass, in pursuance of an Order made at a Meeting at Reading in January last; that he is not concerned in the Execution of it, bpt only as a Surveyor: That the Canal may be a permanent Navigation, except stopt by Frosts, to which both the River and that are equally liable; but the Rapidity of the Stream has some Effect in preventing freezing: That there is a Stream in every Part of the River between Reading and Monkey Island, but it has been froze lately; and that the River, in its present State, may not be so liable to be stopt by Frosts as the Canal, but if Locks are to be built upon it, it will; and that he never kneto the Obstructions by Frosts at Locks removed, except in flight Frosts, but never in a Frost strong enough to freeze the Canal: That he is sure the Canal may be so executed, as by carrying its Level above the Floods, that they cannot aftedl it; and knows one so constructed at Birmingham, and several others.

That the Expence of making the Canal will be about £.51,000, but that Calculations of this Kind have, in many former Instances, turned out fallacious; but he has had more Experience since, and can speak with greater Certainty: — Being asked. If he ever knew or heard of a Canal being executed at the estimated Price ? he said, That he does not know of any completed at present, but he can form an Estimate from what is already done: That Mr. Brindley is concerned in the Trent Canal, the Estimate for which was £. 131,000, and that last Year there was about £. 86,000 expended; and that it hath been Years and a Half in Hand; and he thinks it will greatly exceed the Estimate.

That there will be Flood Gates at the Head of the Canal, if necessary, which, with a regulating Lock, will cost about £. 300: That he cannot say how many Culverts (which he explained to be Brick Arches, to convey the Water under the Canal) will be necessary; that there will not be above Four or Five that will amount to £. 100 a-piece; that some will cost £90, and so down to£ 10; and that there will be One which will cost£. 60; but that he cannot exactly tell how many small ones will be wanted, but thinks about 40 in the Whole; that he cannot speak positively to the Number, but is sure the Expence of them will not exceed £.650: That he knows the principal ones, which would be wanted, but not the small ones, and is pretty sure they won’t exceed that Sum, but cannot say how many Springs they should have to cut away till they cut the Ground, but is sure there won’t be many, and believes there will be none that will require a large Culvert, for the smallest- Culvert will be sufficient for any Spring he ever saw in cutting a Canal: — That the Breadth of the Canal on the Surface will be about 45 Feet, at the Bottom 53 Feet, and the Depth Feet and a Half; and the Land to be paid for will be about 192 Acres, including Towing Paths and Banks; but that some of it will be returned again: — That he' was not himself a competent Judge of die Price of Land there, but had estimated 145 Acres, at £.35 an Acre1; and 47 Acres, which was Waste Ground, at £.10 per Acre; and that he made his Estimate from the Information of Farmers and others, who informed hittt of the Value of Land inthofe Parts: — ‘-That the Fall from the high Ground in Bray Field to Monkey Island; was 1*7

Being asked the Consequence of the Canal’s breaking, he said, It could not possibly break but in Time of Floods, and then it would overflow nothing more than which is at present flooded; that it could not affect the Town of Bray, as the Water would go off as freely by Means of the Four Culverts as it did at present, and would very little delay the clearing the Country of Floods.

Being asked, How the Water can go off so well in the Space of 40 Feet as in Half a Mile ? he said, Not quite so readily, but if the Water stands on a Level on both Sides the Canal, it can have no Effect in drowning the Country; for by Means of the Four Culverts, it will prevent the Water riling many Inches higher, on the higher Side, than on the lower, and the Flood can have no Effect above the Excess of the perpendicular Height on the one Side more than the other: — That the blowing up of Canals must be from the Insufficiency of the Banks, and the Pressure of Water in the Canal, but there never can be a greater Pressure of Water on the Outside than on the Inside, since the Water within will be higher, nod that it nevei can overflow: — That no more Ground will be wanted on the Side of the Canal than for the Culverts, and the Water will be taken from the River

Kennet, which will fall into the Thames again at Monkey Island, and will not take the 12th Part of an Inch Depth from the Thames between the Mouth of the Kennel and Monkey Island: — That it may be prejudicial tq Mills on the River if they are short of Water, but does not know whether they ever are or not; next Sluice or Lock above; and thinks there is to be One Reach of several Miles long, which begins at Reading; and if the Contents of that Reach should make its Way down, the Consequence would be very dreadful, and, if in Summer, to the neighbouring Fields, whereon great Quantities of Corn grow: — Being asked, Whether the Consequence would not be worse, if a Failure was to happen to a Canal of Sixty Feet wide, than to one of Thirty ? he said, If the Lengths and Depths in both Cales were alike, the Quantity from that of Sixty would be Twice as much as that of Thirty, and the Risque would be in the same Proportion.

Being asked, Whether the Danger attending the Works of a Canal of Sixty Feet wide, is not greater than one of Thirty, supposing the greater Canal to be deeper also than the lesser ? he said, That where the Locks are the same Width, the Pressure is the same against them, whether the Canal is wider or narrower; and is only increased in a certain Ratio in proportion to the Depths.

That if the Canal was to go by White Waltham and Old Haywood, Bray would be affected as he has mentioned; but that he now understands that Course is given up: That if the Canal was to go from Old Haywood Two Miles and Six Furlongs towards Monkey and it should break, he thinks it would affect Bray.

Being asked (as he understood the Course of the Canal by Old Haywood was given up) Whether his Evidence relating to that Reach, and the Notion of its breaking at all, applied to affect that Course for the Canal, which the Committee had agreed to adopt ? he said. In the same Degree, and meant that it would affect, supposing the Clnal was to go by Old,

the Length of the Reaches considered: — And being asked. Whether the Reach he mentioned exists or not, and whether his Evidence does not relate to a Reach which does not affect the Course which the Canal is intended to go ? he answered, That neither of them exist; if either did, it would have the same Effect on Bray-, and thinks there is a Reach of Two Miles in the Course of the-intended Canal.

That in a Canal, calculated for Barges of 200 Tons, it would be necessary for the Locks to be wider than for Barges of Thirty Tons.

Being asked. If a Wear, or Towing Bridge, be made across the Thames at Monkey Island, it will not dam back the Water upon the Lands, and affect Bray he said, A Towing Bridge would bring an Inconvenience upon the Trade of the River; and if a Wier was erected, Without a Means of Barges passing, it would operate to the flooding Bray much more than at present.

That whether artificial Canals are liable to ouze, depends entirely on the Strata of Matter they pass through, and the Treatment they receive in the making the m: That many do ouze, and when they do, they affect the Lands adjacent, by making them swampy and rulhy, and renders them of less Value.

Being cross-examined, he was asked, How many Locks would lie erected in the Fall of Seventeen or Eighteen Feet from the Top of the Water in the Canal above that of Bray Meadow ? he said, He did not know; but whether more or leis, the upper Gates, which (hut the Water into the Reach of the Canal, or any Part of the Reach, will be just as liable to Breaches; — and he having laid, that the Level of the Water in the Canal would be Twelve Feet above the Soil in Bray Field, was asked. How he formed his Judgment of the Height of Water above Bray Field, when he did not know the Number of Locks? he said, That the Fall from Holyport Field to Bray Field, being from Seventeen- to Eighteen Feet, and whether there are Seventeen or Eighteen Locks, or but One to defeend through that Space, the Height of Water is the same in both Places $ and the Efledt of a Breach from Holyport Field will operate the fame; and if a Breach in the upper Part, it rulhes over all the lower Locks; but in case of a Breach, there is not more Water let out than between Lock and Lock.

Voi.. 33.

Being asked, Whether any ill Consequence could happen to Bray from a Breach in the First Reach from Reading ? he laid, That confining himself to the Course of the intended Canal, there is a Length of Eleven Miles Seven Furlongs, to which is annexed the Word " Le* " vel" on the Plan; from whence he inferred there would be a Reach of Two Miles; and if the Lock, at the lower End of that Reach should fail, the Consequence must be that the whole Contents, measuring down to the Sill of the upper Gates, must be discharged into the next lower Reach; and the Risque of the adjacent Country on either Side will be more or less, in proportion to the next lower Work's Abilities to sustain that Quantity flowing from a superior Height j if the Banks should fuf* tain it, it carries forward the Risque even down to Bray.

Being asked, Whether he had never heard of Stops being put in long Reaches to prevent these Accidents ? he said, He had; but if a Breach was to happen in a Frost, they may be prevented performing their intended Operation, as it often happens at other Times; and that he has known Floods in Time of Frosts.

That the Stream of the Thames may be so confined as to keep its Channel, though at an extravagant Expence, and if done, there is lcarce a possible Means of preventing Bray from being flooded by the Floods com-' ing down Holyport Brook: — That it was possible to make Culverts under the Canal of 100 or 200 Feet broad, but the Effect of that Width must be in proportion to the Depth of the Canal across the Meadow; but if the Water by Works of Art, could be prevented from overflowing the Town of Bray, it would affect some other Part of the Country, in full as high a Degree as Bray would be relieved.

That be made the Survey and Plan for the amending the River Thames, but is to be no otherwise concerned in carrying the Works into* Execution, than as an Engineer.

To prove the Allegations of the Petition of several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Owners and Occupiers of Mills, Locks, Wharfs, and Warehouses, in the Counties of , Bucks, and Oxford;

Mr. Joseph Nicka/ls, Engineer, being examined, said, That he knows the Locks, Weirs, and Mills to each Lock, on the Thames between the River Kennett and Maidenhead Bridge; and that it is necessary they should be maintained as high and strong as they are at present, for the Purpose of Navigation only: — That there are Eight Locks, and each Lock, and other Works belonging thereto, produces annually, on an Average, ,£. 160, or upwards, for the Service of the Navigation; and that the Navigation is necessary for the Support of those Locks, the Trade of the Mills being greatly inadequate; and that if the Canal from Reading to Monkey island should take place, and a considerable Part of the Trade which now passes the Locks should go thereon, the remaining Part of the Trade would not be sufficient to maintain those Works, paying the same per Ton for Lockage as is now paid for the Mode of tupplying Water; for the Service of the Navigation has so worn the Bed of the River below each respective Work, as to bring on a much greater Expence than would have happened, had those Works been entirely for the Service of the Mills, and that he thinks, as a Means of continuing the Trade of the Navigation and those Mills, it is necessary the Locks should continue to produce the like Income they now do, from the great Expence the Proprietors must be at.

That he attended at several Meetings held at Reading, concerning a Canal to be made from Sunning to Monkey Island, on Behalf of the Lock Owners, to require Satisfaction for the Loss they might sustain; and received for Answer several Times, that ample Satisfaction should be made, if such Canal should take place; but was afterwards told by Mr. Page, who was one of that Meeting, that it was a Doubt in the Minds of the

3 p Well-

2i° Februarii. A. 1771.

Well-wishers to the Canal; whether the Lock Owners had any legal Right to expert Satisfaction: — That he Was at a subsequent Public Meeting, and it was then agreed to make such Satisfaction; but that he was doubtful afterwards, from his Information, whether they would or not; bat that this was mere private Conversion, and that it was proposed at this Public Meeting, that the Lock Owners thou Id be wrote to, to give an Account of the Damages they would sustain, if the Canal took place.

Being asked his Opinion, Whether they are to receive Satisfaction or not ? he said. From what had been told him, it was not meant to make Satisfaction; and thinks it will not be in their Power (from the great Expence the Canal will (land loaded with, if such Satisfaction should be made, and a Means provided for the Continuation of the Trade below Maidenhead down to London on the Old River) to pay for it, confident with the Service of the Public, and the Reduction of the Price of Carriage, such as may be made by the Amendment of the Old divert That as to his Opinion, what Damages the Lock Owners would fudain, he said, from what he had lien published, it appeared to him, that the Proposers of the Canal propose to carry from, and bring to, London, upon the Canal only; and if that should be the Cafe, the LoGk Owners will receive a Damage of near Half their present Income.

Being asked. Whether he had estimated the Profits of the Canal, and its Expences, in order to form his Judgment, whether they could make Satisfaction ? he laid. From his‘Knowledge of Trade he had; and that the Expence of such Satisfaction, and the Amendment of the Old River, mud be from 30 to £. 40,000; and their Edimate for making the Canal, is near £. 50,000; and, from the Quantity of Goods which will be carried thereon, he thinks it will not be sufficient.

That in the Amendment of the Old River, there are several Canals to be made on the Sides thereof, and One of near Three Miles long; and none of the present Locks will be passed through, but will take nearly the same Expence to keep them in Repair, as they mud be kept to the same Height; and that the present Lock Owners will receive the like Income as at present, should the proposed Amendment take place; and that to the Town of Abingdon, a Barge will be capable to pass from Day's Lock thither in Four Hours, which now takes up on an Average, Two or Three Days: That the Toils for passing on such Canals, are to be paid by the Bargemaders, and there will be great Savings by using Horse Towing Paths.

Oxford A Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy,- and Free-Milcways. holders, of the County of Oxford, and Parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have perused a Bill, depending in the House, for tTTe more effectually amending several of the' Mileways leading to the University and City of Oxford-, for making a more commodious Entrance into the said University and City, through the Parish of BridgeJ'et, commonly called Clement; for widening, repairing, or rebuilding, ;for making

a safe and commodious Road from the said Bridge, through the said University and City, to join the great Roads leading to several Places therein mentioned; for cleansing and lighting the Streets, Lanes, and Places, within the said University and City, and the Suburbs thereof, and the Parish of Saint Clement; for removing Nuisancesand Annoyances therefrom; for holding and regulating a Market within the said City, and for other Purposes; and that a Toll is intended to be laid on all Cattle and Carriages patting through the said Mile-ways, to be applied, not only for repairing the several Mileways not included in any Turnpike Act, but to Purposes so various and extensive, as to leave the Petitioners little Reason to hope that they can be executed at an Expence that will not be too burthensome to the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners apprehend the Laws in being are sufficient for the effectual Reparation of the said Mileways and Bridge; and that the laying a Toll upon Travellers, for the paving of Streets, the embellishing or ornamenting any Town, or removing Annoyances therein, is contrary to the Tenor of all the Laws for repairing of Highways, repugnant to Justice, appropriates, as it were, a Tax upon Land, for the local Improvement of a rich and opulent Town and University; and, if adopted by the House, may become an intolerable Grievance: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Coun-Hel, against such Parts of the Bill as may affect them, Vol. 33.

or that they may have stich Relief as to the Hotife shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Rill for the more effectual amending such of the Roads as belong to, and are Part of, the Mileways leading to the University and City of Oxford, and which are not made a Part of any Turnpike Road J for the making a commodious Entrance into the said University and City, through the Parish of Bridgefet, commonly called Saint Clement; for the widening, repairing, or rebuilding, the Bridge called Magdalen Bridge; for making a safe and commodious Road from the said Bridge, through the University and City aforesaid, to join the great Roads leading to Worcester, GloucesterBirmingham, Banbury, Abingdon, Newbury, Southampton, and other Places; for cleansing and lighting the Streets, Lanes, and Places, within the said University and City, and the Suburbs thereof, and the said Parish of Saint Clement-, for removing Nuisances and' Annoyances therefrom, and preventing the like for the future; for holding and regulating a Market within the said City; for impowering Colleges and Corporations to alienate their Estates there; and for other Purposes, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Mr. Vane reported from the Committee, to whom-the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Town of Berwick upon Tweed, and of the several other Persons, whose Hands and Names are thereunto set and subscribed. Owners and Proprietors of Fisheries in the River of Tweed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House j and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the feme was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Anthony Lambert, being examined, feid. That many unwarrantable Practices and Abuses have of late Years been committed in the River of Tweed, and the Rivers and Streams which run into the feme, by taking and killing Salmon Gilfes, Salmon Trouts, and Whit-lings, at unseasonable Times, and by destroying the Spawn, Fry, and young Brood, in the said Rivers and Streams, both in England and Scotland, and Liberties of Berwick upon Tweed: — That he has seen many Hundreds "of Salmon killed out of Season, and great De-struction made amongst the young Fry, which is a great Detriment to the Owners and Occupiers of Fisheries, to the Cities of London and W, and to the Public in general.

That if these Practices were restrained and prevented, Fish would come cheaper and more plenty to Market than at present: — That there is no Power at present in any Person sufficient to restrain and put a Stop to thele illegal Practices by the Laws now in Force, or by the Powers and Authorities vested in the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Town of Berwick upon Tweed, as Conservators of so much of the said River, as. lies in the Counties of Durham and Northumberland, and Berwick, or within the Bounds and Limits thereof; and that if feme Stop be not put to such illegal Proceedings, this valuable Fishery will continue to decrease, to the great Prejudice of the Public.

Mr. Thomas Strangeways confirmed Mr. Lambert's Evidence; and added. He had known most of the Rivers and Streams described in the Petition many Years, and that the Tenants of the upper Part of the River kill many Salmon out of Season, and also destroy the young Fry and Spawn; and that the Public sustain a great Lois by those illegal Practices.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for regulating and improving the Fisheries, in the River of Tweed, and the Rivers and Streams running into the fame: And that Mr. Vane and Sir Thomas do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Wilbraham Bootle reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Gentlemen, Land Owners, Merchants, Traders, and others, being Inhabitants of the County and City of Chester, whole Names are thereunto subscribed; and also, the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, and Traders, of the City of Dublin, passing and trading betwixt Ireland and England-, and also, the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, of "the City of Chester', in Council assembled; and also, the Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation from the Trent to the Mersey, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the First mentioned Petition (no Evidence being produced in Support of any of the Other Petitions) and had directed him to -report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’is Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the First mentioned Petition, the several Acts for improving the Navigation of the River Dee, were read: And Mr. Thomas Lane, being examined, said. That he is Secretary to the Committee for improving the said Navigation:

That the said Navigation, from the City of to

the Sea, has been completed at an Expence of more than j£.8o-,000; but that for want of an Inland Conveyance by Water, to and from the said City, the Inhabitants thereof, and the interior Part of the Country, cannot fully enjoy the Advantages of the said Navigation:

And that* if the -Canal, prayed for in the Petition, were completed, it would encrease the Quantity of Goods for Exportation on the River Dee.

Mr. Samuel West on, being examined, said. That he is an Engineer: — He produced a Plan of the proposed Canal to your Committee, which he said-Was a true Survey, and that the Levels were properly: laid down therein; and said, that the proposed’Canal was practicable according to the Plan laid down:

A1 reltofi Inclosuie.

Chester to Middlenrich, Sec. Navigation.

II Geo. III. $6° Februarii. aoc

He also produced an Estimate of the Expence, amounting to ft.38,650; and said, that the Canal might be completed for that Sum.

Being cross examined, he laid, He had been an Engineer Three Years.

And being asked, What Experience he had as an Engineer, to enable him to make that Estimate ? lie said. He had been employed by Mr. Brindley as a Staff holder, and in levelling: — That he levelled for the Gen-

tlemen about Two Years ago; and that he has undertaken Twenty-six Miles of Cutting upon the Leeds Canal.

That he has no Experience of the Expence of Locks, nor any thing of that Kind, except making Culverts or Arches, of Three, Four, or Six Feet.

That Twenty-seven Locks and Thirty-seven Bridges will be necessary; and that he never was employed, in making Locks or Bridges.

And that One Tunnel will be necessary; and that he never was employed in that Work.

Being asked, If he had ever been employed in valuing Land? lie said. He had not; but has followed Farming.

He added, That he has made near Four Miles of the Leeds Canal, let it out, and did the Whole.

That One Mill will be destroyed by the Water being taken for the proposed Canal; and that he has not calculated the Expence of destroying that Mill.

That he has never carried any Navigation over a River, which must be done in this Cafe; and that an Aqueduct will be required of One hundred Yards long and Sixty Feet high from the Water, over the River Weaver, and another about Two hundred Yards of Banking, Thirty or Forty Feet high from the Water, over the River Walling.

That One hundred and Twenty Yards of Tunnelling will be necessary, of Eighteen Feet high and Nine wide, which will go under One House in the City of Chester; and that he has no Experience in that Work.

That he made all the Estimate without any Assistance: — That he is acquainted with the Value of Land, and thinks his a fair Valuation at Thirty Years Purchase.

That Mr. Brindley's, Agents have acquainted him.with the Expence of making Locks; and that the Tunnelling and Cutting may be done at the Price estimated.

And that the Owner of the Mill he mentioned has consented to part with it, without any Agreement being made as to the Price.

Mr. Yeomans, an Engineer, being examined, said,

That he has been employed in making several Navigations: — That he has looked carefully over the Estimate produced, and was very particular in his Enquiries into the Prices of Materials and Labour, but never law the Ground where the Canal is proposed to be carried: — That Mr. Weston seems to have taken great Pains, and understands the Subject: — That he is not acquainted with the Price of Materials and Labour in that Part of the Country; but if they are as he is informed, the Work may be done for the Prices set down in that Estimate; but that he never carried on any Works under Ground.

Mr. John Lingard produced a Map of the proposed Navigation, a Paper of the Consents of the Proprietors, and also a Field Book, in which is set down the Length of the proposed Canal through each Proprietor’s Land; and acquainted your Committee, that the Proprietors of Fourteen Miles of Land, through which the Canal was proposed to be carried, bad signed their Consent to it.

Mr. James Folliot, a Merchant at Che tier, being examined, said, That a great Trade is carried on at Chester, most of the Manufactures that go to Ireland being lent that Way, particularly in Time of War, to avoid the Danger of the long Sea.

That an inland Navigation to Chester is absolutely necef-1 VOL. 33.

fary for preserving the Trade there; and that a Canal from Chester to Middleivieh would answer that Purpose, and

he thinks would be of public Benefit: — That he has no Doubt about this, as Goods would be conveyed cheaper to Ireland this Way than they can be by Liverpool, that being a greater Distance.

Being asked. What Tonnage the proposed Canal would produce ? he said. That the Goods that go to and from Chejhr by Land, arc at present upwards of 17,000 Tons per Annum, which would go on this Canal; and that probably.a Navigation would double this Quantity:

— That the Carriage of Goods from Sheffield to Chester, through Midd/ewich, is Three Shillings and Six Pence per Hundred Weight, and by Mane heft er Four Shillings: — That the Carriage from Birmingham is Four Shillings, and great Quantities are sent from thence.

That aThoufand Bales of Cloth are sent annually from Gloucestershireand the neighbouring, Counties, which go by Land from Shrezesbury, at Two Shillings />t?r Hundred Weight.

That great Quantities of Merchandize are lent from London by Land Carriage, particularly Wrought Silk, Raw Silk; Broad and Narrow Cloth: — That the Price ot Carriage in Winter is Eight Shillings per Hundred Weight, and in Summer, Seven Shillings for Merchandize; and that Baggage pays Fourteen Shillings.

That if this Navigation was completed, all thele Goods might go upon it, and would go cheaper: — That if the Plan proposed does not take Effect, the City of Chester will lose the Business they have long enjoyed, as the Goods will go to Liverpool by the Canal authorized to be made from the Trent to the Mersey.

That many Ships are employed between Chester and Dublin in: carrying Merchandize; Thirteen constantly, from Ninety to Two hundred and Fifty Tons, which are maintained at a great Expence; and that His Majesty’s Troops are commonly transported that Way: — That the Witness himself employs Six Ships in this Trade; but if this Canal should not be executed, he must: fend them to some other Port.

That about One hundred Tons of Hardware comes from Sheftield to Chester in a Year; upwards of that Weight of Goods from Manchester, including the Woollen Trade of Yorkshire; about Two hundred Tons of Hardware from Birmingham and the neighbouring Places; and about One hundred Tons of Woollen Goods from Oxfordshire, and Parts adjacent.

Being asked. How far it would be from the River Dee to the River Pier fey by a Canal? he answered. About Eight or Nine Miles, the nearest Way, and that this would be more beneficial to the Northern Trade than the Plan now defiled; but he afterwards said, that he thought it would not be so convenient, for that they now fend Goods from those Parts to Chester by Land (though the Carriage to Liverpool is cheaper) for the Benefit of a better Port.

Being asked, Why the Navigation to the would

not be more convenient, as being nearer? he said. It is out of the Way to all Parts, but the North; and although nearer to the Northern Parts, it would not be so commodious: — That a Junction with the would

be a great Way round for the Southern Trade, and attended with extraordinary Expence; and that the Trade of the North is not more than One Tenth, or One Twelfth Part of the Foreign Trade of Chester.

That the Inconvenience of going to the Mersey would be, that when Goods are Water-borne upon that Arm of the Sea called the Alerjey, they will not come to ter, but would go to Liverpool, and Chester would be hurt greatly; and if the Runcorn Gap Navigation were made, and not the other, the Witness thinks the Trade of Chester will be totally ruined, because the new Canals will carry the Goods of all the Kingdom, and they will not come to Chester, having no Communication with it; and this would put Chester in a worse Condition than other Parts of the Kingdom: — That the Trade from

Ihence to Ireland would be loft, as Goods could not be sent thither so cheap as from Liverpool: — That all Goods which now go to Chester would go to Liverpool^ if a Navigation was made thither and none to

Being allied. If it would be worth while to make the Canal, if no new Trade was to be thereby carried to Chester f he said. He does not know that the present Trade would pay fof it, but he believes it would be increased by the Navigation, and the Carriage of Coals alone would pay for it j and that the I ncrease of Trade at Chester would by no Means hurt Liverpool, as the Goods, which he supposes would increase the Trade of would not be carried to Liverpool; and that he confines himself to the Coal Trade principally.

Mr. John Chamberlain, a Merchant at being

examined, said, That a great Trade is carried on there, which is at present increasing, but that they have no Land Carriage to the interior Parts of the Kingdom; and that '' if a Canal were made to Liverpool, and none to Chester, that City would be ruined.

That Chester is well situated for an Intercourse between England and Ireland.

That the Inhabitants of Chester are at present supplied with Coals from Cheshireand Flintshire, which aredelivered

at about Ten Shillings a Ton at Chester; — That the proposed Canal would reduce the Price, not only at Chester, but all the Way to Middlewich; and about the Middle of the intended Canal, they are Fifteen Shillings per Ton in Summer, and Twenty Shillings in Winter.

That the Carriage of Coals would increase the Tonnage between the Trent and the Mersey: — That they would be brought from Hare Castle Hill to the Country about Tetrporly, though not to Chester.

That he apprehends the Junction between the Port of Chester and the Canal carrying on between the Trent and Mersey, would be of great public Utility.

* That Goods coming from the South of England Would be shipped at Chester cheaper than at Liverpool, by One Shilling and Six Pence/> Ton, the Passage being Fifteen Miles shorter; and that he apprehends the Trade to Chester to be about 20,000 Tons ahnually, including Salt and Coals, which would produce about £. 1,$00 per Annum clear.

That he has seen the Eftirfiate of the Expence of making this Canal, and thinks it a.reasonable one; and that he is acquainted with Building in that Country, and the Prices of Materials and Labour, but that he knows nothing of Navigation Works, but was present When Mr. ffefion made his Estimate, and saw Mr. Yeomans and him put down the Prices of Materials and Labour, which were the common Prides in that Part of the Country.

That the City of Chester is a Place of great Trade, pays £. 15,000 per Annum to the King for Imports apd Exports; and that Twelve or Thirteen Ships are employed there in the Dublin Trade Only.

That a Canal from the Trent to the Mersey, and none to Chester, would min that City, as that would carry away all Importation and the Trade to — That

he was of this Opinion Five Years ago, when the Jhitr Navigation Was in Contemplation; and that Application was then intended to be made from Chester, for aClaiife to join that Navigation: — That this was the general Desire at that Time, and the Application for that Purpose was dropped, upon a Presumption that Parliament would give Leave at any Time to make a Canal for that Purpose; which was the only Reason why it was not prosecuted at that Time.

Mr. John Latham, being examined, said, That he is Surveyor of the Port of Chester, and well acquainted With the Trade there: That Thirteen Vessels conftailtly trade from thence to Dublin, and many others occasionally to and from other Ports in Ireland; — and that if this Canal should not take place, not only the greatest Part of the Neighbourhood of Chester will be mined, but all the Inland Counties of North Wales suffer materially; — That all the Import Trade, and Trade 7

from Ireland will be destroyed 1 and that this is not only the nearell Way from London to Ireland, bilt the fafrit Navigation.

That the Navigation of the River Dee will be greatly hurt, and a great Part of the Profits of the Proprietor-. (Which arise from Tonnage) will be ldft, as there will be no Importation to Chester, but for the Use of the Inhabitants themselves.

Being asked, If he did not think that the City o Would not carry on as much Trade from the Navigation* as from this proposed Canal ? Ire laid. He thought not, as there will be a long Land Carriage to Chester, and none to Liverpool; and that Goods would go so much cheaper to Liverpool, that it would carry all the Trade from Chester.

Mr. Fo/liot, being again examined, said, That all that is intended by the Promoters of this Scheme, is to preserve their own Trade; and that he has Authority from the present Subscribers to say, that if the Proprietors of the Staffordshire Navigation are willing to undertake the making of this Canal, they may have the Whole, or any Part of it that they please.

Mr. Chamberlain, being again examined, was asked# What Quantity of Trade he thought would Come annually from Middleivichto Chester ? he said. He apprehended 20,000 Tons, which Cannot come from Runcorn Gap for lets than Two Shillings and Six Pende per Tati incteased Expence: — That he thinks this Canal would increase the Carriage on the Staffordshire Canal, as the Coals uled in making Salt would come that Way, and as Merchants Goods make but a itnall Part of the Carriage; and upon the Whole, he thinks this proposed Canal would be art Advantage to that Navigation.

That the Trade of the North is not more thdn One Tenth of the Southern Trade; and that the Trade from the South would never come to Chester without this Canal, but would be carried to Liverpool.

That the Carriage from Mid to Chester consists chiefly of Coals ana Salt; and that no Coals would come from Runcorn Gap, as the additional TvVo Shillings and Six Pence per Ton would make them too dear; and that

all Goods from Chester to Middleivich, round by would be loaded with this Two Shillings and Six Pence per Ton.

That if this Canal should not be made, and a Communication were made between Chester and Runcorn Gap, it would occasion the same additional Expence of Two Shillings and Six Pence per Ton; for the Distance is about Fifteen Miles, and the Carriage would be about Two Pence per Mile.

That it is Nine Miles from Chester to the Communication with the River Mersey, and it costs Eighteen Pence going the re: — That it is then Six or Eight Miles in a boisterous Arm of the Sea, at the additional Expence of 1 s. per Ton; and that the common Expence from Runcorn Gap to Liverpool is Two Shillings per Ton at prefect.

If a Canal Was made to the Mersey, he thinks Salt would not come cheaper down the and up the

proposed Canal between the Mersey and Dee.

That Salt cannot be conveyed from Norrhwkh to the Mersey for less than Three Shillings and Six Pence, of Four Shillings per Ton; and he thinks it Could not be carried for lets than Five Shillings and Three Pence, as they carty it now to Liverpool.

Being asked, If Chester could not be supplied cheapet with Coals by a Navigation between the Dee and Mersey he said, He thought hot, as Coals are now Ten Shillings per Ton at Chester, and Ten Shillings and Six Pence at Northzvich-, and he thinks they would not go

cheaper to Chester by the proposed Canal from the Mersey to Chester: — That froiiv Chester to by Land is Eight Miles, and from thence to Runcorn about Eight Miles more.

That no Staffordshire Coals are burnt at Chester-but if this Canal was made, Tarporly would be supplied

The Tellers reported to the House, that the Numbers were for the Ayes 155, for the Noes 165, so Mr. Speaker declared, that the Noes had it.

But it having happened, that among the Members who were coming in on the Division, a Stranger, who had continued in the Lobby, after it was cleared, had come in, and was told as One of the Noes, several Members objected to the Validity of the Division, and infilled, that the Question ought to be put again, and the Sense of the House again taken: Mr. Speaker immediately on declaring the Numbers, had ordered the Doors of the House to be locked, in order that no Member might go forth: The Stranger was then brought to the Bar, and examined,.and it appearing that what he had done was from Ignorance and Inadvertency, and without any Intention of passing for a Member on the Division, and being known to several Merftbers as a Man of good Character, he was for the present ordered to be taken from the Bar.

The Question then, " That Mr. Speaker do now " leave the Chairwas again put.

The House divided again.

Mr. Sutton, from the Office of One of His Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, presented to the House, pursuant to their Address to His Majesty,

A Paper, intituled, " Copy of his Catholic Majesty’s " Orders, signified by the Balio Fray, D" Julian de " Arriaga, to Dn Philip Ruiz Puente-, dated Pardo, 7th " February 1771 and Trar.station.

And the Titles of the said Papers were read.

And the said Translation was also read.

The said Papers are preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session; and the said Translation is as followeth; viz.

Translation of his Catholic Majesty’s Orders, signified by the Balio Fray Dn Julian de Arriaga, to D Philip Ruiz Puente;dated Pardo, 7th February 1771.

It being agreed between the King and His Britannic Majesty, by a Convention signed at London, on the 2 2d January last past, by the Prince of and the Earl of Rochford, that the Great Malouine, called by the English, Falkland, should be immediately replaced in

the precise Situation in which it was before it was evacuated by them on the 10th June last Year; I signify to you, by the King’s Order, that, as soon as the Person commissioned by the Court of London, shall present himself to you with this, you order the Delivery of the Port de la Cruzada or Egmond, and its Fort and Dependencies, to be effected; as also, that of all the Artillery, Ammunition, and Effects, that were found there, belonging to His Britannic Majesty, and His Subjects, according to the Inventories signed by George and William Malt by, Esquires, on the lith July of the said Year, at the Time of their quitting the fame; of which I fend you the inclosed Copies, authenticated under my Hand; and that as soon as the one and the other shall be eflfedted with the due Formalities, you cause to retire immediately the Officer and other Subjects of the King, which may be there. God preserve you many Years, Pardo 7 th February 1771.

(Signed)

The Balio Fray, Da de Arriaga.

To Dn Philip Ruiz Puente.

W.kefield Mr. Lascelles reported from the Committee, to whom Paving, the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Inhabitants within the Town and Township of Wakefield, in the County of York, and Owners and Occupiers of Houses and Lands there, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he

read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Johnson, being examined, said, That the Streets, and other public Passages, within the said Town, are very ill paved, repaired, cleansed, and lighted; and the Passages thereof greatly obstructed by various Nuisances and Annoyances: That in many Parts thereof they are so narrow as to be extremely incommodious; and mentioned particularly the Passage opposite the White Hart Inn, in the Road to Leeds, which is so narrow that a Horse cannot pass a Carriage without great Danger; the Way between the North Gate and the Market Place, where Carriages are frequently flopped by Reason of some detached Buildings, which make the Way so narrow that Two Carriages cannot pass; and the Passage from the West Gate to the Market, which is so much cramped by the Two Corner Houses, that Two Carriages cannot pass; and also Kirk Gate, which is rendered very incommodious by the Projection of Shepherd's Garden.

He said further, That, if the said Streets were properly widened, cleansed, paved, and lighted, and the Nuisances and Obstructions removed, it would tend greatly to the Safety and Advantage of the Inhabitants, and be of public Utility.

William Rat cliffe, Esquire, being examined, said, He acts as a Justice of the Peace in that Part of the County of York: That he apprehends the Inhabitants of Wakefield are liable, by Law, to pave the Streets in the Fronts of their respective Houses; but that many of them are too poor to repair them in a proper Manner: That he has known numberless Instances of their being indicted and fined for neglecting to keep their Pavements in Repair, and many of them committed for being unable or unwilling to pay their Fines; but, notwithstanding all that has been done, the Streets remain as bad as ever: And he is of Opinion, they cannot be effectually repaired by the Laws now in being, on Account of the Inability of many of the Inhabitants.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better paving, repairing, cleansing, and lighting, the Streets, Lanes, Alleys, and other public Patfages, within that Part of the Town of Wakefield, in the County of York, which lies within the East End of Bridge, the South Side of Northgate Bar, the North End of Kirkgate Bridge, (except to much thereof as is repaired by the West Riding of the said County of York) and the extreme Part of the Township of Wakefield aforesaid, leading from towards;

for preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein; and for widening and rendering the same more commodious: And that Mr. Lascelles, Sir George Sir

Mr. Pennant reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Merchants and Tradesmen of the Port of Kingston upon Hull, on Behalf of themselves,

and more particularly of those concerned in the Whale Fishery, to Greenland; Davis's Straits, and the Seas adjacent; and also, the Petition of the Royal Boroughs of Scotland; and also, the Petition of the Merchants, and

others, His Majesty’s British Subjects, concerned in the Whale Fishery, were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said last mentioned Petition, no Person having appeared in Support of the Two first mentioned Petitions; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table, together with an Appendix thereunto: Where the same was read; and is as followeth, viz:

A State of the Fasts contained in the said last mentioned Petition, is as follows:

By an Act, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for the further continuing several Acts of Parliament made for the Encouragement of the Whale Fishery, carried on by His Majesty’s Subjects, which sets forth, That divers Acts of Parliament have been made for the Encouragement of His Majesty’s Subjects to carry on and improve the Whale Fishery; which, by the Bounties given by the said Acts, did greatly increase, to the Advantage of the Trade and Navigation of the/e Kingdoms; all the Acts therein recited, together with the Bounties by them granted, are further continued to the 25th Day of December *770, and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament.

And it appeared to your Committee, from the Evidence of Mr. James Mather, That, since the Bounty was granted on Shipping employed in the Whale Fishery, many Ships have entered into that Trade: — That in the Year 1749 only 3 Ships went out, and in 1756 there were 83 sent: — That the Trade has decreased since that Time, owing to the late War, and the Shortness of the Time for which the Bounties were granted, so much, that in the Year 1770 only 53 Ships were employed in it: — That, if the Bounty was further continued, the Number of the Adventurers would be increased more than double: — That each Ship carries, upon an Average, more than 30 Men; so that in 1756, when 83 Ships were employed in that Trade, there were 4,150 Men in the Service, and 300 Apprentices were taken; each Matter being obliged to take an Apprentice for every 50 Tons of his Ship: — That all the Implements ui'ed in this Trade, which formerly were made in Holland, are now made by English Manufacturers; and, if the Bounty is not continued, the Trade cannot as yet go on without it; and the Seamen employed in this Fishery, from the high Price of Wages, will be induced to go into the Dutch Service: — That a Ship of 350 Tons, fitted out for this Fishery, costs about £. 1,500 more than one of the same Burthen for any other Trade; all of which is entirely loft, if file is not employed, because the Articles that cause that Increase of Expence are not fit for any other Purpose; and if such Ship was to return unsuccessful, and there was no Bounty, the Adventurers would, in the present State of the Fishery, lole at least £. 1,200 by the Voyage: And he laid, he had loft £. 700 by One Ship, though he received the Bounty.

Your Committee having proceeded to inquire into the Price of Whalebone and Oil, and the Quantities of each brought from this Fishery, have received Evidence from Mr. Mather: — That last Year the Quantity of Whale Oil brought in was near 2,000 Tons; being almost One-third of the whole Consumption of the Oil of this Kingdom; the Average of Whale Oil is now 18 or £.19 a Ton, that formerly was 27 a Ton. The Quantity of Whalebone brought in last Year was about 100 Ton — the Average Price of Whalebone is now £. 400 a Ton — that it has been formerly fold fdr £. 860 a Ton: — That the Bone brought in by this Fishery, together with what comes from North America, is not yet sufficient to supply this Kingdom, there being large Quantities annually imported from Holland, notwithstanding the Duty of£.84. is. on the Importation of such Bone: — That large Quantities of Seals are taken in this Fishery, the Skins of which are made use of as Leather. — And he concluded his Evidence by saying, he makes no Doubt, but that this Fishery may, in a few Years, supply this Kingdom with its whole Consumption of Whalebone, and even enable the Merchants to export some, if the Bounty on Ships employed in the Greenland Trade is continued for a longer Time than heretofore ic has been.

And he produced an Account of the Number of Ships fitted out for the Whale Fishery, from the Year 1733 to the Year 1770, which your Committee have annexed hereunto.

Mr. William Ward, and Mr. Thomas , confirmed the Whole of Mr. Mather's Evidence.

The above Calculation of Seamen is made at 50 Men for each Ship: — But they generally carry 56. By the Act of Parliament, each Ship of 300 Tons must carry every Voyage an Apprentice for each 50 Tons; that is, Six Apprentices; so that, from the Year 1755 to 1769, this Fishery must have been the Nursery for 5,000 Seamen j and have employed in that Time 40,600 Seamen.

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, Gra- Narrow-ziers, and Farmers, within the Counties of Nottingham, wheeled Leicester, and Derby, on Behalf of themselves and others,

3 M was

226

5° Martii. A. 1771.

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a great Number of heavy Horses are bred in the faifl Counties; and that the Mares kept for continuing that valuable Breed are neceflfarily used by the Owners, in drawing Coals and Lime for Manure, and other hard Exercises, and which is usually performed in the Spring Months, in very bad Roads, when such Mares are either big with Foal, or suckle; and that, by an Act made in the Seventh Year of His present Majesty, to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the several Laws in being, for regulating the Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, the Petitioners are restrained from drawing any narrow-wheeled Waggon on any Turnpike Road with more than Four Plorfes, which Restraint puts the Petitioners and others under insuperable Difficulties; and the Petitioners apprehend, that unless some Relief is given in the Premises, the Breed of the useful Animals above del'cribed will be greatly diminished, if not totally neglected; and that the Petitioners apprehend. Four Horses drawing a heavy Carriage upon a Turnpike Road do more Prejudice to such Road than Six Hoiks would in drawing the same Carriage and Weight, and do not pay lo much Toll; but that, if Liberty was given to draw Six Horses in the like Carriages and Weight, much more Tolls would be received, and the Commissioners thereby enabled to keep the Roacls in much better Repair: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and permit narrow-wheeled Waggons, going for, or loaded with. Coals, or with Lime, or other Things for Manure, so be drawn by a greater Number of Horses than are now by Law allowed; or to give the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Table.
