*11 ^"R. Onslow reported to the House, That their IVl Address of Monday lift (that His Majesty would be graciously pleased to issue His. Royal Proclamation, for apprehending John Wheble and R. Thompson, with a Promise of Reward for the fame) bad been presented to His Majesty; and that His Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, that He will give Directions accordingly.

His Majesty’s Proclamation, iflfued in pursuance of the said Address, is as followeth:

By the KING,

A PROCLAMATION,

For apprehending John W and R. Thompson.

GEORGE R.

Whereas, on the Eighth Day of February last. Complaint being made to the House of Commons, of the printed Newspaper, intituled. The Gazetteer and New Daily Adverlifer, Friday, February 8, 1771, printed

for R. Thompson; and also, of the printed Newspaper,

intituled. The MiddlesexJournal, or Chronicle of Liberty,

from Tuesday, February 5, to Thursday, February 7,

1771, printed*- for J.. IVheble, as misrepresenting the Speeches, and reflecting on several of the Members of the said House, in Contempt of the Order, and in Breach of the Privilege of the said House: It was ordered, That the said J. IVheble and R. Thompson should attend the said House of Commons; and they, not having obeyed the said Order, it was thereupon ordered, by the said House of Commons, That the said John IVheble and R. Thompson should be taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending the said House, or his Deputy: And whereas the said Deputy Serjeant, having informed the House that he had not been able to meet with the said John Wheble and R. , or either of

them, though he had been several Times at their respective Houses, and had made diligent Search after them,

8

to take them into Custody, an humble Address hath been presented to Us, by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, in Parliament assembled, That We would be graciously pleased to issue Our Royal Proclamation for apprehending the said John Wheble and R. Thompson, with a Pro-mi(e of Reward for the same; We have thought fit, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, to ill'ue this-.

Our Royal Proclamation, hereby requiring and commanding all Our loving Subjects whatsoever,. to discover and apprehend, or cause the said John Wheble and

R. Thompson, or either of them, to be discovered and apprehended, and to carry him or them before some of Our Justices of the Peace, or Chief Magistrates of the County, Town, or Place, where lie or they shall be' apprehended; who are respectively required to secure the said John Wheble and R. Thompson, and thereof give speedy Notice to One of Our Principal Secretaries of State, to the End he or they may be forthcoming to be dealt withal, and proceeded against according to Law And for the Prevention of an Escape of the said Joint

Wheble and R. Thompson, or either of them, into Parts beyond the Seas, We do require and command all Our Officers of the Customs, and other Our Officers and Subjects of and in Our respective Ports and Maritime Towns and Places, within, Our Kingdom of Great Britain, that they, and every of them, in their respective Places and Stations, be careful and diligent in the Examination of all Persons that shall pals, or endeavour to pals, beyond the Seas; and if they shall discover the said John Wheble and R. Thompson, or either of them, then to cause him or them to be apprehended and secured, and to give Notice thereof as aforesaid. And We do hereby strictly charge and command all Our loving Subjects, as they will answer the contrary at their Perils, that they do not any ways conceal, but do discover, him or them, the said John Wheble and R.

Thompson, to tire End he or they may be secured. And for the Encouragement of all Persons to be diligent and careful in endeavouring to discover and apprehend the said John Wheble and R. Thompson, We do hereby further declare. That whosoever shall discover and apprehend the said John Wheble, and R. or either

of them, within Three Weeks from the Date thereof, and shall bring him or them, the said Wheble and R. Thompson, before forr\e Justice of the Peace, or Chief Magistrate, as aforesaid, shall have and receive, as a Reward for the Disco very, apprehending, and bringing the said John Wheble and R. Thompson, or either of them, before such Justice of the Peace, or Chief Magistrate, as aforesaid, the Sum of Fifty Pounds for each: which Our Commissioners of Our Treasury are hereby required and directed to pay accordingly.

Given at Our Court at St. James's, the Eighth Day of March, One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-one, in the Eleventh Year of Our Reign.

God save the King.

Mr. Cooper, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to comfider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followed); viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Charge of the Pay and Cloathing of the Militia, in that Part of Great Britain called England, for One Year, beginning the Twenty-fifth Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-one, be defrayed out of the Monies arising by the Land Tax granted for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-one.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That,. towards raffing the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of One million Eight hundred thousand Pounds be raised, by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged upon the First Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament; and such Exchequer Bills, if not discharged, with Interest thereupon, on or before the Fifth Day of April One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-two, to be exchanged, and received in Payment in such Manner as Exchequer Bills have usually been exchanged and received in Payment.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill, or Bills, be brought in, upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Cooper, Sir Charles

Whitworth, the Lord Beauchamp, and Mr. De Grey, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

That in the said Bill there are Clauses, which, the Petitioners conceive, are very improper, and will be very burthensome to the Inhabitants living within the Limits of Long Alley Sewer, wherein the Streets mentioned in the said Bill are situate, and that, by the Law of Sewers, and the . constant Usage of the Petitioners, no Drain or Sewer ought to be cleansed or amended, but on the Preferment of a Jury, who constantly make their Preferments on Oath; but, by one of the aforesaid Clauses, the Commissioners in such Bill are empowered to make Sewers, and cleanse Drains, at their own Will and Pleasure, which the Petitioners conceive to be very arbitrary, and contrary to the Laws of Sewers: And therefore praying, That the said Clauses in the said Bill may be struck out; and in regard as the Petitioners have no Fund whereby to defray any Expences, that the House will take the Matter into their Consideration; without the Petitioners employing any Counsel to attend on their Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Tnrkey A Petition of the Governor and Company of Mer-

Trade. chants of England, trading into the Levant Seas, being

offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read'; Setting forth. That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey, has for a long Series of Years been carried on by a Society of Merchants incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on the said Trade with Safety, and to protest His Majesty’s Subjects in the Turkish Dominions, it has been found necessary that there ftinuld be an AmbalTador lent from England to retide at Constantinople, and that there Ihould be Consuls, Vice Consuls, and other Offi-

cers and Servants, in the other Parts of Turkey, where any British Subjects refiiic, and where the carry oh

Trade 5 the whole Expence whereof has been borne by the Turkey Company; which, together with other necessary Expences incident to the carrying on the said Trade, has of late Years amounted to upwards of f. 10,000 per Annum-, and that the said Trade, to and-from Turkey, once so flourishingi is now, from many unavoidable Events and concurring Circumstances, much reduced; and that the Assistance which was granted to the Petitioners by Parliament, in the last Session, was employed in paying off a considerable Part of the Debt they had incurred; and they had Reason to hope, that they should not now have been under a Necessity of applying for further Assistance, nor should they have troubled the House, but for the great Stagnation of Trade, and Increase of Expence, occasioned by the War which still subsists between the and the Russian

Governments; and that the Petitioners are fenlible, that they should not discharge the Duty incumbent upon them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public, if they did not declare their Inability to support their necessary Expences, unless relieved by Parliament;

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such further Afe fiftance as may be thought necessary and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The several Orders of the Day being read, for the Privilege. Attendance of Brass Crosby, Esquire, Lord Mayor of the City of London, and Richard Oliver, Esquire, Alderman of the City of London, in their Places;

And the Lord Mayor attending accordingly in his Place, acquainted the House, that he had received the Resolution of this House of Friday last, for allowing him Liberty to be heard, by his Counsel, upon all such Points as do not controvert the Privileges of this House; but that finding the Counsel were, by that Resolution, restrained from speaking to many Points material to his Defence, and that the Counsel he could depend upon, and whom he wished to employ, were on the Circuit; he therefore would not give the House the Trouble of hearing Counsel on this Occasion.

Then the Evidence, which, upon Monday lad, was given to the House, by the Deputy Serjeant at Arms attending this House, was read; and the Minutes of what the Lord Mayor had offered to the House, in his Defence, upon Tuesday last, were also read.

And the original Charter, granted to the City of London, upon the 6th Day of March, in the First Year of the Reign of King Edward the Third, was produced, and read.

The House was also moved. That the Resolutions, which, upon the 26th Day of February 1701, were reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Rights, Liberties, and Privileges, of the House of Commons, might Be read.

And the same were, as agreed to by the House, read accordingly; and are as followeth; viz.

" Resolved, That to alTert, that the House of Commonsisnot the only Representatives of the Commons " of England, tends to the Subversion of the Rights and

Privileges of the House of Commons, and the fundamental Constitution of the Government of this " Kingdom.

" Resolved, That to assert, the House of Commons

u have no Power of Commitment, but of their own " Members, tends to the Subversion of the Constitution " of the House of Commons.

" Resolved, That to print or publish any Books

" or Libels, reflecting upon the Proceedings of the " House of Commons, or any Member thereof, for or " relating to his Service therein, is a high Violation " of the Rights and Privileges of the House of Commons.

" Resolved, That it is the undoubted Right of the

People Of England, to petition or address to the King,

" for the calling, fitting, or dissolving, of Parliaments,

and for the redressing of Grievances.

* Resolved, That it is the undoubted Right of every " Subject of England, under any Accusation, either by " Impeachment or otherwise1, to be brought to a speedy '* Trial, in order to be acquitted or condemned."

The House was also moved, That the Resolutions of the House, of the 23d Day of Jamary 1722, in relation to the Complaint of the Proceedings of this House being frequently printed in; News Letters and Papers, might be read.

And the same were read accordingly; and are as followeth; viz.

" Resolved, That no News Writers do presume, in " their Letters, or other Papers, that they disperse as " Minutes, or under any other Denomination, to intermeddle with the Debates, or any other Proceedings,

" of this House.

" Resolved, That no Printer or Publisher of any

printed News Papers do presume to insert in any such " Papers, any Debates, or any other Proceedings, of this " House, or any Committee thereof."

The House was also moved. That the Resolution of the House, of the 13th Day of April 1738, in relation to the Complaint made to the House, of the Publishers of several written and printed News Letters and Papers, might be read.

And the same was read accordingly; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is an high Indignity to, and a notorious Breach of the Privilege of, this House, for " any News Writer, in Letters, or other Papers, (as " Minutes, or under any other Denomination) or for " any Printer or Publisher of any printed News Paper, of any Denomination, to presume to insert in the said " Letters or Papers, or to give therein, any Account " of the Debates, or other Proceedings, of this House, " or any Committee thereof, as well during the Recess, " as the Sitting of Parliament; and that this House " will proceed with the utmost Severity against such. " Offenders."

The House was also moved, That the Resolution of the House, of the 24th Day of November 1763, relating to the Privilege of Parliament, in the same of seditious Libels, might be read.

And the same was read accordingly; and is as followeth; viz.

" Resolved, That Privilege of Parliament does not " extend to the same of writing and publishing seditious " Libels, nor ought to be allowed to obstruct the ordinary Course of the Laws, in the speedy and effectual " Prosecution of so heinous and dangerous an Offence."

Tumult. The House being informed of a tumultuous Crowd assembled in "Palace Yard, and in the Passages leading to the House, who had assaulted several of the Members in their coming to the House:

Several Justices of the Peace of the County of dlesex and City of Westm attending; they were called in; and, at the Bar, Mr. Speaker, by Order of the House, acquainted them. That the House, having received Information of the said riotous Proceedings, did expect that they should go immediately and give the proper Orders for preserving the Peace, and dispersing the Crowd who were assembled about the Passages leading to the House; and that they should return, and give the House an Account of what they had done.

And then they withdrew.

And, after some Time, the House being informed that the said Justices were again attending; they were called in; apd, at the Bar, acquainted the House, That they had endeavoured to put the Orders of the House in Execution; and had proposed to read the Riot Act, but were prevented; and were totally unable to do any thing further towards keeping the Peace.

And the Sheriffs of London and , being

Members of this House, were requested to go themselves, and endeavour to disperse the said Crowd.

And they went accordingly.

And being returned; they, in their Places, informed the House, That they had been amongst the People, and persuaded several of them to go away; that they had di-rested the High Constable to get an additional Number of Constables; that they had lent for the Under Sheriffs, who were coming with further Assistanqe of the Civil Power; that at present the Crowd were considerably dif-perfect; and what remained seemed exceedingly quiet; and that they were of Opinion, that the House need not any longer defer proceeding upon Business.

Clerkenwell Mr. 'Thomas townjkend.Junior, reported from the (S'John) Committee, to whom the Petition of several of the principal Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint John, Clerkenwell, in the County of Middlesex, was referred} That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition* Sir George Poole, Baronet, and Heaton Wilkes, Esquire, being teverally examined, said. That frequent Outrages and Felonies happen in the said Parish, in the Night Time; and that ’ if a well-regulated Watch were kept there* it would tend greatly to the Safety of the Inhabitants.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for paving, repairing, cleansing, and lighting, the Streets* Squares, Lanes, and other Passages, within the Parish of Saint John, Clerkenwell, in the County of Middlesex, and for removing Obstructions and Annoyances therein, is committed; That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, for keeping up and regulating a Nightly Watch within the said Parish.

I He of Wight A Petition of the Churchwardens and Overseers of

Poor, Sec. tj,e Poor of the Parishes of Brooke, Brixton,

Cari/brooke, Saint Helens, Shalfleet, Gat combe,

Arreton, Godskill, and Newchvrch, in the Ifie of Wight,

whose Names are thereunto subscribed* was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for eftahltshing a House or Houses of Industry in the Isle of Wight, for the Reception, Maintenance, and Employment of the Poor belonging to the several Parishes and Places within the said island; and setting forth* That the Inhabitants of the said Parishes are in general Farmers and Graziers, who employ great Numbers of poor Persons in the Cultivation of the said Farms, and are well satisfied with the present Mode of laying on and collecting the Poor Rates, and maintaining and employing the Poor in the said Parishes; and it is apprehended, that the said Bill will be very prejudicial and injurious to the said Parishes: And therefore praying the House, that the said Parishes may not be included in the said Bill; and that they may be heard, by themselves or Cotihfel, against the said Bill; or {nay be otherwise relieved, in such Manner as to the House shall appear just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Count'd, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think lit.

Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported’ from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of/. 650,000 be raised by Way of Lottery; such Lottery to consist of 50,000 Tickets, at £.13 each; and that the Contributors towards the same shall, on or before the 18th Day of this Instant 1771, make a Deposit with the Cashiers of the Bank of England of £. 1. in respetft of the Money to be paid for every such Ticket, as a Security for making the future Payments to the said Cashiers, on or before the Times herein after limited; that is to say, for, and in respect of every such Ticket, £. 2. on or before the 7th Day of June next; £.3. on or before the 10th Day of July next; £. 3. on or before the 21st Day of August next; £. 4. on or before the 3d Day of October next: And that Tickets, as soon as the same can be prepared, dull be delivered to the Contributors so completing their Payments: That the Sum of/. 500,000 shall be divided into Prizes, from each of which Prizes there shall severally be a Deduction after the Rate of ./. 10 for every/. ico, and the Sums remaining, after such Deductions, shall be paid unto the Proprietors of the several fortunate Tickets in the said Lottery, out of any the Aids or Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament, for the Service of the Year 1771, at the Bank of England, in Money, upon Demand, on the First Day of March 1772, or as soon after as Certificates can be made out, without any further or other Deduction whatsoever: And that all the Monies to be received by the said Cashiers shall be paid into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, to be applied, tram Time to Time, Vot. 33.

to such Services as shall then have been voted by this House in this Session of Parliament; and that every Contributor, who shall pay in the Whole of Lis Contribution towards the said Sum. of /. 650,000 on or before the 15th Day of August next, shall be allowed an Interest, by Way of Discount, after the Rate of £. 3 per Centum per Annum, on the Sums so completing his Contribution respectively, to be computed from the Day of completing the fame, to the 3d Day of October next.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be issued and applied the Sum of Six hundred Ninety-one thousand Nine hundred Seventy-seven Pounds Seven Shillings and Nine Pence, remaining in the Receipt of the Exchequer, on the Fifth Day of April 1771,'for the Disposition of Parliament, of the Monies whifch liad then arisen of the Surplusses, ExcessTes, or Overplus Monies, and other Revenues, composing the Fund commonly called The Sinking Fund.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be issued and applied the Sum of One million Six hundred and Fifty thousand Pounds, out of such Monies as shall or may arise, of the Surplusses, Excelics, or Overplus Monies, and other Revenues, composing the Fund, commonly called The Sinking Fund.

Resolved, That jt is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Eighty-nine thousand Six hundred. Fifty-eight Pounds Sixteen Shillings, and Niije Pence Farthing, now remaining in the Exchequer, being the Overplus of the Grants for the Service of the Year 1770, be issued and applied towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty in, this Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That if is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Four hundred thousand Pounds, which, by an Act made in the Ninth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for carrying into Execution certain Proposals made by the East India Company,. for the Payment of the Annual Sum of Four hundred thousand Pounds, for a limited Tipie, in respect of the territorial Acquisitions and Reyenues lately obtained in the East Indify is dire died to be paid within the present Year info the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, by the said Company, be applied towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Twenty Thousand Pounds, out of such Moni.es as have been, or shall be, paid into the Receipt of the Exchequer, on or before the 5th Day of April 1772, of the Produce of all or any of the Duties and Revenues, which by any Act or Acts of Parliament, have been directed to be reserved for the Disposition of Parliament, towards defraying the necessary Expences of defending, protecting, and securing, the -British Colonies and Plantations in America, be applied towards making good such Part of the Supply as hath, been granted to His Majesty, for maintaining His Majesty’s Forces and Garril'ons in the Plantations; and for. Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported isle from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it of Mu. -was referred to consider of proper Methods for raising a Revenue in the Isle of Man to defray the Charges of amending, repairing, and supporting, the several Harbours and Sea Ports in the said Island; the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Duties, payable on Account of the Harbours of the Isle of Man, do cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Duty of One Penny Halfpenny per Ton be laid upon all Ships and Vessels, not being laden, or in Ballast, belonging to any of His Majesty’s Subjects; which, shall arrive or put into any of the Harbours in the said Island.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Duty of Two Pence per Ton be laid upon all such

Ships

33^ 17" Aprili 1771*.

Ships and Vessels, being laden, or having any Cargo on Board, whether they shall break Bulk, or deliver any Part of their Cargo or not.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Duty of One Penny Ton be laid upon all Ships and Vessels, which shall be repaired in any of the Harbours in the said Island.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Pence per Ton be laid upon all Foreign Ships and Vessels, not being laden, or in Ballad only, which shall arrive or put into any of the Harbours in the said Island.

Re/o/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Three Pence per Ton be laid upon all Foreign Ships and Vessels, which shall arrive or put into any of the Harbours in the said Island, without breaking Bulk, or delivering any Part of their Cargoes.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Duty of Two Pence Ton be laid upon all Foreign Ships and Vessels, which shall break Bulk, and deliver any Part of their Cargo.

Re/o/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Duty of Two Pence per Ton be laid upon all such Foreign Ships and Vessels as shall repair in any of the Harbours in the said Island.

Re/o/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence be laid upon every Foreign Ship and Vessel which shall anchor in any of the Bays of the said Island.

Re/b/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence Ton bejaid upon all Spirits imported into the said Island.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Shilling and Six Pence Hogs-head be laid upon all Tobacco imported into the said Island.

Re/o/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Shillings per Hundred Weight be laid upon all Teas imported into the said Island.

Re/o/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Shilling per Hundred Weight be laid upon all Coffee imported into the said Island.

Re/o/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Shillings and Sixpence per Ton be laid upon all Wines imported into the said Island.

Re/o/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Pence per Chalder be laid upon all Coals imported into the said Island, to be reckoned according to the Cocquet at the Port of Exportation.

Re/o/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty after the Rate of Ten Shillings Centum, ad Valorem, be laid upon all Foreign Goods (Wines, Spirits, and Salt excepted) imported into the said Island.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty after the Rate of Five Shillings per Centum, ad Valorem, be laid upon all other Goods, imported from Great Britain or Ireland, into the said Island, except Licensed Goods and Salt for the Fisheries, of above the Value of Five Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Three Pence per Quarter be laid upon all Corn and Grain imported into, or exported from, the said Island.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of One Penny per Hundred Weight be laid upon all Meal and Flour imported into, or exported from, the said Island.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Six Pence per Head be laid upon all Horses, and Black Cattle, imported into, or exported from, the said Island.

Rje/olved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Rates, Duties, and Impositions, be applied, from Time to Time, towards amending, repair-3

ing, and supporting, the several Harbours and Sea Ports in the said Island.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

That a Bill is depending, for establishing Houses of Industry in the Isle of Wight, for the general Reception and Maintenance of the Poor of_ the said Island; and that Petitions have been presented* to the House, by the Officers of the said Parishes, praying to be excepted out of the said Bill; and that such Step was not taken with their Consent, who are the principal Inhabitants of the said several Parishes; and that the Pe-' titioners, having heard the said Bill read and explained, and being convinced of its great Utility, pray, that the same may pass into a Law, under such Rules and Regulations as the House shall think proper, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, on Behalf of the said Bill.

Fishery. was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner’s Ship, called The Lord Molineux, failed from Liverpool, upon the 2 7th of March 1770, duly fitted out, and bound for the Greenland Fishery, and did, in Company with the Betty, of this Port, catch in those Seas Three Whales; and returned to upon the 19th

eft August last, having fully complied with every Requi-fition stipulated by the Act of Parliament to entitle the Petitioner to receive the Bounty on the said Ship; but the Words of the Oath to be taken upon granting a Certificate to receive the Bounty are, " That all the Whale " Fins and Blubber, imported in the said Ship, this pre-feat Voyage, were really and bond side caught and taken " in the said Seas by the Crew of the said Ship only and that the Petitioner, as such Oath could not, with Truth, be literally sworn to, had the Word " only" left out, and inserted, agreeable to the Fast, " by the Crews u of the said Ship, and the Betty, belonging to this Port," to which the Captain and Mate, as required, made Oath; whereby the Bounty is withheld from the Petitioner, as the Lords of the Treasury adjudge themselves not empowered to dispense with any Alteration of the Words or Form which the Law has prescribed: And therefore praying such Relief as to the House shall seem proper.

Mr. Timas Booth, Clerk to Mr. Dobson, being examined, laid. That he knows the Ship, called Lord linr.cc, was fitted out with every Requisite that the Law directs.

Tint the said Ship is of the Burthen of 190 Tons, or thernbouts, and had on board 60 Fithing Lines, of 120 hamom each, 60 Harpoon Irons, and Six Boats, with Seven Men in each, and Two as an additional Number, together with Six Months Provision.

That the said Ship failed from Liverpool on the 27th of March 1770; and did, in Company with the Betty of the said Port, catch Three Whales; and returned to Liverpool on the 19th of August following, where she went through the Examination required by the Adk.

That, upon Application for the Payment of the Bounty for the said Ship, the Master refuted to take the Oath prescribed by the Act of 6th George the Second; which Act was produced, and read; alledging, that l)ie laid Fish Bone and Oil, which he had on Board, ^vas not taken by the said Ship only, but in Company with the Betty from the said Port: And he believes that all the Bone and Oil on board was taken in the Greenland Seas.

That Mr. Dobson has not received the said Bounty; and that the Owner of the said Ship the Betty hath received the Bounty due on the said Ship. And,

A Petition of the Widows of the Commission and Navy Warrant Officers of the Royal Navy, being offered to Officers, be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth. That, for these Seven Years pad, the Petitioners Pensions have gradually decrealed; and are now so greatly diminished, as for these Three Years past they have received considerably less than what they did in Time of War; whereby many Widows have been reduced to insuperable, and lbmc to insupportable Dif-trels; therefore beg the House to take their very unhappy same into Consideration, and make an Addition to their Fund, which is at prefen t so low-, and upon such an uncertain Establishment, that they are not able to raise any Money on the Credit ot their nominal Pen-lions, to procure them only a temporary Relief from the most excruciating Distress; and as the melancholy dif-trelsful Prospect of leaving a beloved Wife, and help-less Children, exposed to a\\ the Milenes and Calamities attendant upon Poverty ant\ Want, can be no Encouragement for a good Officer freely and cheerfully to venture his Life in the Service of his Country, the Petitioners hope, that that ron(lderation, added to the distinguished and ackrtowd d Services rendered to the Public, by their beloved \ but unfortunate Huf-

Sir William Maynard reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several of His Majesty’s Justices of the Peace, atting in and for the County of Essex; and also, the Petition of several Farmers, Graziers, and others, who frequent the Markets and Fairs at '

ford, in the County of Essex; and also, the Petition of the Gentlemen, Landowners, and Occupiers of Land, in the County of Essex, on Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Proprietors and Occupiers of Land in the said County; and also, the Petition of the principal Inhabitants of the Town of Chelmsford, in the County of Essex, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Town; and also, the Petition of Sir William Mildmay of Moulfham Hall, in the County of Essex, Baronet; and also, the Petition of Edward Revenel, of Dean Street, Soho, in the Liberty of Wefi-mhtfter , Esquire, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the Four First-merv-tioned Petitions; and had heard Counsel on Behalf of the Second, Third, and Fourth-mentioned Petitions, no Counsel appearing, or Evidence having been produced, on Behalf of the Two last mentioned Petitions; and that the Committee had directed him to report the Matters of the said Petitions, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the First-mentioned Petition, Mr. William Hillyer,a Surveyor, being examined, said, that he surveyed the Shire House at Chelmsford, last Tuesday and Wednesday, for the last Time — That it is a very old Building, very much out of Repair, and standsupon Eight Columns.

And he produced to your Committee, Plans for a new Gaol and Shire House.

Mr. William Robinson, a Surveyor of the Board of Works, and Mr. Charles Mills, a Builder and Surveyor, being examined, said, That they have surveyed the Sessions House with Mr. Hillyer — That it is out of Repair, in Decay, and worn out.

Being asked, Whether it was in such Decay, that it had better be rebuilt than repaired ? they said, It might be kept up and tied together for some Time, but would not support an additional Building — That it stands on Eight Columns, the Sixoutfide Columns have been decayed at Bottom, and cut off, and are pieced about Four Feet — that they are very much twisted out of an Upright — That the Brest-summer upon the Columns is rotten, and the Gutter Plates that come into this Brest-summer, are fwagged round several Inches, and tied together with Iron; and the main Tye that should have went across, was (topped short upon the Two Center Columns, which has occasioned the Rafters to thrust out the Side Brest-summers — That the Rafters are very much fwagged, and the Tiling lays hollow and round; and that it will be needless to repair it — That it would be unreasonable to think of repairing it, by Reason the Expence would be very great, and it would be a very old Building when done — That they think it would be best to rebuild it, and most for the Interest of the County: — And added, That it would be Money thrown away, to make any material Alterations by Repair.

Mr. Hillyer, being crols examined, said, That he has practised as a Surveyor about 14 or 15 Years, and was bred to the Business — That he was Surveyor to the Margate Public Assembly Room, and all the Build* ing in that Square, except those Sir Edward Hales was building.

Being asked, Whether be was Surveyor only, or the Designer of that Building ? — he said, The Foundation of that Building was dug by some Carpenters — That he

was down there surveying a job for Mr. Bull — That the Proprietor of that Room came and allied his Advice, in Regard to the Cost of that Building — -That he gave his Advice, and made several Alterations in the Plan, and was Chose Surveyor

Being asked, If from his View Of the Shire Hall, lie knows how long it is since it was repaired ? — he said. He should suppose, by the State it is in, many Years — That the Nisi Prius Court has been built since the Assize House, and One Side is supposed to be in the same Decay as the rest of the Building- — That, in examining the Nisi Print Court, he did not rip off the Plaister to search the Timbers; but that there is a Break of Six Foot, in which the Timbers appear in the same State of Decay as the rest of the Building — That the Dimensions of the Nisi Prius Court are Thirty-one Feet by Twenty -seven Feet Six Inches — That he did not measure the Height of it — That the Inside is Twenty-four Inches by Twenty-eight Inches, and the Crown Court is Twenty-six Inches by Twenty-four Inches, or thereabouts — That he did not examine the Repairs of the Inside of the Crown Court, neither did he calculate the Expenreof putting this in Repair; but calculated the Expence of taking it down.

Being asked, How long it would last and serve sufficient for the Purposes it was now used, with a complete Repair ? — he said. If it was thoroughly repaired, it would last 50 or 100 Years, but by thoroughly repairing, he meant rebuilding it — That the Columns might last some Years with proper Security — That he was first called upon to survey this in June or last, and was employed by Mr. — That when be

took that Survey, it was to examine into the State of the Repairs of the Shire Hall; and that he surveyed it Five or Six Times afterwards — That he went down with a Plan to the Quarter Sessions to attend a Committee, and then surveyed it for his own Satisfaction every Time — That he was not paid for the Plan, but presumes he shall — That he carried those Plans to Lord Rockford, and by his Order carried them down to the County; and when he was with the Gentlemen at the Quarter Sessions, after he was approved on as Surveyor, he told them, that if the Building went on, and he was continued Surveyor, at Five per Cent., the Expence of the Plans were included.

Mr. Robinson and Mr. Mills, both informed your Committee, that they are not any ways concerned or interested in the carrying on this Business.

Mr. Robinson said. That he took this Survey last Wednesday, and never took any before.

Being asked, When he went down upon this Survey, what Directions he had with Regard to taking it; and what he apprehended was the Object of it ? — he said, He went down to take a Survey of the Foundation of the new and old Gaol — That when he was at Chelmsford, Mr. Hillyer desired he would examine the Shire House; which he did — He likewise told him, There was a new Shire House intended to be built upon Part of the Premises; but did not desire him to give his Opinion upon the Valuation of the Repairs of the old Shire House.

Mr. Mills, being further examined, said, He went down the Day before Mr. Robinson; and the same Evidence he has now given, he gives.

Mr. Francis Smylhics, Deputy Clerk of the Peace for the County of EJJ'ex, being examined, said, That he had attended almost every Session and Assizes for these Ten Years — That he has known very great Inconveniences arise from the Situation of the Crown Court — That being an open Court, and a very great Traffic of Coaches and other Carriages passing so near, he has known the Business of the Court frequently interrupted and delayed, from the Noise that has been made by Carriages and other Traffic; and besides, it is much too small for the Business of the County.

Beingafked, How near the Corner of the Court House,

all

e

11 Geo. III.

66

all the Carriages, Coaches, Beasts, that dome from Braintree, Booking, Norfolk, Suffolk, &c. pass? — he said. He could not speak as to exact Admeasurement, because he never surveyed it, but they come extremely near, and there is nothing to defend their coming immediately close up to the Piazza of the Court House — That he supposes, the High Road from the Corner of the Court House to the Shops, on the other Side of the Road, to be about Fifteen Feet wide, and believes Two Carriages cannot pass abreast by the Court House: That, in his Judgment, the Nisi Prim Court is too small for holding either the Quarter Sessions or the Assizes — and he has frequently found Inconvenience arising therefrom, both at the Quarter Sessions and Assizes — and that, at the Summer Assizes, by Reason of its being so small, he apprehends it to be extremely unwholesome for the Number of People that resort there — That when the Special Jury or Common Jury have been fitting in the Niff Prius Court, he has known frequent Interruptions in passing through the Midst of that Jury, by Reason of the Avenue being stopt up intirely on One Side of the Court — and that there is no Room in that Assize House, or any Place in which the Grand Jury, doing the Business of the County, can retire to; nor any in the Grown Court.

Being asked. How far the Crown Court is situate from the Gaol ? — he said. The Court House is at One End of the Town, and the Gaol at the other Extremity — That he has frequently seen the Criminal Prisoners brought all together upon a Chain through the Town to the Court House — That at the Time of the Assizes, they are taken up in the Morning to the Court House, they are together put into a small Box and kept till Dinner Time, unless they take their Trials before j and at Dinner Time they are taken back again to the Gaol, and brought up again after Dinner, and taken back again in the Evening — The Prisoners are put promiscuously into this Box — And that he has seen a Clergyman in his Gown and Caffock, against whom no Bill has been found, Handing the re in the Midst of a Number of Felons — That he has heard the Shire House is intended to be built, where feme Houses now stand, near or adjoining to the Church Yard in Chelmsford — And that if it is built there, it will be farther from the present Gaol than it is now, by about Fifty Yards.

Being asked. Whether he himself personally ' heard the Judges complain, that they had felt any Inconvenience ? he said, He never heard any Judge make any Complaint — But has known the Judges of Assize flop Coun-fel and Witnesses, because they could not hear while Carriages were passing by.

Being asked, Whether he ever heard the Judges themselves express a Desire for the Removal of the Shire House ? — be said, He never had the Honour of any Conversation with the Judges — That during the Assizes, he never heard the Judges make any Complaint of the incommodious Situation of the Place.

Being asked, Whether the Inconvenience arising from Carriages going by, proceeds from the Court being an open Court, or from the Situation alone ? — he said, He apprehended the Inconveniences* arose in feme Measure from both — That he believed the doling up of the Court would in feme Measure remedy the Inconvenience arising from the Noise of the Carriages, but would in many other Respects make it still more inconvenient.

Being asked. Whether it would sufficiently remove the Inconvenience of the Noise of the Carriages ? — lie laid, He could not certainly tell — That the Niff Prius Court is a very close Court -, and in Summer Time the Heat thereof is almoftinsupportable to every one that has any Business to do.

Being asked. Whether he had heard the Judges in that Court flop Witnesses and Counsel from any Noise being in the Street ? — he said. He believed he had known the Business of that Court interrupted by Noise of Carriages, but not in l'o great a Degree as the other Vol. 33.

Being asked, In what other Respects doling up the Crown Court would be more inconvenient ? — he said.

He apprehended it would make it more confined, and less capable of receiving the great Number of People that always resort to that Court.

Being asked. Whether he had been acquainted with the Tran fad ions of the justices in Quarter Sessions, or in Committees relative to the Building of a Gaol ? — he laid. He had attended every Quarter Sessions for Five or Six Years pad, and many of their Committees appointed to consider of repairing or rebuilding the Gaol; and consequently had been acquainted with most of their Proceedings: That he did not know that they ever made any Application to Parliament, before this, for rebuilding the Shire Hall.

Being a(ke<j. Whether any Application had been made to him at any Time by any of the Petitioners against this Bill, or their Agents, for Copies of any Orders made relative to this Application to Parliament, and the Purposes of it i — he said. There never had been any Application made to him since he was appointed Deputy Clerk of the Peace; — but said, he received a Letter some Time ago, long before he had any of the Records particularly in his Custody or any Power over the fame, from Mr. John Griffith-, the Purport of which, to the best of his Recollection was, to desire him to ask Mr. Ennewto fend him (Mr. Griffith) a Copy of the Order of Sessions relative to an Application to Parliament, and to give him Notice of the Time of presenting any Petition.

Being asked. Whether Mr. did, or did not, in

that Letter, t.ell him that the Application was on Behalf of those who intended to petition against the Bill ? — he said. He did not recoiled: whether he particularly did or not, but he understood it so.

Being asked what Answer he sent ? — he said. He really could not tell whether he sent any Answer or not; but he acquainted Mr. Ennew with the Purport of it, for, it required no Answer from him: — That he did not know whether Mr. Emiezv sent any Answer, but believed the Copy of the Order wa,s never sent: — That he thought the Shire Hall was inconveniently situated, by being so far from the Gaol.

Being asked, Whether it would be better for the Prisoners to come immediately from a Gaol into a Shire House or not ? — he said. He imagined that either Extreme would be better to be avoided, of a Gaol being too far from, or too near to, a Shire Flail: — That the Road that runs by the Shire Hall is gravelled; and from what he recolledts of the Two Courts, he does not know which is nearest the Road.

John Strutti Esquire, (One of the Justices of the Peace for the County of Effiex) being examined, laid. That he knows the Situation of the Shire House in but not the exact Size: — That he thinks the Situation very inconvenient, and the Size not large enough for the Business of the County: — That attending as a Magistrate, he had frequently known the Business stopt for feme Time by the Noise of Carriages and Droves of Cattle passing in the Road near the Shire House: — That the Grand Jury are obliged to leave the Court, and adjourn to a Public House, having no Room to retire to.

Being cross-examined, he said, He had acted as a Justi’ce of the Peace, for the County of Effiex, Ten or Twelve Years, and did not recollect any Application to Parliament,.before this, for removing the Inconveniences complained of; but knew it had been the Wiflr ?f,many Gentlemen, that the Inconveniences mentioned 1

might be removed: — That he never attended the Assizes at any other Place in England.

Being asked, Whether he thought that the Courts were big enough to contain those that attended upon mere Business ? — he said. It was a Matter he could not answer, but knew that the Grand Jury were frequently incommoded by the Crowd of People attending in and near the Sessions House: — That he never heard the Judges personally make any Complaint of the Situation of the Court House: — That he thought the Inconveniences arising from the Situation and Smallness of the Shire House so great, as to make it necessary to pull down the present Court House, and to build a new one j and added, that he never heard any Methods proposed to remove these Inconveniences without pulling it down.

Mr. Christopher Griffienhoofe, a Surgeon and Apothecary at Chelmsford, being examined, said, That he has lived there Forty Years and upwards, and is acquainted with the Road between the Court House in Chelmsford and the Houses on the opposite Side: — That he has heard of many Accidents, which have happened in or near the same: — That he was sent for to one Gentleman, who was overturned in a Whiskey, Major Barry S' Leger, and apprehended that Accident happened by the Narrowness of the Road: — That he never was sent for ,to any other Person that happened any Accident thereThat to his Knowledge there has been no Alteration made in that Part of the Road since the Accident he mentioned happened: and thinks, if the Road had been made wider he should have known it.

Being cross-examined, he said. That the Accident, he had mentioned, happened in January 1769, between One and Two o’Clock in the Day-time :~*-That that Part of the Road, in his Opinion, is a narrow and dangerous Road,

Being asked. Whether that Road could be made wider, otherwise than by pulling down the Shire Hall ? — he said. It might, by pulling down the Sheds opposite, and Part of a Dwelling House adjoining to the Sheds.

Being asked, Whether he ever surveyed this Spot with an Intention to form any Opinion as to widening the Road ? — he said, That since the Matter has been in Debate, he had surveyed it and stept it: — That the Measure of it is about Fifteen Feet or Fifteen Feet and a Half; but never took any exact Measure of it: — That it is a hollow Road; and he does not believe it can be widened without pulling down Part of a House.

SIR,

" As I promised to give an Answer to the Questions " you asked me on Wednesday last, at the Desire of the " Committee appointed to rebuild the Gaol for the " County of Essex, Whether I would fell the Bell Inn, " in Chelmsford, for the Purpose of building upon those " Premises a County Gaol; and, if I would, what would be my Terms? In answer, I beg you will acquaint the " Gentlemen of the Committee, that I have no Desire " to fell any Part of my Property in the County of " Essex-, but if it be deemed of Utility to the County, " I shall then be glad to oblige the Gentlemen concerned, by felling the Bell Inn, which is now in Lease " to a good Tenant for Twenty-one Years, from " F>ay 1764, and consequently the present Lease will " not expire till Lady Day 1785; It is now let only for £ 3° Per Annum to the pretent Tenant, upon Account of his having laid out a considerable Sum of 4‘ Money towards the Repairing the said Premises, but was formerly let for £. 40 per AnnumIf therelore, under these Circumstances, the Gentlemen are " desirous of purchasing my Interest, subject to that " Lease, I will part with it for the Sum of One thousand Guineas; but for the Purpose of building a Gaol only, and not to be applied to any other Use: The " Premises are Freehold, except ihc Hog Pens in the " Front of the House, which are Copyhold, and held <* of Sir William Mildmay, Baronet. I must beg to be " favoured with an Answer as soon as you conveniently can.

" I am, Sir,

" Your humble Servant,

" Rich. Tyson."

To the worshipful the Justices assembled at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace at Chelmsford.

Gentlemen,

By an Order of this Court, dated Tuesday the Eleventh Day of July 1769, I was directed to survey the Estate belonging to Dr. Richard Tyson, called the Inn, ia

Chelmsford, in order to fee whether the same would be convenient for erecting a large and commodious Gaol thereon, in as cheap a Manner as on the Ground where the old Gaol now (lands, with the adjoining Premises lately proposed to be added thereto; and also to survey the Ground belonging to Sir William Mildmay, Baronet, called Brick Field, in Chelmsford, in like Manner, for the" same Purpose; and prepare Estimates thereof; and deliver the fame, and report my Opinion thereon; at the next General Quarter Sessions of the Peace*

In consequence of the said Order; I have surveyed and examined the Premises; and I find the Expence of the Foundation will be the same in each of the Three Places mentioned in the Order.

H avingcaufed the Ground to be opened where the old Gaol now (lands, and the adjoining Premises proposed to be added thereto, in Seven different Parts, 1 found, at the Depth of about Five Feet, a Stratum of good hard Gravel, mixed with a small Portion of Loam.

I likewise caused the Ground to* be opened at the Brick Field, where I found a fine Bed of hard Gravel; and there is no room to doubt of there being a very good Foundation at the Bell Inn; but as the Tenant refused to let his Ground be dug, I could not have it opened as I did the other Places.

I have estimated the Value of the different Premises to be purchased, which are as follows; viz.

1" The Be//Inn.

The Ground belonging to the Bell Inn is very extensive, but its Shape is inconvenient for the Purpose of eroding a large and commodious Gaol; it extends from the Front next the Market, about 670 Feet in Length to the River, and does not exceed 82 Feet in Breadth, except in that Part next the River, where at the Time of Floods the Water overflows.

This narrow Form mull create unavoidable Inconveniences in the Construction of a Building which requires the freed Communication to its several Parts, at the same Time that the different Sorts of Prisoners, Debtors and Felons, Men and Women, should be kept entirely separate; but as the Entrance to the Gaol, if eroded on this Spot, must be in the narrowed Side or End of the Building, the Parts next such Entrance mull necessarily, in some Measure, be Passages tothofe which are more distant; whereas, if the Plan was more, extended in Breadth, the Entrance, by being more central to the whole Building, would open a much freer Communication to all its several Parts,

Therefore, I am of Opinion, that the Estate of Dr. Richard Tyson, called the Bell Inn, is not so convenient fur eroding thereon a large and commodious Gaol, as a

Piece

ii Geo. III. 6°

Piece of Ground where the Plan might be more extended in Breadth; and, as the Whole of theie Premises must be purchased, it appears by the foregoing Estimate, that it cannot be erected so cheap upon this Spot, as upon that on which the present Gaol now stands, together with the adjoining Premises proposed to be added thereto.

The Ground belonging to Sir William Baro-

net, called Brick Field, in Chelmsford, is an extensive Field, any Part of which would be convenient for the Purpose of erecting a large and commodious Gaol, with all its Appurtenances, which might be built on this Spot, as appears by the foregoing Estimate, much cheaper than on either of the other Two Places.

All which 1 beg leave to l'ubmit to this worshipful Court.

And the Witness being asked, Whether, in pursuance of the Orders of the Quarter Sessions, Advertisements had been inserted in the public Newspapers ? — he said.

were made publicly in the Court of Quarter Sessions---

That he attended the Committee of the House of Commons in 1769, as prosecuting a Petition from the Borough of CoLchester, against the Bill for rebuilding the Gaol at Chelmsford.

Being asked, Whether it was an Agreement, that there should be a County Meeting called, and that the High Sheriff should publish an Advertisement for that Purpose ? — he said, He did not know that there was any such Agreement entered into; but had heard there was same such Conversation between Sir Anthony and Daniel Matthew, Esquire, who was then High Sheriff — That there was no County Meeting advertised for, or called, before the last Act passed.

And the Witness said. That this Letter was communicated to the Justices; but believed nothing was done in consequence of it — That he had attended every Quarter Sessions for these Five Years past; but did not remember what the Bench said when this Answer was delivered to them.

Being asked. Whether, upon that Answer being lent, there was any other Surveyor appointed ? — he said. There has been another Surveyor appointed since, but not in consequence of that Answer, to the best of his Knowledge and Belief — That he never heard any Reason given why another Surveyor was appointed.

Being asked. Whether there was another Surveyor appointed the same Sessions ? — he laid, he believed not; but desired Leave to refer to the Order of Sessions.

Being crols-examined, he said, he did not attend at every Committee of the Justices relative to this Business, since it commenced — That he attended for Mr. Ennew, who was then Deputy Clerk of the Peace — That there were no Books kept for entering the Proceedings of the Committee; but that the Accounts of the Business there done, was taken down in Writing — That he did not know whether Mr. Rawlins made any Report or not — And that he could not tell whether he was present at the Meeting when Mr. Ra attended, without re-

ferring to the Entries of the Committees — He said, he is acquainted with the Hand Writing of every Gentleman who signed the Resolution of the Committee held at Chelmsford, in January 1768, having frequently leen

Whereas the common Gapl of the County of Essex, situate at Chelmsford in the said County, is in a very unwholesome, obnoxious, and inconvenient Place, and is too small, and being a Very ancient Building, and greatly gone to Decay, is so incapable of being repaired) that it is necessary a new Gaol should be built.

Hereupon your Petitioners cannot forbear expressing their Surprize, that such Allegations, relating to the Place on which such Gaol now stands, should be inserted in the Preamble of the Bill, being Matters not complained of, nor contained in the Prayer of your Petition j and as the Surveyor above appointed has not yet made any Report of his Survey of the present Spot; and we being totally unapprifed that such Objections to the Situation of the old Gaol were intended to be thus previously alledged, the Truth of which might have been invalidated by the Evidence of Fadts and Experience, if due Notice had been given; and conceiving ourselves materially interested in the Event, as most likely to be first affected by any Annoyance that may happen by altering the Situation of the said Gaol; we do therefore now most humbly beg Leave to repre-l'ent, and doubt not but we shall be able to prove, that the present Situation of the old Gaol, adjoining to the wide, deep, and running Stream of a large River, is the most proper Place for a Gaol, with Regard to Health, Conveniency.and Safety, the three essential Points Chiefly to be considered in erecting any Building for that Purpose. And We cannot but remark, that a very recent Instance of the confined Felons conspiring, and attempting to set the Gaol on Fire, in order to make their Escape, was prevented by the Means of so 'much Water being near at Hand, which is almost evident Proof of the Utility of such a Situation.

And your Petitioners beg Leave further to observe, that in and by the said printed Bill, such general and extensive Powers are proposed to be vested in the Justices of the Peace, to compel the Sale of Property for the Purpost of building a Gaol, that, wfere it not for the Confidence we repole in the Wisdom and Justice of this Court, might create an Alarm of a most threatening Danger to our common Liberties, since such cornpulfory Powers thereby proposed, without Exception or Restrictions, might authorize the building of the Gaol in any "Place detrimental to private Property, and even in our ^public Market Place, to the Annoyance of its Neighbourhood, and in prejudice to the Rights, Franchises, ’and Emoluments, this Town is entitled to enjoy, and has Time out of Mind enjoyed, of holding a Market once in every Week, and of keeping Fairs at certain allotted Times in the Year, in the said common Market Place, to which the Inhabitants of the adjoining County resort, for the Sale or Purchase of Proyilioris and other Necessaries of Life, and whereby the Tradesmen in the Town, and the Farmers in its Neighbourhood, gain a mutual Benefit for the Support of themselves and their Families, in the general Intercourse of Commerce and Dealing with one another; But should a Gaol be built at or near the Place of so common a Resort, it might deter People from coming to our Market, for Fear of the many malignant and pestilential Distempers which the unhappy Wretches under so close‘a Confinement ate liable ufito. And we are' sorry to find, that the Proposel and Re-cofnmendation that has lately been publicly offered, for building the 'Gaol in this Market Pl^cep has already . infused alarming Apprehensions into the Minds1 bf many People. ''; ‘ j""1- 1

Your Petitioners therefore most humbly pray for the Concurrence of this Court, in making timely Application to the Committee of file House of Commons, to whom the said Bill is' referred, for procuring such - VoL; 33.

Amendment to the said Preamble as may be consistent to the Resolutions of the last General Quarter Sessions, and the Prayer of your Petition, in order that we may not be precluded or restrained, by any implied Construe-tion of the above recited Allegations, from proving, that the Place whereon the present Gaol is situated is neither unwholesome, obnoxious, or inconvenient. And as to the Objection that has been urged) of the present Building being too small, it is obviated, by the voluntary Offers made) by the Proprietors of the Houses and Lands next adjoining, to fell their Premises, to be disposed or made use of towards the Enlargement of the Place, for the Erection of a more spacious Building; Or, in case any material Objection, not yet suggested, should arise to its present Situation, we humbly hope no other will be fixed upon, that may any ways annoy the Health and Safety of the Inhabitants, or be prejudicial to their Market, and to the Rights, Franchises, and Emoluments appertaining thereto. And your Petitioners shall ever pray, (ffc.

The humble Representation of the Inhabitants of the Town of Chelmsford, whose Names are hereunto subscribed.

We the Inhabitants of the Town of Chelmsford, cannot forbear expressing our great Surprize, as well as deep Concern, at the many Attempts that have been often made, and are now repeated, towards removing the County Gaol from the River, and rebuilding it in the Town, adjoining to the Market Place; which Situation for a Gaol, we have frequently and earnestly remonstrated, would prove an Annoyance to our Market, offensive to the People resorting thereto, and prejudicial to the Inhabitants, and the principal Part of this Town.

We had great Reason to hope, when the Legislature had passed an Act, the last Sessions of Parliament, to authorize the Building a new Gaol, on the Ground adjoining to, and communicating with, the old one, that all former Contests about the Situation would have been finally terminated, and Peace and Tranquillity restored to our Town and its Neighbourhood; but bn the contrary, after all the Trouble and Expence that has been created to ourselves and the County; after all the Rea-fons and Arguments which have been offered, and attended to with Candour and Impartiality, by the honourable the House of Commons; after the fullest Evidence given by the most eminent Surveyors in Favour of the old Place, as preferable to any other in or near the Town; and even after the Law above mentioned had been passed, to fix the Gaol on its former Foundation; we are fprry to find, that, notwithstanding all these Circumftinces, a Committee of Justices, appointed foconsider of an.Explanation and Amendment of some inaccurate Clauses in the above Act, have agreed, by ' a Majority of One Vote only, to propose t6 this Court, to make another Application to Parliament, to repeal and annul the very Law, which, but a few1 Months before, had been passed upon a former Application from this Court. '

Our Concern' has yet been farther increased, upon hearing, that they not only propose removing the Gaol to the Market Place, but pulling down and.destroying the White Horse Inn, a large, convenient, and well accustomed Inti, situate on the East Side of the Market, in order tp give Place to a Gaol to be built in the room of it — Herice we must beg Leave to suggest, that as Markets are necessary for the Sale the common Provisions bf Life, so Inns near the Market are necessary, for the Reception and Accommodation of those who deal-in the Sale of those Provisions: and to this Purpose, we cannot but take Notice, that the said White Horse Inn, now proposed to be demolished, is of great Convenience to the Farmers, Millers, and others, coming to fell or buy the several Sorts of Co'rn and Grain; to Which Inn, accordingly, great Numbers resort, and dine every Market Day, it being the if Place of Rendezvous, whefe, at appointed Times, they- are to be found, and where they finish the Bargain, they agree for in open Market; should such a respectable Body of Men be driven from this Place of Accommodation, we are fearful they may look out for other Markets, to the Diminution of this, and to the Prejudice of the Town in general: And, with respect to trltefe Premises themselves, belonging to the Whitt being im-

proper for the Construction of such Gaol; We appeal to the Testimony of the Surveyor appointed by this Court to examine them; as we are informed, that the Grounds Containing the Back Yard1, Garden, and Bowling Green, are top small, and the Soil 'too('fWatiipy, for the Erection of a sufficient, strong,. and ample'Edifice; and no good Water to be procured, but through Pipes from a Distance, if any can be procured it all; for we

w O ' J 1 . '

confide in the Protection of the Law, that none will be taken from the Springs that now help to fill the Reservoir of Water, from which the Town has by Prescription the (ole Right of being supplied.

Lajlly, We most humbly submit to your Consideration, as the Guardians and Trustees of the County Revenues, the Expences which will be created by thus pulling down old, and erecting new. Buildings, and purchasing the Grounds sufficient for such Purposes, which must be paid by Rates levied on the Land-owners of this County; and how greatly must these Rates be augmented, from the additional Expences incurred by the many Disputes and Oppositions instigated on this Occasion ? We, the Inhabitants of this Town, have already expended large Sums, raised by our Voluntary Contributions, to avoid the Nuisances as above; the County in general must pay considerably more, to defray the additional Expences of these renewed Disputes; hence the Freeholders at large, on whom such encreased Rates must be levied, will become interested in the Event; On their Behalf therefore, as well as of ourselves, we humbly entreat the Interposition of this Court, to oppose any Application to Parliament, for altering the Situation of the Gaol, from the Place whereon it is now by Law authorized to be rebuilt.

Being asked, Whether, at that Quarter Session, when he attended by Order, he did or did not offer to give his Opinion with regard to the Propriety of the Situ* ation of the old Gaol, in preference to any other Situation ? — he answered, That upon the Subject of-draining the Gaol, he remembered that he said. He was going to compare it with the old Spot, but was told, by l'ome of the Gentlemen upon the Bench, that he need not say any thing with regard to the old Spot, or something . to that Effect.

Being asked, Whether, if he had not been stopt, he intended to have given his Opinion on the Preference - of the Situation of the old Gaol ? — he said, He meant . only at that Time to have spoke what occurred to him, with respect to the Comparison of draining the one Place and the other, and should have only said, that the Circumstance of the River being so near the old Gaol, would have been the Means of the Gaol being drained and kept clean.

Being asked. Whether he was ever examined at any other Time, touching the Propriety of the Situation of the old. Gaol ? — he laid. He was, at a Committee of the House of Commons last Session, when the Bill was depending for rebuilding Chelmsford Gaol — That the Opinion he gave at that Time, with regard to the Propriety of the Scite of the old Gaol, was, that it was the Place which he should prefer — and that he was of the same Opinion now.

Being asked, the Grounds of his Opinion ? — he said. The principal Advantage which that Place appeared to him to have, over all others, wa6 the Nearness of a very deep River, which would be a Means of carrying away all Manner of Filth, and which, he apprehended, was of great Consequence to a Building of that Nature — That the Ground is situated in a Manner out of the Town, distant at least from the principal Part of the Town, and would therefore be of less Annoyance to the Inhabitants and, with the Addition of very small Pieces of Ground, it would become a very large and commodious Spot; wanting only in Breadth a very little, in its present Form — That close to it there is a very copious Spring, by which he thought the Gaol might be supplied plentifully with Water.

Being asked. Whether he had ever formed any Plan for building a Gaol upon this Scite ? — he said, He had, which he produced to your Committee — That he proposed, by his Plan, to new build Part of the Gaol upon the new purchased Ground; and when the new built Part was fit, to remove the Prisoners into it, and afterwards go on in pulling down the old Part, and finishing the whole Building — That he had made an Estimate of the Expence of building it, which he believed was £.8,000.

Being asked. What he estimated the Purchases necessary at ? — he said, £.496 — That he examined the Scite of the White Horse Inn, the first Time he went down; but. said, It was so long since, be could not (peak particularly to it.

Being asked, Whether a Gaol to be built upon that Ground, with the Purchase of the Ground, would not cofl a great deal more than the Gaol on the Plan he had proposed ? he answered. That he imagined the Purchase of the Ground would be more; but as to the Building, it would depend upon the Plan — That he had seen the Plan of a Gaol produced by Mr. , as recom-

mended by Lord Rochford; and from the short View he had of it, he imagined, as it was much more extended, it would undoubtedly cost much more than the Plan he produced — That he thought there could not be any great Difference between the Two Spots, with respect to Health; and added, that Experience had shewn the old Spot was very healthy — That the Gaol

being removed to the White Horse Inn, would be bringing it up to the principal Part of the Town, the Market Place.

Being cross-examined; he said, That the Nature of the Soil on the old Spot is a strong loomy Gravel, about Five or Six Feet deep from the Surface; and was of Opinion, it would not be necessary to pile for the Foundation of a Gaol there; for by giving proper'Footings to the Walls, he thought that Soil would be a very good Foundation; and added. That the Expence of making proper Footings was very inconsiderable — That he is not acquainted with the Soil at the White Horse Inn.

Being asked. Whether he was not one Time of Opinion, that some Piling would be necessary ? — he said. He had not had the Ground opened at first, therefore could not judge whether it would be necessary — but that having seen the Soil, he was always of Opinion, it would make a good Foundation without Piling — Thdt he was not present himself when it was opened, and had only Samples of the Earth, produced by the Person who dug it.

Being asked. Whether he saw this Spot after the Holes were opened ? — he said, He did not; and that if it was left entirely to him to build a Gaol in or about Chelmsford, he should prefer the old Spot.

Being asked. Whether the Stratum of loomy Gravel was observed by himself, or reported to him by those who bored it ? — he answered. By those who bored it; and that he had Samples of it brought by the same Person — and from this, he had made his Calculation of the Foundation, and the Propriety of building the Gaol there — That he did not taste the Water of the Spring he mentioned — That it was a Pump, but did not know bow deep the Spring lay that supplied it, nor what Quantity of Water that Well would bold — That he did not make any Observation how high, in Floods, the Water flowed from the River to the Gaol — That if the new Gaol was raised to a proper Height, It would not prevent the Facility of draining — And that he would raise it about Three or Four Feet — But that Three Feet worild be enough — And that he imagined, there would not be any Occasion to raise the new Gaol that Height at the White Horse, for the Sake of draining it — That to the best of his Opinion, the Surface Pf the present Gaol, from the Surface of the Water, when he surveyed it, was about Two Feet — That the Floor of the present Gaol is below the Highway; but that hfe could not pretend to say how many Feet, as he never considered the Level with respect to the Road; neither did he dig, bore, or try, the Ground at the White Horse Inn, which is very near the Conduit at ’, and

may be easily supplied with Water from thence — That it will be proper to build the Gaol with Bricks — That he does not know the exact Price, but has heard they are 2 2 s.a Thousand; and does not know the Price of Cartage — And that, if there should be Brick Earth found at the White Horse Inn, so as to make a sufficient Quantity of Bricks to build a new1 Gaol, it would certainly be a great Saving.
