Mr. Robert Baldwyn, a Surveyor and Architect, being examined, said. That he had been concerned in building the Earl of Egremont's, the Earl of the Duke

of York's, and the Earl of Leicester'% Houses, and many other Things of less Consequence — That he had like-wife been Deputy Surveyor of Black Friars Bridge — and that he was concerned, and had the ordering all the Foundations of the Piers and Abutments of that Bridge, except One of the middle Piers, that was built before he had any Concern with the Bridge.

Being *fked, Whether he at any Time engaged with Mr. Dance ? — he answered, Yes, next June will be Three Years — That since he engaged with him, he had been concerned in every Building Mr. Dance had been engaged in — That he was now engaged in building Newgate — That he knows Chelmsford — That the First Time he went there was the 18th of February 1769, when he went down with Mr. Dance, to survey several Spots of Ground, in order to fee which was pro-pereft for eretting a Gaol on — That the Places he then viewed, were The Swan, The Dolphin, Mr. s.

The Bell, Two Fields belonging to Mr. and an Orchard opposite the Workhouse — That he likewise looked at the White Horse Premises, but was acquainted they were not to be purchased; the Gentleman to whom they belonged being not of Age, and therefore took but a very flight Survey of them-r-That, ;upon that Survey, he never drew up any Report.

Being asked, Whether he was at any Time examined, touching the Opinion he formed upon that Survey ? — he said. Yes, about Midsummer 1769, at the Quarter Sessions; and was asked several Questions by most of the Gentlemen then on the Bench.

Being asked. Whether he was examined as to the Propriety of the Situation of the present Gaol ? — he said. He believed the Whole of the Questions then asked him, were entirely confined to that and nothing else; and was of Opinion, that, with the Purchases of Grounds and Houses adjoining the old Gaol, it would be preferable to any of the other Places he had been shewn — That since that Time, he had taken a particular Survey of the Scite of the Whi Horse Inn, and of the Scite of the present Gaol — had made different Plans; One with only purchasing the Premises belonging to the Executors of Mr. Pocklington — The other Two Designs comprehend purchasing Mr. s, Mr.

Wade's, Mr. Ricket's, and Sir William Premises, as well as those of Mr. — and that

he apprehended either of the Three Designs sufficient for a County Gaol for Essex.

He then produced to your Committee Three Plans.

And being shewn One of them, and asked, Whether, in the executing that Plan, he proposed building and finishing the new Gaol before he meddled with the old one, or in what Way he proposed to execute it ? — he said, He intended to build that Part of the Gaol intended to be inhabited by the Keeper, the Wards for the Felons, the Wards for the Debtors, and to have inclosed both the Felons and Debtors Courts — That there would then remain the Debtors Hall, One of the Debtors Wards, Two Staircases, and the , Turnkey’s Room, unbuilt — That, when the Two Courts, and Wards for Felons and Debtors, were built, and fit to be inhabited, after the Prisoners in the present Gaol were removed into that of the new one, he then intended to take down the present Gaol, together with the Houses in Front next the Road, and make use of the Materials in the remaining Part of the Building unbuilt.

And being asked. What would be the Expence of the Gaol, built by that Plan, with the Purchases necessary to be made for that Purpose, taking in the Advantage or Value of what the old Materials used or sold would amount to ? — he said, Supposing the Building to have Stone Fronts next the Road and River, it would then cost about £. 8,740, including the Purchases; which

Purchases would amount to the Sum of 539. 8 besides the Gratuity for quitting a Lease, which he imagines will be 15 or £. 16 — That a Gaol built in the Manner he now represented would hold from 30 to 40 Felons; and might, upon an Emergency, hold 10 more — That it will hold also from 50 to 60 Debtors; and may be extended to hold 60 Felons.

Being asked, Whether he had considered the Exten-fion of the Plan for that Purpose ? — he said. He had considered a larger Plan of a Gaol, supposing it to be built One Story in Height only, by which Means the Areas or Courts of the Gaol would admit to be larger than those of a Gaol of Two Stories in Height: Which he produced to your Committee.

And being asked, Whether this Plan would require more Purchases ? — he said, None, except that Piece of Sir William Mildmay's, which was necessiiry to be taken in in this Plan, but might be omitted in the others.

Being asked, What would be the Difference of the Felons Wards, between this and the Plan N° 2, as to the Numbers they would hold ? — he said. There is One Ward more, and Nine Cells — and that this will hold Threescore Felons, or more: That the Expence of executing this Pian, including Purchases, will be about £. 9,670.

That the Front of the present Gaol is close to the Road.

That he never was in the Gaol.

Being asked, Whether the Circumstance of such a River flowing by the Gaol, is not of any, and what Utility, in respect to cleansing the Gaol, and making it wholesome, in any and what Degree, and supplying it with Water ? — he said. That in general, where there is a living Stream or flowing Water, it is looked upon as a wholesome Situation — That the River Can, which flows by the Gaol, when in Motion, must be attended with the same Conveniences he had before referred to, and supplying it with Water — And that, in his Opinion, it would contribute to the Health of the Prisoners; for when the Water was in Motion, it would be a Means of preventing Stagnation of the Air — And believed the Width of this River, by the Side of the Gaol, to be about 30 Feet.

Being cross-examined, he said, That no Part of the River Chelmer runs near the Gaol; and that, at the Time he l'urveyed the River Chelmer for a Navigation, he did not l'urvey the River Can — That Moulsham Mill is supplied by the Chelmer and the Can.

And the Witqefs said. That there certainly is not so proper a Place for building a Gaol in or about -

ford, because the same Advantages cannot be had upon any other Spot — That it is One very great Advantage for a Gaol to stand at a great Distance from the Courts of Justice j because, if any epidemic Fever should be in the Gaol, the Air will blow off the infectious Particles, and bring them more safe and sweet into the Courts — For there are many fatal Examples now upon Record, of the Prisoners being immediately brought from a Place of Confinement into Courts of Justice 1 — That he alludes to many Places, and the Bailey in particular — That the White tiorfe Inn stands in the principal Part of the Market — and he thinks the Sciteof that Inn, or the Grounds belonging to it, is a very improper Situation for a Gaol; for its being in the principal Part of the Market will certainly spoil that Market} for an infectious Gaol Fever happening the re, would terrify and drive the Farmers to other Market Towns — That his Business calls him daily among those Farmers, Who are at this Time in the greatest Fear and Consternation — That about 20 Years ago the malignant Small Pox came into the Town, and had such an Effect upon the Markets, that it destroyed them for some Time — The Markets for some Days were kept at the Red , a Quarter of a Mile out of the Town — Therefore, if the Small Pox had such an Effect upon the Farmers Minds, a Gaol Fever would have much more — That he does not think the Scite of the Inn is a whole -

some Place for erecting a Gaol upon, being surrounded with Houses and Buildings on every Side, except the East — That on the East of the White Premiers there is a Bowling Green, a Garden, and a flat Meadow; but he did not examine the Nature of the Soil on the East of the Bowling Green, but it is Meadow Land — That there are several stagnate Ditches next, or adjacent to the White llorfe Premises — That the Drains of all the upper Part of the East Side of the Town fall into those Ditches, which Ditches are ge^ nerally full of stagnate Mud — At this Time there is hardly a Foot of Water over the Surface of the Mud in any of them — -Some of them have from 3 Feet of Mud to 10 Feet — That he thinks those Ditches would certainly contribute to the Unhealthfulness of a Gaol at the Scue of the White Horse Inn, and obstruct the Drams from any Gaol built there — That a Gaol at tic White Horse Premises can be supplied with Water from no Place properly, but from the Conduit at Chelmsford, which must ruin the Town; for

which he gave Four following Reasons: First, the Current of Water that runs from the Conduit, runs through all the Yards of that Part of the Town that is called The Middle R, which forms the principal Part of the High Street, and all the Back Street; it carries away all the Filth from the Necell'aries, and other Filth belonging to their Houses, which Houses would not be habitable without the Convenience of that Water, the Current being so large, it carries off all this Filth without the least Inconvenience to the rest of the Inhabitants of the Town. — Secondly, It is so contrived at the Conduit, that the Inhabitants can turn it to every Street and every Part of the Town, by which Convenience the Town is kept perfectly clean all the Winter, and in hot dry WeatheF, in Summer, it is kept cool. — Thirdly, With respect to Fires, it is of the utmost Consequence, he having seen many Fires, since he had lived in that Town, quickly extinguished by that Water — That One Instance happened little more than a Year ago, of a very rapid Fire breaking out in the Wool Pack Inn Yard, which is in the very Middle of the Town — A Quantity of Mulch from the Common Dunghill, being laid across the Street, will, in a few Minutes, form a Pond of Water from Two to Three Feet deep, and supply any Demand from Three Engines, which was then the Cafe; for notwithstanding the Fire was very rapid, it was completely extinguished in little less than an Hour; without Which Convenience, the greatest Part of the Town would have been burnt down. — Fourthly, That he looks upon the Town of Chelmsford, in its present State, to be a remarkable healthy Town; and believes it is chiefly owing to that Current of Water running through the Middle of it; for the Town of Chelmsford lies very low; That Two Rivers run, One on each Side of it; and it is chiefly surrounded by low Meadows, and many stagnate Ditches; therefore the Exhalations from the Rivers, Meadows, and Ditches, must be very great, and would certainly form a large Body of stagnate Air in that large Street, which must soon be very unhealthy; but this Current of Water puts that Air in a continual Motion, and carries it off — That if Water is not brought from the Conduit to the White Horse Inn, he believes it can be brought from no other Place but Burgess , the Fountain Head of the Conduit at C; and what little waste Water may be found there will be quite inadequate to the Use of the Gaol — That the Fountain Head is near a Mile from the While , and the Water must be brought through the Grounds of John Wallingery Esquire, chiefly — Through One Field, belonging to Mil's , and another to

Mr. Jeph of Chelmsford — That a Gaol built on the White Horse Premises, would annoy and injure the Inhabitants of the Town in a very particular Manner,

11 Geo. III. 6° Mai. 393

ner, as a Gaol built there must be surrounded with very high Walls for the Security of the Prisoners; which high Walls, and the surrounding Building, must flop all free Circulation of Air; therefore the Air must be stagnant; and stagnant Air being often re-spired by the Number of Prisoners confined there, will soon become putrid, and of Course generate infectious and malignant Fevers; which must be exceeding dangerous, not only to the Inhabitants near it, but to the Town in general, and the Farmers and others frequenting the Market — This can never happen at the old Gaol, because the Principles that generate those infectious Fevers cannot cxift there, from the Vicinity of the large deep River, and the constant Circulation of Air that is upon the old Spot — That he can prove for upwards of Thirty Years (having constantly attended the Gaolers and their Families, and many of the principal Debtors, which makes him so thoroughly and well acquainted with the old Situation) that there is no other Spot, in or near the Town of that can be equal to the old Spot; because no other Place can have the Advantages that the old Spot has; and, notwithstanding Two very great Inconveniencies that attend the present Gaol, which are that of being ancient, and much too small; yet Time, the Father of Knowledge, has proved the Healthfulness of this Situation, as the Number of Burials taken from the Church Register will sufficiently prove — -That he never did hear any Complaints, from the Inhabitants of Chelmsford, on Account of the Prisoners being taken through the Town, at the Assizes, from the Gaol to the Court Houses, or of any infectious Distemper being communicated, or caught thereby- — -That he never had declared his Opinion, that any other Place or Situation, in or about Chelmsford, was equal or preferable to the old Spot; and so far from saying any such Thing to any Man living, he never lo much as thought it — That he does not believe it possible for a Gaol at the White Horse Premises to be drained of Filth, the Declivity or Fall of Ground down to the Meadows below, being so very little; that the human Excrement, when in Quantities, very soon undergoes a Fermentation, and becomes ib extremely tenacious, that even a large Stream of Water would not carry it off, where the Drains are so flat — That the White Horse Premises is about 18 Feet from the Church Yard — The Town -in general are for the old Spot, as well as the County at large.

In Answer to the 2d, 3d, and 4th mentioned Petitions, Mr. John Phillips, being examined, said, That he is Carpenter to the Board of Works, and has been in Business ever since the Year 1736 — That he has viewed the Two Places, at the Desire of the Justices of Essex — That, on the 18th of February last, he went with Mr. Robinson to Chelmsford, and viewed the Two Spots be-

fore mentioned; on One of which, he was told, a new Gaol was intended to be built — and did declare, — That a new Gaol may be built at either Place — ,

That the Body of such Building, from the Ground Floor upwards, will be the same at both Places — 3 Consequently the Difference will only lay in making the Support, or Legs, for the before-mentioned Super-struttions — 4 llily.If done at the White Horse Inn, and the Level of the Ground Floor is made Two Feet above Ground at the Entrance, according to a printed Plan now in his Hand, marked D, or any other Plan that may be agreed upon; which, at the Distance of not more than Seven Feet downwards from the said Ground Floor, will terminate upon a Foundation of Gravel, which, in his Opinion, will be sufficient to sustain the Weight of the whole Building — 5thly, If it is done on the Scite of the old Gaol, and the Ground Floor made Level with the Road Or Street, a good Foundation, in his Opinion, cannot be found at less than 13 Feet downwards from the said Ground Floor, and that an Uncertainty, without piling and planking. — The Witness begs it might be observed — That if the Level of the Ground Floor, at the White Horse Inn, ffrould be made higher -than Two Feet above Ground, the Expence of building on that Spot will increase — That if the Level of the Ground Floor, at the Scite of the old Gaol, should be lower than the Road or Street, the Expence of building the re will decrease — But whatever Plan may be agreed upon, for a new Gaol at , the Expence of building it will be greater on the Scite of the old Gaol, than at the White Horse Inn — For Example, If the Plan D, should be built on the Scite of the old Gaol, it would cost, including wharfing the River £. 3,000 more than at the White Horse Inn — That he was also desired to view the Shire House, which he did, and upon Examination it plainly appeared, that some necessary Repairs were wanting, which can easily be done, and so in Proportion for a greater or lesser Plan — That the Difference between Footing and Piling is, that Footing may be, of either-Brick or Timber, but we generally apply it tq Timber, that lays flatways upon the Ground, instead of being drove as Piles- — Planking is the Fame — Piling is a Piece of Timber drove , perpendicularly down;

that would obstruct any Gentleman's House: The Ground of the White Horse Inn lying so much above the Meadows, that it would be sufficiently drained, let the Ground be what it would — That there was a Ditch at the left Hand of the Garden, next the Road, that was dry, only the common Run of the Drain of the Inn- — That he did not observe whether the other, at the Bottom of the Garden, was stagnate or not; nor is it Material to the Building, in his Opinion — That he did not particularly observe any other Ditches — There is a little Ditch, or Drain, on the Right Hand, he believes, but is not sure — That he was as attentive to those Premises as the other, but he does not know with Precision the Number of Ditches; for this Reason, As the Ground at the White Horse Inn is considerably above the Branch of the River; and, in his Opinion, the Drain to it would meet no Obstruction — That the Difference of the Level between One Part of the Horse Premises, and the other, at. the Bowling Gree, the Extent of the Premises, he thinks, is 7 Feet — That, according to Mr. Hillyer's Plan, the Gaol is intended to be built at the White Horse, from the Street to the Bowling , and upon Part of the Bowling Green — That no Part of the GaoJ comes up to the Street, according to the Plan D; but he cannot tell the Distance of that Part of the Wall facing the Street, to the Street.

Being asked, Why be apprehends there is no Spring on the old Spot ? — he said, He could onlyanswer for the Two Holes he bored, because in those Two Holes there did not appear any Strata of Ground that would produce a Spring — That he means only the Spot he saw, which was near the old Pump, near the Back Ground — That he viewed the Grounds, which he was told were intended to be purchased, near the Gaol.

Being asked. Whether he observed any Springs there ? — he said. He did not examine any there — That there may be, for a,ught he knows — No doubt there are Springs every where — That he saw One Pump, and One in the Gaol, but does not remember seeing Two other Pumps — That it was late when the Well was opened; and Mr. Hillyer said, he would bring an Account of it — That a Gaol properly built, on the White Horse Premises, he thinks, will not be attended with great Inconveniences to the Inhabitants of Chelmsford — That he believes a Gaol built in the Heart of the Town of Chelmsford will probably be attended with greater Inconveniency to the Inhabitants, in case of an epidemical Distemper therein, than a Gaol built oa the old Spot, at the End of the Town, because a Gaol built in the Center of a Town, surrounded by Inhabitants, in case of an epidemical Distemper, will be more dangerous than if the Gaol is at the End of the Town, — That it, was in regard to Magnificence and Duration that he was of Opinion to pull down the Shire House, in case it should be necessary to add Grand and Petty Jury, and Record Rooms, rather than add them to the present Building.

Being asked, If he was of" Opinion, that a Gaol, thus situated before the Entrance into Chelmsford, and parted from the Town by this River, is more dangerous, and would be a greater Annoyance ro the Inhabitants of Chelmsford, in case of an infectious Gaol Distemper, than a Gaol' built on the White Horse Premises, although the White Horse Premises adjoin to the Market Place, and is surrounded by the Houses of the Inhabitants, and such Musket Place is the usual Resort of Persons frequenting the Markets and Fairs? — he said, I think the White Horse Premises more open than the old Spot is; and, from its Situation, a better Air, and capable of being much better drained — I think there is less Danger to the Inhabitants from a Gaol being built there — should think they would be equally dangerous to the Inhabitants; but the White Horse being nearest the Market Place, the Infection at the White Horse would be more dangerous to the People attending the Market.

Being asked. Whether a Brick Kiln, and making Bricks, at the White Horse, would- not in -any Degree be an Annoyance to the Inhabitants of the Town of Chelmsford? — he said, Not any material one, because it is only for Part of a Summer — That the Bricks would be made next the Branch of the River which is not near the Town.

Mr. Charles Mills, Surveyor and Carpenter,' being examined, said. He went to Chelmsford on the 12th of February, and was there, with a proper Man along

with him to bore the Ground — That he (aw Six Holes bored, and flood by the Man the whole Time — Upon the old Spot, the Holes lie bored were from 10 to 12 Feet deep, and he found it all to be marlhy except Three or Four Feet from the Surface, where he found a Sort‘of Sand Three or Four Inches thick, and the Soil rather drier than the other; but the lower he went, he.looked upon the Foundation to be worfc, it was quite Mud and Water — After they had done boring, he tried Two of the Holes, and put his Rule down, and found Water, and that Water was level with the Water in the River, as near as he could guess by putting his Rule down — - That he did not bore or examine the Grounds adjoining to the present Gaol; but went into them, and observed them to be upon the same Level j and apprehends them to be the same Soil — That he went to the White , and there bored; at about 20 Inches, or Two Feet, he found Ground Mould; near 3 Feet deeper a Brick Earth, and then a Gravel — That he went no further, thinking it to be a very good Foundation — That he opened the Ground with a Spade, and found the Strata of the Earth the same as where he bored — That where he bored at the old Spot, he found no Soil that he could depend on as a good Foundation for a County Gaol, or any Building at all; and he would not risque his Credit and Character by so doing — That he would not put any Brick Work upon that Foundation, until he had‘planked and piled it — That he apprehends the Wells, adjoining to the old Gaol, are supplied with Water by the Draining from that mar (by Ground; but he nevbr bored the fame.

Being asked, Whether he calculated the Expence of making good the Foundation, in the Manner he spoke of, from his own Observations, or from the Observations of anybody else ? — he said. From his own Observations, with Mr. Phillips, Mr. Robinson, and Mr. Hillyer.

Mr. William Hillyer, being again examined, said. He had made an Estimate for carrying into Execution the Plans produced by him — That the Expence of the Gaol is £.12,784 at the White Horse, exclusive of Purchase; and the Estimate of the Assize House is £.9,704, exclusive of Purchase; and that he can find several eminent People of Credit, to execute both, and give proper Security to execute them according to his Estimate.

Being crols-examined, he was asked. What Number of Houses he intends to pull down, for carrying into Execution his Plan of the Court Houses ? — and said. He thought there are Eight little Houses or Tenements, which he values at £. 2,000, to be purchased.

Being asked. Whether he drew any Plans or made any Estimates, for improving or enlarging the present Court Houses, without pulling them down ? — he laid. He had not.

Mr. Seymour reported from the Committee, appointed, Privile upon Thursday the 28th Day of March last, to esquire

into the Causes and Occasions of the Riots and Tumults of the Persons who assembled on several Days, in the Avenues leading to this House, and attacked the Persons of the Members coming to attend their Duty in Parliament; That the Committee had enquired accordingly, and had directed him to report a State of the Evidence to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Saunders Welsh, Esquire, a Justice of the Peace, said.

He attended at the House, on Wednesday the 27th of March, when the Mob was very disorderly, hooting and applauding the Members alternately — That he attentively examined the Mob, but did not know any one Person; from whence he conjectures that they came from the Eastern Part of the Town — That there appeared to be Management in their Disposition, being drawn up 8 or 10 deep; and the Pelting came from those in the hindermost Ranks, who were concealed by . the Persons in Front — That the Magistrates made Use of both Threats and Persuasions to disperse the Mob, but without any Effect; nor was any Impression made, till some Gentlemen came down with the Sheriffs; upon whose Interposition great Numbers of the Mob went away, and all was tolerably quiet during the Remainder of the Day — That he saw no other Act of Violence but pelting with Dirt, norobserved any Person particularly active, except a tall Man in White, and a short Man dressed in Blue, who appeared to be Directors of the Mob; but they flood in a Place where it was almost impossible to come at them — That one Man was taken up on the Steps of the Court of King’s Bench, who was brought afterwards to Guildhall, and committed to the Gate-house.

That he thinks Four Fifths of them went away when the Sheriffs came down; but that he did not fee any particular Signal for their Departure.

That he knows of no Liquor or Provisions carried to the Mob; but there was some Bread and Cheese and Beer given to the Constables.

That there are but 80 Constables for the City and Liberty of Westminster, who are appointed by the Deputy High Steward and Burgesses; and that People of the better Sort usually hire Men of mean Condition to officiate for them — That he thinks the Number of Constables insufficient; and that it is impossible to collect . the whole Number together; but it would be more easy to collect them, if they were not suffered to hire Deputies.

That there was an Execution at Tyburn on the 27th of March, which he looked upon as an unfortunate Circumstance, many of the Mob coming from thence to Westminster — That the Constables came likewise from Tyburn, and complained of the Hardness of their Duty; and that he thinks an additional Number of Constables will tend to the Preservation of the Peace.

Charles Marsh, Esquire, another Justice of the Peace,

confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Welsh, except that he said, he could not observe any thing like Discipline among the Mob. And,

William Keeling, Esquire, confirmed Mr. s Evidence in every Particular.

Your Committee then proceeded to examine into the Dispersion of the Hand Bills: And,

Anthony Wrangham, a Stationer, who disperses News-

papers, being examined, said, He knew nothing of the Distributirtn of Hand Bills.

Rice Williams, Newlman in Street, Covent

den, laid, He law a Hand Bill in his Shop; but he was lure none were dispersed in his Papers, because he folded them all up, and delivered them himself; and he enquired of his Servants, whether Anybody had been there to put in any Bills, and they said Nobody had.

Edward Langaridge, a Porter at the Temple Gate, said. That he had about 200 Hand Bills to attend my Lord Mayor upon his Return — That he does not know the Man from whom he received them — That he met him in Saint Paul’s Church Yard, and gave him Two Shillings for delivering the m; which he did to Anybody he met: That he has seen the Man since, but had no Conversation with him — That he was a thin Man, appeared in a good plain Dress of Second Mourning.

John Stevens, a Temple Porter, said. That he only delivered Hand Bills, the 29th of March, for the London Packet, and no other.

Mr. John Jackson, a Constable, said, he attended the Houl'c of Commons on the 25th of March, and was the Person who Michael Keys struck, who was afterwards apprehended by One of the Constables, and carried into the Lobby, and then to the Guildhall — That the Witness took no Notice of Keys when he struck him, but striking another Constable, he was then taken into Custody; but knows nothing of any Ringleader.

William Lawrence, a Constable, said, That attending his Duty, on the Day Lord North was assaulted, a Man struck a Constable; upon which the Witness said, Why don’t you take him into Custody ? upon which he struck the Witness, who upon that took him into Custody; but he knows nothing of any Ringleader.

Peter Stenhouse,a Constable of Covent Garden Parish,

said, he attended the Parliament House on the 28th of March, when His Majesty came to the House of Peers — That they took a Man into Custody about Two o’clock, in Parliament Street, for crying out, " No " Lord Mayor, no King," while His Majesty was passing by — That they took him before Sir John Fielding, and the Witness indicted him at the last Quarter Session, but the Bill was not found — That he laid no other Charge against him than that of making a Noise, and hilling the King; and he did not perceive any Person particularly active in the Mob.

After which, His Majesty was pleased to make a most Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth j' viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

As the State of Public Business no longer requires your Attendance, I think it right, at this Season of the Year, to put an End to the present Session of Parliament.

The Satisfaction I have obtained from his Catholic Majesty, for the Injury I had received, together with the Proofs which the Courts of France and Spain have given Me, by laying aside their Armaments, of their sincere Disposition to preserve the general Tranquillity of Europe, have enabled Me to reduce My Forces by Sea and Land. The Zeal with which you exerted yourselves, upon the Apprehension of a Rupture with Spain, mull convince the World of your affectionate Attachment to Me, and of your constant Regard for the true Interests of your Country. On that Support I shall always rely for the Defence of My Honour, and for the Security of the Rights of My People.

With regard to the Troubles which still agitate some Parts of the Continent, My Endeavours have never been wanting to bring them to an Endj and in those Endeavours, you may be allured, I shall persevere.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

It was with real Concern that I found Myself called upon, by the Situation of Public Affairs, to alk of My faithful Commons more than ordinary Supplies for the Service of the current Year; and I cannot sufficiently thank you for the Unanimity, Chearful-ness, and Public Spirit, with which they have been granted.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

While we acknowledge the Goodness of Divine Providence, in preserving Us from those Calamities with which some Parts of Europe have been afflicted, let Me exhort you to employ your bell Endeavours, in your several Stations and Countries, to render the national Happiness complete, by discouraging and supprelfing all groundlels Suspicions, and domestic Disturbances. 1 have no other Object, and I can have no other Interest, than to reign in the Hearts of a free and happy People: And it is My earnest Wilh, that My Subjects may not be prevented, by any Mistakes, or Animosities amongil themselves, from enjoying, in the fullest Extent, the Blelfings of a mild and legal Government. The Support of Our excellent Constitution is Our common Duty and Interest: By that Standard I would wish My People to try all Public

Principles and Professions; and to look upon those as their most dangerous Enemies, who, under any Pretence whatsoever, would persuade them to violate those Laws, and undermine that Authority, which the Constitution has provided for the Purpose of preserving the general Liberty and Happiness.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, said,

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued to Tuesday the 23d Day of July next, to be then here held; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday the 23d Day of July next.

That the House had attended The King’ His Majesty in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

v

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It gives Me much Satisfaction, that nothing in the Situation of Our Affairs, either Foreign or Domestic, has obliged Me to require your Attendance earlier than might have been confident with your private Convenience; and that, now you are met together, you will find yourselves at Liberty to give your whole Attention to the Establishment of wife and useful Regulations of Law, and to the Extension of our Commercial Advan- -tages.

The Performance of the Engagement of the King of Spain, in the Restitution of Port Egmont and Falkland's Island, and the repeated Assurances I have received of the pacific Disposition of that Court, as well as of other Powers, pro'mise to My Subjects the Continuance of Peace: And We may, with the greater Confidence, hope, that We shall not be disturbed in the Enjoyment of this Blessing; as there is no Reason to apprehend that We shall become involved in the Troubles which dill unhappily prevail in one Part of Europe.

The Danger of the farther spreading of the infectious Sickness in Europe is, I trust, very much abated: But I mull recommend it to you, not to suffer Our Happi-

5 M nets.

410 21 JanuariiA. 1774,

ness, in having been hitherto preserved from so dreadful a Calamity, to lessen yo»K Vigilance in the Use of e*ery reasonabl* Precaution fof Our Safety.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the Estimates for the Service of the current Year to be laid before you. I make no Doubt but you will fee the Propriety of maintaining a respectable Establishment of My Naval Forces. I am pleased, however, to find, that 1 shall be under no Necessity of asking of you, at this Time, any extraordinary Aid.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Concerns of this Country are so various and ex»-tensive, as to require the most vigilant and active Attention; and some of them, as wellfrom Remoteness of Place as from other Circumstances, are so peculiarly liable to Abuses, and exposed to Danger, that the Interposition of the Legislature, for their Protection, may become necessary. If in any such Instances, either for supplying Defects, or remedying Abuses, you shall find it requisite to provide any new Laws, you may depend upon My ready Concurrence, in whatever may best coo-tribute to the Attainment of those salutary Ends.

Refolotion Refdved, That an humble Address be presented to His for Address. Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His most gracious Speech from the Throne:

To offer our Congratulations to His Majesty, on the Birth of another Prince, and on the happy Recovery of the Queen ;who is still more endeared to this Nation by every new Pledge of Security for the Happiness we enjoy under His Majesty’s auspicious Government, as well as by Her own amiable Virtues:

To return His Majesty our Thanks for His gracious Communication of the Assurances He has received from the King of Spain, as well as from other Powers, of their Disposition to maintain the public Tranquillity; and to declare our Satisfaction at the fair Prospect which those Assurances, and the Performance of his Catholic Majesty’s Engagement, by the Restitution of Port Egmont and Falkland's Island, afford His Majesty’s Subjects of the Continuance of Peace; at the same Time, expressing our Confidence, that the Respect derived to this Nation, by the Moderation and Firmness of His Majesty’s Conduit, will continue to preserve His Majesty’s Dominions from the Calamities of War, which still unhappily prevail in the distant Parts of Europe:

To acknowledge His Majesty’s paternal Care, in the Precautions He has taken to preserve this Kingdom from the infectious Sickness with which We have of late been alarmed; and though we have the Satisfaction to find, that, by the Blessing of Providence, the Danger of its spreading is now ditninished, wc will not be negligent, on our Part, in taking such Measures as may, from Time to Time, appear best calculated to secure this Nation from the Visitation of so dreadful an Evil:

That His Majesty’s faithful Commons will chearfully grant to His Majesty such Supplies as shall be found necessary for the Service of the current Year; and will be careful to make l'ufficient Provision for the Establishment of a respectable Naval Force, on which, they are truly sensible, the Security, as well as the Importance, of this Nation must ever principally depend:

To allure His Majesty, that we will not fail, during this Season of Tranquillity, to employ our Time in making such Provisions as may be found necessary for the Improvement of our Laws, and the Extension of our Commerce; and that we will give the most vigilant and active Attention to those important 'Concerns recommended to us by His Majesty; and wherever it shall be found that, with respect to any of these, either from the Remoteness of their Situation from the Seat of Government, or from other Circumstances, such Abuses

A Petition of William Lowndes Stone, Esquire, Lord of the Manors of North Crawley, in the County of Bucks, the Reverend 'Thomas Lowndes, Clerk, Rector of the Parish and Parish Church of North Crawley aforesaid, and of several other Owners of Lands and Estates within the said Manors and Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there are, within the said Manors and Parish, several Open Common Fields, Meadows, and Waste Grounds, which, in their present Situation, are incapable of any considerable Improvement; but, if divided, and specific Shares thereof allotted to the Petitioners and others, according to their respective Interests therein, the same might be considerably improved: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration; and that Leave be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Lands and Grounds, in such Manner, and subject to such Regulations, as the House shall think fit.

The Lord Hinchingbrook reported from the Committee, appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to His Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, return Your Majesty our humble Thanks for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

It is with unfeigned Joy we beg Leave to offer to Your Majesty our Congratulations on the Birth of another Prince, and on the happy Recovery of the Queen; who is still more endeared to this Nation by every new Pledge of Security for the Happiness we enjoy under Your Majesty’s auspicious Government, as well as by Her Majesty’s amiable Virtues.

We return Your Majesty our warmest Thanks, for Your gracious Communication of the Assurances Your Majesty has received from the King of Spain, as well

as from other Powers, of their Disposition to maintain the Public Tranquillity; and we cannot but feel the greatest Satisfaction at the fair Pro!pert which those Assurances, and the Performance of his Catholick Majesty’s Engagement, by the Restitution of Port Egmont and Falkland's Island, afford Your Majesty’s Subjects of the Continuance of Peace: At the same Time, we have the greatest Confidence, that the Respect derived to this Nation, from the Moderation and Firmncfs of Your Majesty’s Conduct, will continue to preserve Your Majesty’s Dominions from the Calamities of War, which still unhappily prevail in the distant Parts of Europe.

We acknowledge with Gratitude Your Majesty’s paternal Care, in the Precautions Your Majesty has taken to preserve this Kingdom from the infectious Sickness with which we have of late been alarmed; and though we have the Satisfaction to find, that, by the Blessing of Providence, the Danger of its spreading is now diminished, we will not be negligent, on our Part, in taking such Measures as may, from Time to Time, appear bell calculated to secure this Nation from the Visitation of so dreadful an Evil.

Your Majesty’s faithful Commons will chearfully grant to Your Majesty such Supplies as shall be found necessary for the Service of the current Year; and we will be careful to make sufficient Provision for the Establishment of a respectable Naval Force, on which, we are truly sensible, the Security, as well as the Importance, of this Nation must ever principally depend.

We assure Your Majesty, that we will not fail, during thisSeafon of Tranquillity, to employ our Time in making such Provisions as may be found necessary for the Improvement of our Laws, and the Extension of our Commerce: And Your Majesty may rely on our vigilant and active Attention to those important Concerns recommended to us by Your Majesty; and wherever it shall be found, that, with respect to any of these, either from the Remoteness of their Situation from the Seat of Government, or from other Circumstances, such Abuses prevail as expose them to Danger, we shall think it our Duty to endeavour, by every Regulation in our Power, to remedy those Evils, which may, in their Consequences, so essentially affect the Interest and Honour of this Country.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to His Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by the whole House.

tJAial Order*. Ordered, That all Persons wh<5 will question any Re-

turns of Members to serve in Parliament do question the same within Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen Days^iext after any new Return shall be brought in; and that all Members who are returned for Two or more Places do make their Election by this Day Three Weeks for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place; and if any Thing shall come in question touching the Return or Election of any Member, he is to withdraw during the Time the Matter is in Debate; and that all Members returned upon Double Returns do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Vol. 33.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same isdeclared to be a High Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That, in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient Time, to be appointed by the House, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members; giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners or their Agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from Time to Time, take into his Custody any Stranger, or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber, every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take Care, that from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple Bar and Westminster Hall shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstructions be. made, by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take Care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster Hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance, by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster , and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Postmaster General.

room of Fane William Sharpe, Esquire, deceased, IVII-liam Skrine, Esquire, and tire Petitioner, were Candidates; and that, at the said Election, Mr. David Horn-don presided, and acted as the Portreeve and Returning Officer of the said Borough; and that the Petitioner was duly elected by a Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned; nevertheless the said David Horndou partially and illegally refuted to accept the Suffrages of several qualified Persons, who offered to vote, and gave their Votes for the Petitioner; and admitted others who were not qualified to vote for the said William Skrine, by which, and other unfair, unwarrantable, and illegal Practices and Proceedings, previous to and at the said Election, a l'mall colourable Majority was procured in Favour of the said William Skrine; and the said Portreeve did thereupon think fit todeclare and return the said William Skrine duly elected to represent the said Borough, in Wrong of the Petitioner, and in manifest and open Violation of the Rights of Election: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to afford him such Relief as tire Nature and Circumstances of his same shall appear to deserve.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Monday the 24th Day of February next, at One of the Clock in the Afternoon.

A' Petition of the Magistrates and Council of the Glasgow City of Glasgow, was presented to the House. arboar.

And a Member returned upon a new Writ, having Member taken the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declara- tworn. tion, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, and having delivered in to the Clerk of the House, an Account of his Qualification, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Qualification, according to the Laws made fqr.those Purposes;

The said Petition Was read; Set ting'forth, That the Glasgow Harbour of Port Glasgow has of late Years been greatly H*d>our> choked and filled up, whereby Vessels of Burthen are hindered from getting into the Piers and Quays, and are thereby exposed to many Dangers and Inconveniences; and that the Trade of the said City and Port has of late Years increased, and the Ships and Vessels trading to and from the same are now more numerous, and of larger Dimensions than heretofore, and the Quays and Piers are not sufficient for the Reception and convenient Lying of the Ships and Vessels resorting thereto, nor for the requisite and convenient Dispatch in loading /and unloading the fame; which Dangers and Inconveniences render the deepening, cleaning, and scouring, of the said Harbour, and the building and erecting new and additional Piers, Breasts, Jettees, and Quays, highly necessary; and that certain Rules and Regulations should be established, for regulating Ships and Vessels trading or coming into, or going out of, the Harbour aforesaid:

And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for deepening, cleaning, scouring, preserving, and maintaining, the said Harbour of Port Glasgow, and for enlarging and improving the Quays and Piers within the said Harbour, and for building and erecting new and additional Breasts, Jettees, and Piers, and for regulating all Ships, Vessels, Barks, or Lighters, trading or coming into, and going out of, the Harbour aforesaid; and for exacting, collecting, levying, and receiving, such Tolls, Rates, and Duties, from all Ships,

Vessels, Barks, and Lighters, coming into, and going out of, the said Harbour, as shall be judged reasonable and expedient; and for giving to the said Magistrates and Council of the City of Glasgow and their Successors in Office, such other Powers, Grants, and Privileges, as shall be necessary for executing and completing the Works aforesaid, and for maintaining, upholding, and keeping the same in Repair.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Haddcoham A Petition of the Commissioners for putting in Exe-Level cution an Act of Parliament, made in the Thirteenth Draioagf. Year of the Reign of his Majesty King George the First. intituled, An Act for the effectual Draining and Preservation of Haddenham , in the Iste of

and of several other Owners and Occupiers of Fen Lands and Low Grounds in the said Level, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in pursuance of the said Act, the Lands and Grounds therein mentioned have been assessed and rated at One Shilling per Acre; and that several Engines, and other Works, for draining the fame, have been erected; but that the said Engines and Works are, by Length of Time, and other Accidents, become so ruinous and decayed, that the present Tax is insufficient for that Purpose, whereby the said Commissioners have been obliged to contract several Debts, which now remain unpaid, and which cannot be discharged, nor the necessary Works for Draining renewed and maintained, without the further Aid of Parliament; and that the Powers and Authorities given by the said Act are not sufficient for the effectual Draining and Preservation of the said Level: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for laying such farther Tax upon the Lands and Grounds in the said Level, and aho for granting such farther Powers and Authorities, for the better draining and preserving the fame, as to the House shall seem meet.

Sum shall be granted for that Purpose; and for Twenty Years past no more than £. 150 appears to >have been applied thereto; and the Petitioners are informed, that no further Assistance is to be expected from that Trust, which they apprehend is contrary to the Intentions of the said Act of the Third of his late Majesty; and representing to the House, That the said Act has been executed in a Manner extremely partial, and contrary to the Interest of the Petitioners, a Toll Bar having Ireen erected at the End of the Town of Chatham, and that the Toll Bar next Canterbury is placed at least Three Miles distant from that City; and that divers Exemptions are granted in Favour of Goods passing through the Canterbury Bar, which are subject to a Toll at Chatham; and that the said Road from Rochester to Chatham is of Public Utility, particularly to His Majesty’s Dock Yard, Office of Ordnance, and Barracks, is in a very ruinous Condition, and cannot be repaired by the ordinary Course of Law: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made, in the said intended Act, for the Petitioners Relief, by ascertaining the Sum to be paid by the said Trust, removing the said Gate the same Distance from the said Town of Chatham, as the said other Gate is distant from the City of Canterbury, or in such other Manner as to the House shall leem just and reasonable.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

William Curtis, being examined, said, That the Town of Islington is very populous, and daily increasing in Buildings, and the Number of Inhabitants: — That frequent Robberies, Murders, and other Outrages, are committed there; several Instances of which he mentioned to the Committee; and added, That the lighting the said Town, and establishing a regular Nightly Watch, would be the most probable Means of preventing such Enormities for the future.

Hammond Cross, Esquire, and Mr. D. confirmed the above Evidence.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts were read: And,

Mr. Benjamin Barnsley, Clerk to the said Trustees, being examined, laid, The Acts have been put in Execution, and the Roads repaired, but that the Sum of £.3,400 is owing on the Credit thereof: That the said Acts have been found deficient in many Respects, particularly there is no Power to widen the Road, nor to erect Side Gates to prevent Evasion of the Tolls: And he added, That the said Road cannot be continued in good Repair, and made commodious, nor the Money owing thereon be paid off, unless the Powers of the said Acts are enlarged, and the Term further continued.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers of Two Acts, made in the Twenty-sixth and Twenty-ninth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for repairing and widening Old Street Road, in the Parishes of Saint Luke and Saint Leonard, Shoreditch, in the County of Middlesex: And that Sir Richard Glynn, Mr. and Mr. Alderman Harley, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

That a Sum, not exceeding One Thousand Two hundred and Eighty-one Pounds and Sixpence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge for Allowances to the several Officers and private Gentlemen of the Two Troops of Horse Guards Reduced, and to the Superannuated Gentlemen of the Fdur Troops of Horse Guards, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-two.

Rfolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Twenty-four thousand Eight hundred and Thirteen Pounds Twelve Shillings and Sixpence, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account, towards defraying the Charge of Out Pensioners of Chelsea Hospital, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-two.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred and Fifteen thousand Eight hundred and Eighty-three Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for the Charge of the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-two.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty-two thousand Four hundred and Ninety-eight Pounds Six Shillings and Three Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Expence of Services performed by the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, and not pravided for by Parliament, in One thousand Seven hundred’ and Seventy-one.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and vGreat Commonalty, of the Town and Borough of Great (Norfolk) Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, was presented to Haven, &c. the House, and read y Setting forth, That the Haven and Piers belonging to the said Town and Borough; have for many Years been repaired and maintained by the Duty imposed by several Acts upon Coals, and other Goods and Merchandizes, imported into the said Haven; and that, by an Act made in the Twenty-third Year of his late Majesty’s Reign for repairing, improving, and maintaining the Haven and Piers of Great,

and other Purposes, the Duties payable by an Act of the Twentieth Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty, were discontinued, and, in lieu. thereqf, new Duties were thereby granted, to be applied for such Uses and Purposes as is therein mentioned; and that the said last mentioned Act is now near expiring, and the said Haven and Piers mull in a shortTimc fall into utter and irreparable Decay, and the Navigation of the Rivers emptying themselves into the said Haven be subject to great Obstructions and Annoyances, and r.ot only Ships wintering in the said Haven, but also the said Town, be exposed to frequent and terrible Accidents by Fire, if the said Act is not further continued and enforced:

And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the said Act for such further Term, and with such additional Powers and Authorities for the better effecting the several Purposes of the said Act, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Town/hMr. Walpole, &c.: And they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Ormfide thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and inclosure. read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are Proprietors of Houses and Lands within the Manor of Great Ormftde, in the Parish of Ormfide, in the County of West-moreland-, and that there are several Tracts or Parcels of Common and Waste Grounds within the said Manor, whereon the Petitioners are entitled to Right of Common; and that, if the same were divided into specifio Allotments, and inclosed, a considerable Advantage would accrue to every Person interested therein: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given tq bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Common and Waste Grounds, under such Rules, Regulations, and Provisoes, as to the House shall ieem meet.

I.vmeRrgis A Petition of the Mayor and Capital Burgesses of

Land Tax. the Borough of Lymein the County of Dor ft, and of the principal Inhabitants now residing the rein, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Parish of Lyme Regis confifis of Two Divisions, namely, the Borough, and a Tything called ;and that, when

the Land Tax was established, in the Fourth Year of the Reign of King IVilli and Queen Mary, the said Borough confided of a great many good Houses, inhabited by substantial Merchants, who carried on an extensive Foreign Commerce, and who then manifested their Zeal for the Government, by assessing, on the Houses, Lands, Salaries, and Personal Estate, within the said Borough, at the Rate of Four Shillings in the Pound, the Sum of Four Imndred and Seven Pounds E'ght Shillings; and Colway Tything was then assessed at the further Sum of One hundred and Twenty Pounds Ten Shillings; which several Sums, or a due Proportion thereof, adequate to the Quantum of the Land Tax, have been Yearly assessed thereon everfince; and that, since that Time, the Trade and Commerce carried on by the Inhabitants of the said Borough have greatly decreased; and above One hundred and Eighteen Houses (which, when the Land Tax was firtF established, were inhabited) have since fallen to Ruin; and many other Houses have been burnt down, and not rebuilt; and t several others, together with several Acres of Land, washed away by the Violence of the Sea; by reason whereof, the remaining Houses and Lands within the said Borough are diminished above One full Third Part in Value; and that the said full Sum of Four hundred and Seven Pounds Eight Shillings, or a due Proportion thereof, adequate to the Quantum of the Land Tax, hath, ever since the first Institution, been Yearly assessed on the said Borough; which now amounts to the Sum of Six Shillings in the Pound, and upwards, on the full Rack Rents of the Houfqs and Lands in the said Borough; which, the Inhabitants being unable to pay, have been Yearly returned Insuper by the Receiver General of the said Tax, in divers large Sums of Money, amounting, within the Space of Fifteen Years past, to the Sum of One thousand Three hundred and Sixty-tive Pounds, or thereabouts; for Non-payment whereof, Process hath issued Half-yearly against them, out of His Majesty’s Court of Exchequer, whereon divers large Sums of Money, not less than One Shilling in the Pound, and for the most Part, every Half-year, have been returned, as Issues forfeited by them for Nonpayment of the said Itfupmany of which Sums they have been obliged to pay; and further Issues will be returned against them every Half-year in future; and that, by reason of their Inability to pay the whole Sums so Yearly assessed on them, new will be returned

against them every Year, whereon new Issues will be returned against them; and that the levying such Issues will tend greatly to the further Impoverishment of the Petitioners, in regard that, notwithstanding the Payment thereof, they will be still liable to Process for the whole Sums, which already have been, or hereafter shall be, so returned Insuper; and that, as such Deficiences will be Yearly increasing, and the Inhabitants more and more unable to pay the same, the Consequence thereof will be, that the few Persons of Property, who now live in the said Borough, will remove thereout, and the little Trade now carried on there mud inevitably fink, and the few remaining Inhabitants be rendered wholly unable to pay their Proportion of the said Tax: And therefore praying the House, to give the Petitioners such Relief, as w^ll with respect to the several Insupert already returned against them, and the

Issues forfeited thereupon, as also with respect to the future Assessments on the said Borough, as the particular Circumstances occasioning the Hardship of their same shall require, and as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Daniel Fox, of Binfield, in the County of Berks, Esquire, and Elizabeth Caroline, his Wife, Lord of the Manor of Sandhurst, in the Forest of J'or, in the same County, being offered to be. presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, gives His Consent, as far as His Majesty’s Interest is concerned, that the House may do therein as they shall think fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That Queen Elizabeth did, by Letters Patent, dated the 16th Day of February, in the Fourth Year of her Reign, in Consideration of £. 248, grant to Sir John Malon. and his Heirs, her Lordship or Manor of

5 ♦

Sandhurst, in the County of Berks, by such Defections as are therein mentioned, and together with alt Lands, Commons, Wastes, Waftrith, Places, Heath, Grounds, Moors, Marshes, Woods, Underwoods, Waters, Pifcaries, Fishings, Ponds, Pools, and all Rents and Services, as well of Free as of Customary Tenements and Tenants, by Copy of Court Roll, and all Fines and Amerciaments of the Tenants of the Lordship and Manor aforesaid, Free Warrens, and all other her Rights, Jurisdictions, Franchises, Liberties, Privileges, Profits, Commodities, Emoluments, and Hereditaments whatsoever, with their Appurtenances, in the Town, Fields, Parishes, or Hamlets, of Sandhurst, or elsewhere, in the said County, to the said Lordship or Manor of Sandhurst, and other the Premises, belonging or appertaining; and did also grant to the said Sir John Majon, his Heirs and Assigns, all Manner of Woods, Underwoods, and Trees, whatsoever, growing and being in and upon the said Lordship, Manor, and Premises, and every Part thereof, and all the Ground and Soil of the same Woods, Underwoods, and Trees, and the Rents, Services, Reversions, Emoluments, and Annual Profits whatsoever, reserved upon any Demise or Grant of the said Lordship, Manor, and Premises, or any Part thereof, except as therein excepted, for ever to be holden, of her Majesty, her Heirs and Successors, as of her Manor of East Greenwich, in the County of Kent; and that the said Manor and Waste Lands do, by the Petitioner’s Marriage Settlement, now stand limited to the Use of the Petitioners and their Assigns respectively, for their natural Lives, and the Life of the Survivor of them, with Remainder to their Children, in such Manner as they shall appoint; with Remainder to the Survivor of the Petitioners, his or her Heirs and Assigns; but the Petitioners have not any Issue, and are now in Possession of the said Manor and Premises, with the Appurtenances, and the Owners of the Ground and Soil of the Wastes of the said Manor; and that the said Manor is in the Bailiwick of in the County of Berks, and within the Bounds of the Forest of Windsor-, and the Petitioners, and those under whom they claim, as Owners of the Soil of the Waste Lands, did, for many Years, annually cut, dig, and carry away, from the Wastes of the said Manor, Turves, Peat, Heath, and Fern, growing thereon; and the Benefit arising therefrom was the foie Advantage arising to the Petitioners, as Owners of the said Manor and Waste Lands, except some small Quit Rents; but, in the Year 1763, an Information was exhibited against the Petitioners, and their Workmen, complaining, that the getting of such Turves, Pear, Heath, and Fern, was a Prejudice to the Vert and Covert for His Majesty’s Deer, and praying an Injunction, to restrain the Petitioners from cutting the fame; and that, upon filing such Information, and before the Petitioners had put in an Answer thereto, the Court of Exchequer ordered an Injunction to issue, until the Petitioners should answer the Information; and that the Petitioners put in their Answer to the said Information, and infilled, that the Matters in question were not within the Jurisdiction of the Court of Exchequer, but ought to be determined in the Forest Courts; and that the Petitioners had a Right to cut, dig, and carry away. Turves, Peat, Heath, and Fern, and to dispose of the fame, so as they did not prejudice the Vert and Covert for His Majesty’s Deer; and that such cutting and carrying away, in the Manner the same had been exercised in the Year 1763, and* before, was no Prejudice thereto; and that the Waste Lands lying within the said Manor contain 3,600 Acres, and upwards; and not only the Petitioners, but those under whom they claim, did, for a great Number of Years previous to the granting the said Injunction, cut Peat and Turves from the Waste of the said Manor, and fold the fame, whereby many of the Inhabitants of the neighbouring Parishes, and particularly the Poor in that Neighbourhood, were supplied with Fuel on reasonable

Mr. John Brownes Clerk to the Register of the said Corporation, informed your Committee, That the Debt of the said Corporation, upon Account of the said Middle and South Levels, is increased to £. 30,700.

Mr. Richard Dunthorne, being examined, said. That great Damage had been done to the principal Works made for the Preservation of the said Middle and South Levels, by the Floods of last Winter; and that such Works could not be preserved from the ordinary Revenue of the said Corporation, nor without borrowing more Money for that Purpose.

Mr. John Browne further said. That at a General Meeting of the said Corporation at , on the 20th of April last, it was declared to be the unanimous Opinion of the Board, that an Application should be made to Parliament, for borrowing the further Sum of £. 12,000. '

Mr. Richard Dunthorne further said. That he apprehended, that the Power to borrow the said further Sum, to be applied to the principal Works of the said Corporation in the said Middle and South Levels, might not only be for the Benefit of the Country in general, but of the Creditors of the said Corporation, provided such Part of the said 95,000 Acres, as lie within the said Middle and South Levels, are charged with a further Tax than the gradual single Acre l ax, wherewith the same are charged by the said Act of the 29th Year of King George the Second, during such Time as such additional Debt, or any Part thereof, shall remain due from the said Corporation.

Roger Kynaston, Esquire, informed your Committee, That the Trustees for repairing and widening the said Bridge, have caused a considerable Part thereof to be rebuilt, and have nearly expended the whole Money 1'ubscribed, but that there is no Likelihood that a sufficient Sum will be raised by voluntary Subscription for completing the fame, and performing the necessary Works directed to be done by the said Act; therefore, unless some other Provision is made for raising Money, the Purposes of the said Act cannot be carried into Execution; and that the Act wants amending in several Respects.

And he further said. That there are Five different Roads which lead into the Town of which

are all repaired by particular Acts of Parliament, and that the finishing the said Bridge will be of Advantage to Travellers making use of those Roads: And,

Mr. William Jones, Clerk to the Trustees for widening and repairing the said Bridge, being examined, said. That Application had been made to the Trustees of the aforesaid Roads, and that they are willing to give up a certain Proportion of the Tolls collected thereon, to be applied towards finishing the said Bridge, provided the Terms of the said Acts are further continued.

And being asked, if the Creditors under the said Acts were contenting thereto ? he said. That the Trustees are the principal Creditors; and that no Creditor could object to it, because their Securities would be benefited by continuing the Terms of the Acts.

Mr. Kynaston, being again examined, confirmed Mr. Jones's Evidence.

Mr. Vaiifiltart reported from the Committee, to whom MaidenVad the Petition of the Mayor, Bridgemasters, and Buigeftes, ®,ld8e* of the Town of Maydenheth otherwise Maidenhead, in the County of Berks, under their Common Seal, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Robert Taylor, Esquire, a Surveyor, being examined, said, That he had lately surveyed the Bridge at Maidenhead-, that it is a narrow wooden Strudture, very old and lo much decayed, as to be unsafe for the Passage of heavy Carriages; that it would be a great Convenience to the Public, and of general Utility, if a Stone Bridge of a proper Width was built there: And he produced a Plan of a Bridge, the Expence of building which, he informed the Committee, would amount to £. i6,oco or thereabouts. And,

Mr. James Payne, Toy/n Clerk of Maidenhead, being examined, said, That the present Bridge is the Property of the said Corporation, who are authorized by their Charter to take certain Tolls therein mentioned, for the Passage of Cattle, Carriages, and Goods; a List of which he produced, and also a List of those now taken — And the Witness said, The Bridge stands in the High Road to Bath, and the average Income of the Tolls taken at it is £. 70 per Annum, which is not near sufficient to defray the Expence of building a new Bridge.

Mr. John Gould, being examined, said, That the Tolls now taken are not sufficient to keep the present Bridge in Repair, and that it will very soon become impal-fable.

Mr. Richard Lovegrove, being examined, said, That the Bridge is so narrow', that Carriages meeting on it are obliged to draw back, to the great Danger and Inconvenience of all Persons travelling that Road.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a Bridge over the River Thames, near the Town of Maidenhead, in the County of Berks: And that Mr. Vanjittart and Admiral Craven do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The said Writ and Return were read.

And the said Mr. Harmood, and Samuel Long, being severally called in, were, at the Bar, examined, touching the Delay in the Execution of the said Writ.

And then they were severally directed to withdraw.

And the said Samuel Long having, in his Examination, informed the House, that the said Writ had been taken from him by Valentine Morris, Esquire, before he could deliver it to the Sheriff of the said County; and it appearing, by the Receipt of the Sheriff endorsed upon the Writ, that the said Writ, though issued on the 4th Day of June, was not delivered to him till the 2ift Day of June.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That Valentine Morris, Esquire, do attend this House upon Friday Sevennight, the 28th Day of this Instant February, to give an Account to the House, of his having taken the Writ for the last Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Monmouth, from the Messenger who was lent down to deliver the said Writ to the Sheriff;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by adding at the End thereof the Words " and of the Delay in the Execution of the said Writ."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Then the main Question, so amended, being put;

Ordered, That Valentine Morris, Esquire, do attend this House upon Friday Sevennight, the 28th Day of this Instant February, to give an Account to the House, of his having taken the Writ for the last Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Monmouth, from the Messenger who was sent down to deliver the said Writ to the Sheriff, and of the Delay in the Execution of the said Writ.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. The L,ord North acquainted the House, that he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House, and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGER.

His Majesty, being desirous, from paternal Affection to His own Family, and anxious Concern for the future Welfare of His People, and the Honour and Dignity of His Crown, that the Right of approving all Marriages in the Royal Family (which ever has belonged to the Kings of this Realm, as a Matter of public Concern-) may be made effectual, recommends to both Houses of Parliament, to take into their serious Consideration whether it may not be wife and expedient to supply the Defect of the Laws now in being, and, by (ome new Provision, more effectually to guard the Descendants of his late Majesty King George the Second (other than the Issue of Princesses who have married, or may hereafter marry', into Foreign Families) from marrying without the Approbation of His Majesty, His Heirs or Successors, first had and obtained.

G. R.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the humble Thanks of this House, for His most gracious Message;

To allure His Majesty', that His faithful Commons, impressed with a just Sense, as well of His Majesty’s paternal Affection to His Family, as His anxious Concern for the future Welfare of His People, and the Honour and Dignity of His Crown, will not fail to take His Majesty’s Message into their most serious Consideration.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s Most honourable Privy Council.

A Petition of the Right Reverend John Lord Bishop of Durham, was presented to the House, and read; Bridge. Setting forth, That, by the Violence of the Flood, upon the 17th of November last, in the River Tyne, the Bridge across the said River, from the Town of Gates-head, in the County of Durham, to the Town of Nexv-cast/e, was broken down in several Parts thereof, and rendered impafiable, and which, the Petitioner apprehends, should be repaired with all possible Expedition; and that, as One Third Part thereof hath of Right been, and ought to be, maintained by the Bishop of Durham for the Time being, the Petitioner conceives, that the gross Sum necessary to be employed therein ought to be raised out of, or secured upon, the Possessions of the See of Durham, or some competent Part thereof; and that the Petitioner and his Successors ought not to bear any greater Burthen than shall depend upon, or relate to, the Interest, or Annual Charge, resulting from the Principal Money so to be raised for the Purpose aforesaid: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Petitioner and his Sue-cessors effectually to repair the said Part of the said Bridge, and, for that Purpose, to raise out of, or charge upon the Possessions of the said See, or some competent Part thereof, such Sum of Money as will be sufficient for that Purpose, in such Manner, and under such Rules; Restrictions, and Directions, as to the House shall seem most meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Major Egerton, Mr. Vane, &c.:

And they are to tfteet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the'Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.
