An Act to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the several Statutes now in being, for the Amendment and Preservation of the Public Highways of this Kingdom, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, as relates to Carriages drawn on the said Public Highways, by Horses and other Bealls of Draught; and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House;

That the Committee had considered the Matters to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Resolu-tions of the Committee were read; and ate as followeth; viz.

ReJ'olved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Carriages with Wheels of the Breadth of Six

Inches

260 Februarii. A. 1772.

Inches ought to be encouraged to pass on all Turnpike Roads, in preference to Carriages with narrower Wheels.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Four Wheel Carriages, with Wheels of the Breadth of Six Inches, and drawn by Six Horses, Mules, or Asses, be permitted to pass on all Turnpike Roads, on Payment of the Tolls, for every Horse, Mule, or A Is, drawing the fame, which are payable on every such Horse, Mule, or Als, drawing Narrow Wheel Carriages.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Carts with Wheels of the Breadth of Six Inches, and drawn by Four Horses, Mules, or Asses, be permitted to pals on all Turnpike Roads, on Payment of the Tolls, for every Horse, Mule, or Afs, drawing the fame, which are payable on every Horse, Mule, or Afs, drawing Narrow Wheel Carriages.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Two foregoing Resolutions shall not extend to Common Stage Waggons, or Carts, employed in carrying Goods by any Common Waggoner or Carrier, which are now subject to be regulated in the Price of their Carriage by an Act, passed in the Third Year of King William and Queen Mary, intituled, An Act for the better repairing and amending the Highways, and for settling the Rates of Carriage of Goods.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Provision be made, that Carriages having the Wheels of the Breadth of Nine Inches, may be permitted to be drawn on Turnpike Roads, by any Number of Oxen, or other Neat Cattle, in Pairs, not exceeding Two Oxen or other Neat Cattle for One Horse, as far as the Number of Horses permitted by Law to draw in such Carriages, on Payment, for every Pair of Oxen or Neat Cattle, the same Tolls that are now payable for every Horse, Mule, or Afs, drawing such Waggons.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Encouragement be given to Waggons and Carts, having Rollers of Sixteen Inches broad, to go upon all '1'urnpike Roads.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Waggons and Carts, having Rollers of Sixteen Inches broad, be exempted from the Payment of Tolls for Three Years.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Seven-night, the 9th Day of March next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

That great Progress has been made towards making and finishing the said Harbour, which, when done, will be very useful and commodious, and a considerable Sum of Money hath been expended in carrying on the said Works; and that several Sums of Money have been raisijd, by Sale of Annuities chargeable on the Duties imposed by the said Act, and another Act made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, by which the Sum off. 50,000 by the said First-mentioned Act authorized to be raised by Sale of Annuities, is increased to £. 70,000, and the Whole of the Annuities now payable in respect thereof, to the surviving Annuitants, amount together to the Yearly Sum of £.4,482 1 Of.; and that, from the Time of the first collecting of the said Duties, until very lately, all Ships and other Vessels passing by the said Harbour, whether they passed through the Downs or not, were considered as liable to the Payment of the fame; but it hath been lately judicially determined, that such Ships and Vessels passing by the said Harbour, and not passing through the Downs, are not, by the said First-mentioned Act, subject to the Payment of the said Duties; and that, since the said Determination, the Duties have fallen short of railing Money sufficient to answer the Purposes intended by the said Act, although the Petitioners have settled and imposed the Duties by the said Act directed to the full Amount thereof, which hath been, and Hill continue to be, a Burthen upon the Trade of this Kingdom, and principally on the City of London: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, to amend and explain the said Act made in the Twenty-sixth Year of his said late Majesty’s Reign; and that the Duties thereby authorized to be collected may be charged on all Ships coming into, or passing through, the Narrow Seas between Doves- and Calais, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, at the Expence of £. 10,453, fegaBy fitted out the above-mentioned Private' Ship of War, of which William Fofier was Commander, who proceeded upon his Cruize from the Port of London, an<i on the 26th of December 1756, fairly and legally toolc the above-mentioned Prize, after a long and obstinate Engagement, more than Five Leagues distant from any Part of the Territories of Spain; and that Captain Fofier, on the 24th of January following, carried the Priie into the Bay of Cadiz, where the French Prisoners, in the Presence of the Frenth Consul, acknowledged the Legality of the Capture; and that# on the 28th of February, the Prize was legally condemned at on the voluntary Evidence of the French Officers and Marines; and that, on the ad of March, the Prize was violently taken from the lawful Captors, with the most unparalleled Acts of Barbarity, whereby One of His Majesty’s Subjects was killed, and Seven wounded, by the Spaniards, in the Bay of Cadiz; and that Captain Fofier was seized in the House of the British Consul at Cadiz, and forced to a very close and dismal Prison, as also were his Officers and Crew, who were confined there several Days, without any Allowance, even of Bread or Water, being treated worse than Felons, though they had given no kind of Offence; and that the Governor of Cadiz restored the Prize to the French, after she had been legally condemned; and the British Colours struek, with the greatest Mark of Contempt, by treading them under Foot, kicking them about, and tearing them to Pieces; and that His Majesty’s Consul at Cadiz acquainted Sir Benjamin Keene, by Letter of the 5th of March, th3t he was in the greatest Consternation imaginable; because, fays the Consul, " I have seen the Flag of my Royal Matter " insulted, our Nation degraded, our Treaties violated,

" the Lustre of our Sovereign’s Crown tarnished and " despised, and my House invaded; and as there is no Minister here of greater Dignity than myself, I consider the Affront and Insult, done and offered to my " Person, as an Indignity on the Sacred Person of my " Royal Matter;" and that the British Consul at Cadiz and Captain Fofier protested against this illegal and arbitrary Way of Proceeding, which. Sir Benjamin Keene said, " was so irregular, unreasonable, and unprecedented, that it would neither bear Light nor Justification;" and that His Majesty’s Minister, the Secretary of the Etnbafly, and Consuls in havfc in

A Petition of John Thoru/ou, Robert Nett let on, John Lodge, Thomas IV,jlker, Bast on Long, Thomas Nash, John Dorr ten, John Blackburn, James Mathias, Jonas Fowler Walker, John Anthony Rucker, John SYnith% and Andrew Thomson, Esquires, on Behalf of themselves and

others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That divers of the Petitioners, and others, in June 1756. formed themselves into a Society (called The Marine Society) and, in consequence thereof, they coiledted by voluntary Donations and Subscriptions, during the late War with France and Spain, the Sum of 23,692. 7 s,2 d-which was expended in cloathing and fitting out 5,451 Landsmen Volunteers, to serve as Seamen on Board His Majesty’s Fleet, and 5,174 poor Roys, as Servants to the Officers in the Navy j and that, at the Close of the late War, the said Society also provided in the most safe and satisfactory Manner, by Rand and Sea, for all the Boys who applied for Relief after being discharged from the King’s Ships; and that, since the Commencement of the Peace, the Petitioners (with Part of the Interest of a Legacy bequeathed to them by the Will of William Hicks, late an English Merchant, in

Hamburgh, deceased, and further voluntary Donations and Subscriptions) have placed out to Officers in the King’s Ships, and to the Merchant Service, 1,132 more distrefi'ed Boys; and that the Affairs and Pufiness of this Society, have been conduced and managed, from Time to Time, with the utrpost Order and (Economy; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that a Society of this Nature, countenanced and 1'upported by the Raws of this Realm, and established upon a respectable and permanent Foundation, and veiled with proper Povvers, for enabling them to carry into Execution their charit?

able JDesigns, of cloathing, fitting out, and apprenticing, or placing out, poor distressed Boys' who have not any visible Means of Support, and who shall voluntarily offer themselves for the Service of the Navy, and of other Ships and Vessels, the Property of, and belonging to.

Great Britain, would be of considerable Use and Ad-r vantage to these Kingdoms: And therefore praying.

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for incorporating the Petitioners, and their Successors, to be elected in such Manner as in the Bill is intended to be mentioned, or as Parliament shall think proper, and for veiling them with due cpnftitutional Powers, for the more effectually carrying on the charitable and useful Designs aforesaid.

Irving’s A Petition of Charles Irving, one of the Surgeons of Sea Water. His Majesty’s Royal Navy, being offered to be prefen ted to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, from a close, unwearied Attention, and Application, to discover a plain and practicable Method of making Sea Water fresh, and fit for drinking, hath, at a very considerable Expence, happily discovered a Method of rendering Sea Water fresh, wholesome, and agreeable to the Taste, and that the Process thereof is plain and simple, and may be carried on at Sea without Difficulty, or any Inconvenience or Hindrance whatsoever to the Business of the Ship; and that the Petitioner hath communicated to the Commissioners of the Admiralty, the Officers of the Royal Navy, to the East India Company, and several others, the Whole of such Process, from which, by repeated Experiments made at it has been

ascertained, that a Quantity of Fresh Water, sufficient fofcthe daily Supply of any Ship or Transport, may be distilled from Sea Water, without any Ingredient whatsoever, and with a very small, if any, Addition to the Fuel necessary for the ordinary Business of the Ship; and that not only the Quality of such Water, but also the Practicability, and great Ease, of producing it from Sea Water in sufficient Quantities, have, as the Petitioner apprehends, been fully proved, as well by the said Experiments as by frequent Practice in the Course of a long Voyage; and, inasmuch as the Petitioner has relinquished all other Pursuits, in order more effectually to make practicable, and to introduce into general Use, so great a National Benefit, and hath thereby impaired his own private Fortune; therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant such public

Reward’to the Petitioner for this l)ifcovery as the Importance thereof shall -deserve.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; And that they do examine, and stale to the House, the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition:

And it is referred to Sir George Colelrooke, Lord Howe,

&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Recordsj and all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.

India, East: A Petition of Gregore late of Bengal, in

Administration the East Indies, on Behalf of himself and others, was of Justice. presentC(j to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner, who is an Armenian Christian, and Native of IfpItalian, in Persia, has for many Years resided in India as a Merchant, particularly in the Provinces of Bengal and its Dependancies, where those of his Nation have ever been allowed to carry on Trade, according to the ancient Usages of those Countries, and even were indulged with certain Privileges in that respect; and that the Petitioner, who has ever strictly conformed himself to the Usages of those respective Countries, has, with many others of his Nation, of late been greatly impeded in their Business as Merchants, by the most cruel, destructive, and injurious, Regulations, and grievously oppressed by long and cruel Imprisonments, and otherwise, by the nominal Nabobs, and other Servants of the English East India Company in Bengal, notwithstanding the Petitioner never in any Degree injured the said Company, nor was ever guilty of any Breach of the Laws, either of or this Nation, to the known Justice of which lad he has already applied for Satisfaction for the great Losses and Injuries he has sustained i and that, when the Petitioner and others have been injured and oppressed by such Imprisonments within the Districts to which His Majesty’s Charter of Justice granted to the said Company is not allowed to extend, they have applied to the said nominal Nabobs of Bengal for Justice, who have referred them and the Petitioner to the President or Secret Committees of Calcutta in Bengal, alledging such Imprisonments to have been effected by their Orders; and when, on the Part of the Petitioner and such other Persons, Application has been made for Justice at Calcutta, to the said Company’s Governor and President of the Secret Committees, they have been referred back to the said Nabobs; and in this grievous Situation, without ever being able to know of what Crime he was accused, the Petitioner by such Evasions, has been ruined, and left without any other Remedy than the precarious Redress which be may possibly obtain from the Courts of Law in this Country, under all the Disadvantages of seeking Justice

in a Foreign Land, at such a Distance from the Scene of Action, without Friends or Money; and that the Petitioner, upon his Arrival in England, was advised to apply to the Directors of the East India Company for Redress, in consequence of the Injuries he had sustained by their Servants Abroad; which the Petitioner accordingly did, in the most humble Manner, but has never yet been able to obtain any satisfactory Answer from that Board; and that the Petitioner is about to return to his Family and Business in Bengal, where, Vol. 33.

535

under the present double Governriient, he is apprehen-five his Person, Property, and Family, as well as the rest of his Nation, will be exposed to greater Hard ships than before, on account of his having applied for Justice in England, unless protected by some effectual Regulations of Government by the British Legislature: Arid therefore praying the House to take this same into Co'nsideration, and grant such Relief in the Premises, with respect to the future Security of Persons and Property in as to the House shall (eem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie u|>oh the Table.

The said Valentine Morris, Esquire, was called in to

against him, " That lie had taken the Writ for the last " Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Monmouth,

" from the Mefl'enger who was sent down to deliver the " said Writ to the Sheriff, and of the Delay in the " Execution of the said Writ;"

He acknowledged, that the said Writ did come into his Hands on the 5th Day of June last, and was not delivered to the Sheriff till the aiftof the same Month; but allured the House, that he did not take the Writ from the Mefl'enger by force; but that the said Meflfen-ger did freely deliver the same to him: That, when he took the Writ, he did not mean thereby to delay the Election; bur l'ome Doubts arising with respect to the Place of Election, and whether the County Court ought not to be held at Monmouth, which he said he much wished, fearing the re would not be a fair Election at Nezvport that he sent several Exprefies to London for the Opinion of Counsel, which delayed the Delivery of the Writ; and that tire said Delay had been very detrimental to his Interest at the Time of the Election; and added, that no Person was blameable for any Part of this Tran fad ion but himself and Samuel Long the Mefl'enger:

And then he was directed to withdraw.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That Valentine Morris, Esquire, having taken the Writ for the last Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Monmouth, from the Mefl'enger who was sent down to deliver the same to the Sheriff, and having delayed the Delivery thereof for Fifteen Days, is thereby guilty of a Violation of the Law, and a Breach of the Privilege of this House; ,

And the previous Question being proposed, That that Question be now put;

The same was, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

Then the main Question being put;

Resolved, That Valentine Morris, Esquire, having taken the Writ for the last Elect ion of a Knight of the Shire to lerve in this present Parliament for the County of Monmouth, from the Mefl'enger who was sent down to deliver the same to the Sheriff', and having delayed the Delivery thereof for Fifteen Days, is thereby guilty of a Violation of the Law, and a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Resolved, That the said Mr. Morris, having acknowledged his Offence, and submitted himself to the House, he be called in, and acquainted by Mr. Speaker, That the House, notwithstanding the Greatness of the Offence, taking Notice of the very full and ingenuous Manner in which he hath acknowledged thp fame, and expressed his Concern for it, doth forbear to proceed any farther against him; and that he be discharged from any further Attendance on this House.

A Petition, of several Owners and Proprietors of Chalk Chalk Wharfs, on the River Thames, and of several Matters and Owners of Colliers and Coasting Vessels, Thame*, in Behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act, made in the Sixth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, for the better Regulation of Laftage and Bailaftage in the River Thames, no greater Quantity of Chalk, or Chalk Rubbish, is allowed to be shipped, transported, or carried as Ballast, from London, or any Part of the River Thames, in any One Year, than 3,000 Tons, or of Flints, and other Commodities enumerated in, the said Act, than 2,000 Tons; and that on the River Thames, between London Bridge and the main Sea, there are several considerable Lime Wharfs, which carry on a very extensive Trade, to London, Westminster, and the Maritime Counties; and that Flints are sold to the Manufacturers of English China or Hardware Chalk, for the Purpose of burning into Lime, or of mending River and Sea Banks, and Chalk Rubbish for the Manure

6 X and

Building* tnd Party Walls.

538 29° Februarii.A. 1773.

and Improvement of Lands; and that the Prices of Flints and Chalk are so high and considerable, it is apprehended that no Mailers of Colliers, or Coalling Vessels, would carry them as Ballad, to be flung into the Sea like common Ballad; and that the Chalk Rubbish is, by the Maders of Coaders and Colliers, sold to the Farmers, for the Purpose of manuring their Land, at the Rate of Two Shillings and Sixpence or Three Shillings a Load; and if not allowed to be taken and carried away from the Lime Wharfs, on board the Colliers and Coaders, mud be removed by Land Carriage at an enormous Expence, or else the Lime and Chalk Works would be choaked up and destroyed; and that the Quantity of Flints, Chalk, and Chalk Rubbish, allowed by the said Act to be transported on board of Vessels as Ballad, is so small and inconsiderable, as to operate but little in removing the Difficulties with which the Lime Trade is burthened, owing, in a great Measure, to this Restriction; and that if a Quantity, not exceeding in One Year 23,000 Tons of Flints, Chalk, and Chalk Rubbish, was allowed to be transported on board of Coaders or Colliers as Ballad, subject to the Regulations prescribed by the said Act, the Proprietors of the Lime Whaifs on the River would be enabled to fell their Lime without an advanced Price, the Manufacturers and Farmers would be supplied with a necessery Article for carrying on their Manufactures, and for improving and manuring their Land, the Maders and Owners of Colliers and Coading Vessels would more easily find Freights for their Ships, and the Public in general would be considerably benefited, by the Increase of Trade, Corn, and other Provisions: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Con-Jkleration, and to give them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and date to the House, the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition:

And it is referred to Mr. Serjeant Sir Robert

Ladbroke, &c.: And they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Younger, Richard Miller Jon, John Rawlinson, and Robert Dodson, Merchants, being Commissioners and Trustees nominated and appointed in, by virtue and in pursuance of, an Act of Parliament, made and passed in the Twenty third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for improving the Navigation of the River Loyne otherwise called Lane, and for building a Quay or Wharf near the Town of Lancaster, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and also of the several other Pep-ions, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Merchants and Traders residing within the Town of Lancaster aforesaid, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition} and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read, whereby it appeared. That One Moiety of the Duties granted thereby expired on the 30th Day of April last: That the Commissioners and Trustees appointed to execute the said Act, are restrained from borrowing any further Sum than £.2,000; and that they are impowered to contract for the Purchase of a certain Building, called The Weigh House, for the Purpose of widening the Road to the new Quay, or Wharf; but have no Power to compel the Proprietors to sell the same.

Mr. William Barrow, being examined, produced an Account of the Receipt and Disbursements of the said Commissioners, by which it appeared, that 2,000 had been borrowed upon the Credit of the said Act, £. 1,100 of which still remains owing upon Bond,

It also appeared by the said Account, that since the Expiration of the said Moiety of the Duties, the Debt is increasing.

The Witness then informed your Committee, That the remaining Moiety of the said Duties is insufficient for carrying on the Works already begun , and that other Works are still necessary for improving the said Navigation.

That it will be necessary, for completing the Purposes of the said Act, to purchase certain Common Pastures or Waste Grounds, near the said River, and also the said Weigh House, which was formerly Part of the Custom House, but is now a Warehouse for Pots:

That the said Act is defective in many Particulars} and that the good Purposes thereby intended cannot be carried into Execution, unless the Commissioners are impowered to borrow a further Sum of Money,

William Lindow, Esquire, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Barrow.

A Petition of the Mayor and Commonalty of the AJr

City of York, and of the Gentlemen and Mer- and Calder chants in the same City, Traders, Owners of Vessels, River!, and others, interested in, or affected by, the Navigation of the Rivers Air and Calder, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That, by virtue of an Act, passed in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of King William the Third, for making the said Rivers navigable, the Tolls and Duties thereby authorized to betaken were vested in the original Undertakers of the said Navigation; and the present Proprietors thereof, claiming under them, are impowered by the said Act to take the Tolls therein mentioned, for Goods carried upon the said Rivers, within the Limits of the said Navigation; and that, by the Increase of the Woollen Manufactures in that Part of the County of York, and the great Increase of Exports from Leeds, Wakefield, and other ;Places, the Yearly Profits of the said Navigation are, and have been for several Years past, very considerable, and are Hill increasing,; and that the said Proprietors might have easily prevented any Impediments, occasioned by. Shoals, and other such Obstructions, in the said Rivers, but the Powers vested in the said Proprietors by virtue of the said Act have been of late very much abused by the Lessee or Agents of the said Proprietors; and that the Peri- -tioners have the great eft Realbn to apprehend, that the real Object of the Proprietors, and the Farmers of the Tolls and Duties, is to facilitate the Design of qoav pleting a Monopoly of the Trade upon the said River:

And therefore praying. That the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves(or. Counsel, against the Petition of, and the Bill applied ;Jor by, the Proprietors of the said

Navigation, or such Parts thereof as may affect t-hq Interest of the Petitioners; ancj that they may ,have lycli further or other Relief in the Premises, as may be' suitable to the Nature of their Cafe, and as the House shall think proper.

That, by divers Acts of Parliament and Charters, the Laftage and Ballastage of all Ships and Vessels in the River Thames is granted to the Petitioners, for clcanlrng and depthening the said River; and the Petitioners apprehend, that if so large a Quantity as 23,000 Tons of Flints, Chalk, and Chalk Rubbish, should Yearly be allowed to be transported, on board of Coasters and Colliers, as Ballad, the same would greatly tend to prejudice the Navigation of the River Thames, and be very injurious to the Trade of this Kingdom, and the Navy of England: And therefore praying. To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Edward Hawkins, being examined, said. That the public Passages within the said Parish are very ill paved, and insufficiently cleansed, and in general greatly obstructed by Nuisances and Encroachments; and it would be a great Benefit to the Inhabitants if they were properly paved and cleansed, and such Obstructions and Nuisances removed.

Then an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for lighting the said Parish, and for regulating the Nightly Watch and Beadles, was read: And,

Mr. William Carter, being examined, laid. That it will be convenient for the Parishioners of the said Parish, if the Provisions for these Purposes were consolidated with the Provisions for the first above mentioned Purposes.

Dissentient.

Because the Liberty of Marriage is a natural Right inherent in Mankind.

Because this Right is confirmed and enforced by the Holy Scriptures, which declare marriage to be of divine Institution, and deny to none the Benefit of that Institution.

Because the Law of Nature and divine Institutions are not reversible by the Power of human Legislatures.

Because there is a total Difference between regulating the Mode of exercising a Right derived from the Law of Nature, and alTuming, or granting, a discretionary Power of taking it quite away.

Because though we think it expedient and agreeable to the Dictates of Reason, that Minors should not marry without the Content of their Parents or Guardians, and that such Content should be necessary to render tjieir Marriages good and valid, as it likewise is in the Exercise of all their other Rights during the Term of their Nonage, it can no more be inferred from thence, that we acknowlege a Right to continue such Restraint throughout their whole Lives, than that we acknowlege a Right to keep Men or Women in a State of endless Nonage, which, unless in the same of Idiots, or incurable Lunaticks, would be absurd, unjust, and a manifest Violation of the Law of Nature.

Because if a perpetual Restraint upon Marriage, or Power given to restrain it, without Limitation of Time or Age, be contrary to the natural and divine Laws (as we apprehend it to be) a Law authorizing such Restraint, or conferring such a Power, must be null and void in itself.

Because in any Case, where the Right of succeeding to the Crown of these Realms may come to depend on the Force or Invalidity of the Power given by this Bill, an Appeal made against it would probably bring upon the Royal Family and the Nation, all the Miseries and Horrors of civil War.

Because, though the placing such a Power in the King, with the Interposition of both Houses of Parliament, is a better Security against the Abuse of it, than if it had been entrusted to the King alone, yet it may be so used, in corrupt or violent Times, as to be made in some Cafes a perpetual Negative on the Freedom of Marriage.

Because, if the Power be grievous and contrary to the inherent Rights of Mankind, the Grievance is increased by the infinite Number of Persons over whom, in the Course of Time, it is likely to extend.

Because we are convinced, that all the good Purposes and Objects of the Bill, which we have greatly at Heart, might have been answered without giving that Perpetuity of Restraint over the Freedom of Marriage, which we think ourselves bound in Conscience to oppose. Radnor, Temple, Abingdon,

Clifton, Lyttelton, Craven.

And because the Bill is essentially wanting to its avowed Purpose, in having provided no Guard against the greater Evil, the improper Marriages of the Princes on the Throne. Radnor.

Manner, that it never has been submitted to the Consideration of the Freeholders; and the Petitioners have the strongest Reason to believe, that not only they, but the greatest Part of the Shire, will be much aggrieved should the said Bill pass into a Law: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, until the Approbation and Concurrence of the Noblemen and Gentlemen, Freeholders of the Shire, shall have been obtained, in the usual fair and regular Manner, at a general Meeting of the Freeholders of the County, held for that Purpose, or to allow the Petitioners to be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Bill pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Bill for repairing and widening the Roads from the Confines of the County of , at or near

Bang house IValls, to Compton's Lanes and Eymouth, and from the Town of Eccles to , and from IV/iite-

law Muir to Compton's Lanes, in the County of Berwick, is committed; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel upon their laid Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

That the said Parishes are of very considerable Extent, and contain a great Number of Inhabitants, and adjoin or are near to the said Manor of Sandhurst; and the Petitioners and others. Inhabitants of the said Parishes, for a great Number of Years previous to the Year 1763, were supplied with Turves and Peat for Fuel at a reasonable Rate, which was a great Advantage and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the said Parishes, and especially to the Poor, as Coal and Wood for Fuel are sold at a high Rate, and the Quantity of Fuel produced is very insufficient for the necessary Consumption of the Inhabitants; and that, since the Year 1763, when, as the Petitioners have beep in-Vot. 33.

formed, Daniel Fox, and Elizabeth Caroline hi*

- Wife, Lord of the said Manor, were restrained from cutting Turves and Peat for Sale from the Waste Lands of the said Manor, the Inhabitants of the said Parishes have been put to considerable Expence and Inconvenience, in purchasing Coal and Wood for Fuel; and that the Petitioners conceive it will be of great Advantage, not only to the Petitioners, but to all the Inhabitants of the neighbouring Parishes, if the Lord of the said Manor for the Time being is . permitted to cut Turves and Peat from the Waste Lands of the said Manor, for Sale: And therefore praying the House, That the said Bill may pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Bill to restrain the Lord of the Manor of Sandhurst, in the County of Berks, for the Time being, from cutting Turves, Peat,

Counties of Lincoln and Northampton, was referred; 1 That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Full wood Saunderson, being examined, said, That the Great Bank of the River Welland, from Spalding High Bridge, through Cohabit, PeakCropland, and

is supported and repaired at the Expence of the Corporation of Bedford Level, Charles Orby , Esquire, and the Adventurers of Deeping Fen.

That the said Bank is too low, and not of sufficient Strength to refill the Waters in Times of Floods; and that if it were made of a sufficient Height and Strength, the Value of tire adjacent Low Grounds would be greatly increased.

That the present Road along the said Bank, and from thence to the Turnpike Road, between Peterborough and Lincoln, is in a ruinous Condition, much too narrow, and inrpaflaole in case of Floods ;and if the same was made safe and commodious, at all Seasons, it would be of great public Advantage: And,

That he apprehends, that the said Road and Rank may be more effectually made and kept in Repair, under the Direction of Commissioners, than by the Laws now in being.

Sir Francis Vincent reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Justices of the Peace for the County of Surrey, was referred; That the Commit-’ tee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Francis Lawson, Esquire, Clerk of the Peace for the County of

Surrey, being examined, said, That the House of Correction in the Borough of Southwark, in the said County of Surrey, is too small, unhealthy, inconvenient, and

unsafe, and was presented as such by the Grand Inquest, at the Assizes at Kingston in April 1770 (which Preferment was produced to your Committee) in consequence whereof, a Committee was appointed by the Justices of the Peace at the Quarter Sessions, to inquire into the State of the said Prison; which Committee reported, That it was absolutely necessary to rebuild the same in a more convenient Situation; and the said Justices, at the last Quarter Session, agreed that a new House of Correction should be built, and the old Building fold — And he produced to your Committee the Report of the said Committee, and the Resolution of the said Justices thereupon.

He further said, That the County of Surrey are possessed of an Acre of Ground, in Saint George's Fields, called White Lyon or Hangman's over which the Owners of Lands in the said" Fields have a Right of Common for their Cattle, at certain Times of the Year, promiseuously with the other Lands, which Piece of Ground is very conveniently situated for the Purpose of erecting the said intended House of Correction; but that by Reason of the Right of Common, claimed as abovementioned, which is not of any Value to the Persons entitled thereto, the County cannot use the same for that Purpose, neither has the County ever received the least Emolument therefrom, the greatest Part of it having many Years been employed as a common Layftall or Dunghill.

Mr.....Gwil/et, a Surveyor, being examined, confirmed the above Evidence, so far as relates to the Condition of the present House of Correction; and added. That as none of the Apartments in the said Prison are separated from one another, Offenders of both Sexes, and for all Crimes, are confined together, which is productive of many Evils, and Inconveniences.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to extinguish the Right of Common upon an Acre of Ground, called White Lyon or Hangman's Acre, in Saint George's Fields, in the County of Surrey: And that Sir Francis Vincent, Mr. Onslow, Mr. Howard, and Sir Joseph Mawbey, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Baldwyn reported from the Committee, to whom Severn

the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, Towinj and Manufacttlrers, residing at Bridgnorth, Brofeley, a Madeley, and Coalhrookdale, in the Count of Salop, and also of the Owners of Barges and Vessels navigated upon the River Severn, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Samuel Jones, an Owner of Vessels navigating on the said River, being examined, laid. That the Navigation between Bewdley Bridge, and a Place called The Meadow Wharf, at Coalbrookdale, in the County c-f Salop, is much

impeded for want of a Towing Path sufficiently broad for the Use of Horses along the Sides of the said River, between the Places aforesaid.

That the present Method of Towing Vessels is with Men, who frequently refuse; and when all the Vessels are employed, there is a great Want of such Men, which hath frequently cauled Delays and Inconveniences: That all Vessels (of which there are between Four and Five hundred employed in the Goal Trade) may navigate between the said Limits at all Times; and by haling of Vessels with Horses, inllead of Men, it would save near Half the present Expence, as it requires Thirty Men to a loaded Vessel, which might be done with.

Three Horses, and be more certain, and less detrimental to the Land Owners, as Men frequently trespals on the Lands, by which the Farmers suffer.

Mr. John White informed the Committee, That he

believes Three-fourths of the Owners of Lands are consenting to the present Application.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making and keeping in Repair a Road or Passage for Horses, on the Banks of the River Severn, between Bewdley Bridge, and a Place called Meadow Wharf, at Coalhrookdale, for haling and drawing Vessels along the said River; and for making Compensation to the Owners of Lands, for as much Ground as may be necessary for that Purpose: And that Mr. Baldwyn, the Lord Pigot, Major Whitmore, and Mr. Gilbert, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Jtamfgate Mr. Alderman Trecothick reported from the Com-

Harbow. mitteo, to whom the Petition of the several Persons whole Names are thereunto fubforibed, being Trustees appointed in pursuance of an Act, made in t he Twenty- ’ second Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, intituled.

An Act for enlarging and maintaining the Harbour of Ramsgate; and for clearifing, amending, and preserving, ^he Haven of Sanehbich, was referred; That the Committee bad examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as foilow-eth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read; whereby it appeared, that all Foreign Ships are* made liable to the same Rates as Ships cleared out or entered in any of the B Ports: And, Mr. John Scott,- Secretary to the said Trustees, said, That the Works have been begun, and carried on, and great Progress made towards completing the said Harbour, which, when finished, will be very useful and commodious, and be of public Utility; in which Works Upwards of £. 120,000 has been expended.

Then another Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for enlarging the Powers granted by the said Act of the 2ad of his late Majesty, was read; whereby it appeared, That the several Sums of Money raised by Annuities, in respect whereof Annuities were then charged upon the said Rates and Duties, amounted to the Sum of £.46,999. 5 4 which; by

the said Act, was increased to^". 70,000: And,

Mr. Scutti nformed your Committee, That the Annual Amount of the Annuities now payable to the Annuitants now existing, is-£. 4,482 10 j.: And,

John Barker, Esquire, one of the Trustees, being asked, how much Money had been borrowed in pur-iuance of the last mentioned Act ? he laid, between Eleven and Twelve Thousand Pounds only, the Trustees ' Vol. 33.

not thinking it eligible to borrow any more, the Security not being so good as if the Act, applied for in the Year 1769, had passed.

Then Mr. Scott, being again examined, said, That from the first collecting of the Rates imposed by the first-mentioned Act, all Ships, as well Foreign as passing on the Outside the Goodwin Sands, have paid the Duties till within thele few Years, it having been determined at the Aflizesat Bodmin, in May 1769,'" That " Shipping failing between the Goodwin Sands and the " Coast of France, are not within the Preamble or " Letter of the Act, or within the actual Benefit of it;" in consequence of which Determination the Payment of the Dunes, which were never refuted before, are now greatly evaded, rendered precarious, and in Danger of being loft.

And he produced to your Committee an Account of Receipts and Disbursements of the said Trustees, from Midsummer 176110 Midsummer 1771, which is hereunto annexed.

And Mr. Evans, Deputy Secretary to the Trustees,

said. That, according to his Calculation, the Duties paid by Foreign Ships in 1760, at Three pence a Ton, amounted to £.850; and in 1771, at Sixpence, about £. 700.

Thomas Nuthall, Esquire, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Scott; and added, That the Rates have been raised from Three Pence Three Farthings to Sixpence a Ton, which is the whole Duty allowed by the Act, and is so great a Burthen, that Ships which used to pay the Three Pence Three Farthings, refuse to pay the Sixpence, pretending the y come round the Goodwin, and therefore not liable to the Rate; by which Means the Revenue falls considerably short of what was intended.

Mr. Stephen Reed, a Filot, being examined , as' to the Utility of the Harbour, said. That a great many Ships, Foreign as well as English, from Three hundred Tons downwards, some drawing Thirteen Feet Water, have been brought into Ramsgate in Distress, many of which have been alhore upon the Goodwin Sands; and one of which, a Ship belonging to Hamburgh,'Of One hundred and-Fifty Tons Burthen, the Witness said he saw bn‘ Shore there, and went on Board; that all her Crew’ had left her, and he brought her into Ramsgate, when after having’ been -repaired, was taken away by the Owners. — He likewise informed your Committee of a Dnntzick Ship, of Four hundred Tons, in Ditfr<*fs, which had passed’ the Back of the Goodwin, the Master whereof wanted to go into Dover Piet; but being'informed there was not Water enough, was obliged to> come into Ramsgate,-where she got'bbw Rigging and

Sails', was fitted oof, and failed again without taking out any Part of her Cargo.

Then lie-produced a Plan of fhoHaibour, which he explained to your Committee; and said, That at the-Pier Heads, at low Water, there is Four or Five Feet Water, and within the Pier Heads from Ten to Fourteen and Fifteen Feet at High Water; and that the Harbour is capable of being made deeper. Then,

Mr. Thomas Preston, a Mason, being examined, said. That the Works remaining to be done for completing the said Harbour will amount to between Fifteen and Twenty Thousand Pounds.

And Mr. Evans produced several Letters from thfc Collectors of the Out Ports to the Secretary, which were read; Whereby it appeared,- that several Matters of Ships havie refused paying the Ramsgate Duty, alledging, that they did not go through the Downs, therefore were not compellable to pay: And,

John Barker, Esquire, being again examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence, with respect'to the Evasion of the Duty, the Utility of the Harbour, and the Decline of* the Income of the Sixpence Duty, in proportion to that of Three Pence; and added, That unless the Duties are put under some more certain Regulation* the Harbour must go to Dellrudion.

A Petition of Leonard Thompson, of Sheriff Hutton, in the County of York, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner observes, by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented, by the Matter, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Corporation of the Trinity House of Deptford Stroud, for Leave to bring in a Bill to veil in them the Duties granted by an Act of the Sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for taking down, removing, and rebuilding, certain Light-houses, near the Spurn Point, at the Mouth of the Humber-, and also a Petition of John for Leave

to bring in a Bill to repeal certain Clauses in the said Act, and for altering and amending other Clauses, so as to enable him to build and erect the said Lighthouses; and that the Petitioner is Tenant for Life of One-fourth Part of the Premises, with such Remainders over, as in the said Act are mentioned; and that the Petitioner, in pursuance of the said Act, has taken down the old Light-houses, and erected Two Temporary Lights, at a great Expence, and would have proceeded to erect Two new Lighthouses, with suitable Offices and Conveniences, but was not able to borrow Money sufficient for that Purpose, on Credit of the said Tolls and Duties, owing (as the Petitioner believes) to the vexatious Disturbances and Obstructions of the said John and

his Agents; and that the Petitioner applied to the said Corporation, who thereupon undertook, and are now proceeding in erecting the Two new Lighthouses, according to the said Act; and that the Petitioner hopes, Provision may be made in the said Bill for repaying the ’Petitioner all his Expences and Disbursements already incurred; and that the Petitioner’s Life Estateinthp laid Lighthouses and Duties be not thereby impeached, or subjected to any further Payment than the Interest of the Money charged or to be charged on the said Fourth Part: And therefore praying, That the Petitioner may be heard, by himself or his Counsel, against the said Petition of the said John Angell; and that the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and protest the Property of the Petitioner, and grant him such further and other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Matter, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Corporation of the Trinity House of Deptford Second, is referred; and that they do examine the Matter of this Petition ;. and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Criminal Sir Charles Bunbttry reported from the Committee, Laws, who were appointed to consider of so much of the Criminal Laws, as relate to Capital Offencesand to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House, That they had considered the same accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the Housej and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

ReJ'ohed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Seventh Year of Henry the Seventh, intituled. The Penalty of a Captain or Soldier, retained to serve the King in his intended "Wars not doing their Duty, as subjects Offenders to Death, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the-First and Second Years of Philip and Mary, intituled, An Act against certain Persons, calling themselves Egyptians, as subjects Offenders to Death, be repealed.

RcJ'ohed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Fifth Year of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, An Act for further Punishment of Vagabonds calling themselves Egyptians, as subjects Offenders to Death, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the 35th Year of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, An Act to retain her Majesty’s Subjects in their due Obedience, as subjects Offenders to Death, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 39th Year of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, An Act for taking away of Clergy from Offenders against a certain Statute made in the 3d Year of Henry the Seventh, concerning the taking away of Women against their Wills unlawfully, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the 21st Year of ‘ James the First, intituled, An Act to prevent the destroying and murdering Bastard Children, as subjects the Offender to Death, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Ninth Year of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act to make an Attempt on the Life of a Privy Counsellor, in the Execution of his Office, to be Felony without Benefit of Clergy, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Ninth Year of George the Second, intituled, An Act for building a Bridge across the River Thames, from New Palace Yard, in the City of Westminster, to the opposite Shore, in the County of Surrey, as subjects the Offender to Death, be repealed.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

Mr. Dundas reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Tanners in and near the City of London, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Tanners in Great Britain-, and also, the Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, and Commonalty, of the Art or Mystery of the Curriers, of the City of London, were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petitions; a Slate whereof they had directed him to report to the House; and be read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth:

A State of the Matter of Fad contained in the said Petitions is as followeth; viz.

An Act of the Ninth Year of His present Majesty, for permitting the free Importation of certain Raw Hides and Skins from Ireland, and the British Plantations in America, was read: And an Account of the Raw Hides and Skins exported since the Commencement of the said Act, to Christmas 1771, was laid before your Committee, which Account is annexed in the Appendix, N° I; by which it appears, that the Number of Raw Hides exported from the 5th of July 1769 were 27,431, and no Calf Skins; and the Raw Hides imported were 287,494, with 50,778 Dozen and Seven Calf Skins.

That your Committee could find no better Way of ascertaining the Increase of Slaughter, than by an Account of Neat Cattle Annually fold in Market

for Forty Years last pall, by which it appears, that the Number of Cattle so fold have increased in some Degree; but from the Year 1769 to the Year 1771, the Time mentioned in the Petition, Slaughter has increased from 82,131 to 93,573; which Account is annexed in the Appendix, N° II.

It appeared, by the Evidence of Mr. James Warm and Mr. Isaac Miller, Tanners, that Raw Hides are reduced in Price 15 or 20 per Cent, in the last Three Years; and Mr. Warne, who is a Facftor as well as,a Tanner, said, he had Reason to believe, that the Slaughter of Cattle near London was increased, as his Commissions for Raw Hides have considerably dccreased in the last Year, which he apprehends are supplied by the Slaughter in their own Markets: And by an Account produced by Mr. Robert Bell, it appeared, that from the Year 1769, the Time mentioned in the Petition, Hides had been reduced from 31 s. 4 to 22 Hundred Weight.

By an Account produced by Mr. Isaac Miller, extracted from his Bcwks for Thirty Years, antecedent to the Alt of the Ninth of His Majesty, for allowing the Importation of Raw Hides Duty-free, it appeared that the Price of Oak Bark at London had risen from £. 5 for a Load of Hatch, by which is meant 45 Hundred Weight of Bark, to f. 8. 5. for which it fold in the Year 1768; and the same Bark in 1769 fold from £.8. to to £.9. 5.; in the Year 1770 from to

That from an Account from the Navy Office, it appeared that several Contracts had been made for Winter-felled Timber, for the Use of His Majesty’s Navy, whereby it is agreed, that £.7. 5 j. in the hundred Pounds, over and above the Prices contracted for, is allowed to lie paid for Winter-felled Timber (that is. Timber felled between the First of December and the 15th of February) but from an Observation at the Bottom of the said Account, it appears that no Winter-felled Timber has been delivered into His Majesty’s Yards in consequence of those Contracts; but the Date of the First Contrail of this Kind appears to be so late as the toth of September last, so that there has been little more than Three Months Time for the Execution of these Contrails: The said Account is annexed in the Appendix, N° VII.

From the Evidence of Mr. ‘Thomas , a Tanner in Sussex, it appeared that Timber was felled in many

different Parts of that County in Winter, by which the Bark was loft; and that the Time for barking Timber is April, May, and some Part of June.

By the Ail of the 20th Charles the Second, Cap. 5, it appeared that a Duty of One Shilling per Hundred Weight was laid on all Leather exported j and by the Ail of the 9th of Queen ACap. n, an Excise of One Penny per Pound is laid upon all tanned Leather, and an additional Halfpenny by an Act of the 10th Year of her said Majesty’s Reign, Cap. 26; and by the said Ail a Drawback is allowed of Two-thirds, or One Penny in the Pound, upon Exportation j and the Duty

of Excise appeared by the Evidence of several Dealers in Leather to amount to about per Cent. Two-thirds of which is drawn back upon Exportation, so that the Excise paid upon exported Leather amounts to about Five per Cent, to which must be added, the said Duty of One Shilling per Hundred Weight, granted by the Ail of the 20th of Charles the Second.

And it appeared by the Evidence of Mr. William Newman, that he has exported great Quantities of Leather to Italy and up the Straits, but that he has been obliged' to refuse Orders, to the Amount of several thousand Hides in a 'Year, because the Merchants can be supplied with the same in Ireland, from 10 to 15 Cent, cheaper than he can do it; that there is no Excise or Duty on Leather in Ireland, which he apprehends to be the principal Reason of their under-felling the Englishr, to which may be added, the Scarcity of Inhabitants in that Country, and the great Slaughter on account of viilualling Ships for Foreign Trade.

Wilts, or some or one of them, on Behalf of themselves and others. Owners and Occupiers of Land in the said Parishes and places, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have been informed, that a Bill is depending, to authorize the Lord of the Manor of Sandhurst, for the Time being, to cut Turves, Peat, Heath, and Fern, Annually, upon such Quantity of Land, Part of the Waste Lands of the said Manor, as in the said Bill is mentioned, and to felland dispose of such Turves, Peat, Heath, and Fern; and alledging, That the said Parishes. are of very considerable Extent, and contain a great Number of Inhabitants, and adjoin, or are near to, the said Manor; and the Petitioners and others. Inhabitants of the said Parishes, for a great Number of Years previous to the Year-1763, were supplied with Turves and Peat for Fuel purchased of the Lord of the said Manor, for the Time being, from the Waste Lands of the said Manor, at a reasonable Rate, which was a great Advantage and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the faicT Parishes and Places, and especially to the Poor, as Coal and Wood for Fuel are sold at a high Rate, and the Quantity of Fuel produced is very insufficient for the necessary Consumption of the Inhabitants; and that, since the Year 1763, when, as the Petitioners have been informed, Daniel Fox and Elizablth Caroline his Wife, Lord of the said Manor, were restrained from cuttingTurves and Peat for Sale, from the Waste Lands of the said Manor, the Inhabitants of the said Parishes and Places have been put to considerable Expence and Inconvenience, in purchasing Coal and Wood for Fuel; and that the Petitioners conceive, it will be of great Advantage not only to them, but to all the Inhabitants of the neighbouring Parishes, if the Lord of the said Manor, for the Time being, is permitted to cut Turves and Peat, from the Waste Lands of the said Manor, for Sale, as the Inhabitants will not only be thereby in a great Measure relieved from the Inconvenience they have long laboured under, by being again supplied with Turves and Peat for Fuel, and the Price of other Fuel will, by such Sale, as the Petitioners apprehend, be reduced in the said Parishes and Places:

And therefore praying, that the said Bill may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Bill to restrain the Lord of the Manor of Sandhurst, in the County of , for the Time

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty, for taking down and removing certain Lighthouses, Rinding near the Spurn Point, at the Mouth of the Humber, and for erecting other fit and convenient Lighthouses instead thereof, was read: And,

Mr. William Hammond, being examined, said. That pursuant to the Directions of the said Act, Mr. son has taken down the old Lighthouses at the Spur* Point, and built temporary Lights at his own Expence, to the Amount of about £. 600; which Lights are now kept burning: And,

Mr. Charles Wyldbore, chief Clerk to the Trinity House of Deptford Strond, being examined, said, that the Elti-mate for building the temporary Lights was —

That Application had been made to the Trinity House by Mr. Thompjvn, to take the Lighthouses under their Care, which they contented to do, and had proceeded to erect Two new ones, according to a Plan made by Mr. Smeaton, which he produced to the Committee, and entered into a Contraft with Mr. Taylor, an Architect, which was also produced, for building the same according to an Estimate given in by him, amounting to £.3,300; and that they had appointed the said Mr. Smeaton Surveyor of the Works, with a Salary of co per Ann.; and he further laid, That the Trinity House have already expended upwards of £. 1,000 on and about the said Lighthouses: Then,

Mr. William Taylor, the Person contracted with, informed your Committee, That he had begun to execute his Contraft, and had completed the Foundation of One of the Lighthouses, and provided Materials for the other: That he has been very frequently obstructed in carrying on the Works by Mr. Angell'% Agents, was compelled to quit the House lent him by Mr.

and was served with a Writ on the 13th of last June, at the Suit of the said Mr. An; the Consequence of which was, intimidating a great many of his People — That Mr. Worth, Agent for Mr. Angell, told him, he was going to erect Lights there himself, and in last discharged the Witness’s People from working; telling them, they should be prosecuted with the utmost Severity for a Trespass; and said, He had Directions from Mr. Angell to destroy them and their Works: — That he repeatedly interrupted the Workmen, compelled them to lay down their Burthens, and threw the Materials about — That he inveigled away the Witness’s Men, by ottering double Wages, and threatened the Witness so far, as to make it necessary for him to keep a Guard Night and Day, and several of his Workmen left him — That Mr. Worth hired or 13 People, and began to dig on the Spot where the Witness meant to erect the High Light — That the Witness and his People watched their Motions, and kept themselves on their Defence, and desired him to desist — That Mr. Worth told him he should not live long on the Spurn Point-, but on being asked, if he meant to shoot the Witness, he gave no Answer: — That the Witness then applied to the Justices of the Peace, who granted an Order for Mr. Worth's Appearance at Beverley Sefixons, to which he was bound, but did not appear — and that the Matter has since been removed by Certiorari into the King’s Bench, but nothing has been done upon it; Arfti the Witness concluded his Evidence with saying, that the abovementioned Obstructions were the Caules why the Works did not go on so expeditiously as they ought to have done.

Upon his cross Examination, he was asked, Whether he had ever seen Mr. Worth before he met him on the Spurn Point, or whether he knew, of his having any Connections in that Neighbourhood ? To which he an* fwered. That he did not know that he had any Connections there: — That he told him he lived in,

That the Petitioners conceive the Grounds belonging to Their Majesties within the said Manor might be greatly improved, if the Footpath or Lane leading from Richmond Green to the River ’Thames was (hut up and di(-continued, which will be of no Inconvenience to the Petitioners, as there is another Footpath leading from the said Green down Palace Lane to the River Thames, and along the Banks thereof, to Two Foot Ferries belonging to His Majesty, one called Railhead Ferry, and the other Isleworth Church Ferry; and that the Petitioners have Reason to believe. Their Majesties are willing to amend the said Palace Lane, and raise the Banks of the said River to the said Ferries in such Manner as that the same shall be passable at all Times, in case the said Lane which divides the Ground before-mentioned shall be {hut up and discontinued: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the said Bill, for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as the House shall think fit.

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Mer- Turkey chants of England, trading into the Levant Seas, being Comply, offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth. That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has, for a long Series of Years, been carried on by a Society of Merchants, incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on the said Trade with* Safety, and to proteCfc His Majesty’s Subjects in the T Dominions, it has been found necessary that there should be an Am* baflador sent from England to reflde at Confiantinople \ and that there should be Consuls, Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, in the other Parts of Turkey, where any British Subjects reside, and where the English carry on Trade, the whole Expence whereof has been borne by the Turkey Company, which, together with other necessary Expences incident to the carrying on the said Trade, has of late Years amounted to upwards of £. 10,000 per Annum; and that the said Trade to and from Turkey, once so flourishing, is now, from many unavoidable Events and concurring Circumstances, much reduced; and that the Assistance which was granted to the Petitioners in the last Session, was employed in paying off a Part of the Debt which they had incurred, and in supporting their necessary Expences; and they had Reason to hope, that they should not now have been under a Necessity of applying for farther Assistance, nor should they now have troubled the House, but for the great Stagnation of Trade and Increase of Expence occasioned by the War which still subsists between the Turkifit and the Russian Governments; and that the Petitioners are sensible that they should not discharge the Duty incumbent upon them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public, if they did not declare their Inability to support their necessary Expences, unless relieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Confident* tion, and to grant them such further Assistance as may be thought necessary and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

cott, Somerton, Pitney, Wearn, Wootton, and Long Sutton, in the County of Somerset, having Right of Common on King's Sedgmoor, in the same County, were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had heard the Petitioners, on the Two first mentioned Petitions, by their Counsel; and that the Committee had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. William Fairchild, a Surveyor, being examined, said. That he had surveyed and measured the said Moor, called Sedgmoor, and contains about Eighteen thousand Acres; which, in general, is a Morals, by reason of the Waters, Handing on it, and in some Winters is very deep; but Part of it, next to the present Rhines and Ditches, is pretty dry; that the Whole is nearly on a Level, and is low in Comparison to the adjoining Lands; that it is seldom fit for Cattle more than Two or Three Months in the Year with Safety; that they generally put Black Cattle and Sheep thereon, but is certain Destruction to Sheep, and in its present State is not worth more than Eighteen Pence an Acre, but if drained, and rendered dry and healthy, and divided into distinct Commons, it would in Two or Three Years, be worth Twenty-five Shillings an Acre; and if divided into particular Inclosures, and properly divided among the separate Owners, in a Term of Years the Whole would be worth Thirty Shillings an Acre, or more, some Part being worth that at present, and would be an Advantage to the Public: — That the said Moor is from Ten to Twelve Miles in Length, and on an Average, Two Miles Three Quarters in Breadth; that he could not say whether it is easy to prevent Trespasses, but suppoles it might be done by Persons having the Care of it: — That he has taken the Levels instrumentally, and finds it capable of being drained; that the Fall from Bradney Bridge, the lowell Part of the Moor, to a Place called Nine Streams, will be between Fifteen and Sixteen Feet, which is about Three Miles in Length. — Being asked, What Fall there is in the present Drain ? he said, The Northern Part of the Moor is lower than the Mouth of the Cloys, which are meant to drain the Moor — That the making Drains for draining the Moor, will contribute, and may be made Part of the Drains for dividing the Commons — That the Expence of draining the said Moor would amount to about Two thousand Pounds; but said, he was not a Judge of the Expence of dividing it.

Being cross examined, he said, He had been acquainted with the Moor Ten Years, and had beer, on it many Times, but could not say how often, though had been there in surveying Estates in the Neighbourhood, and plcafuring, such as Horse Races. — Being asked. Whether he had Occasion to make any Observation on the Moor till the present Application to Parliament ?

he

12 Geo. III. 2° jdprilis.

he said. He had not measured it, but had observed it:

— That he had often rode across the Moor, and observed the Grass and Soil: — And being asked, Whether he had ever been on Half the Acres in his Life ? he said. He did not know but he might in crossing it at several Times, and there was no Part of it he had not viewed; and he judges of the Nature of the Soil by the Rhines and Ditches, and by what he fees upon the Ground: — That he does not know the Number of Cattle or Sheep fed on the Moor. — Being asked. Whether he knew Cattle rot on the Moor ? he said, He had seen Sheep dead thereon; and that there are some large Flocks of Sheep, but could not say there are many: — That during the Summer Three Months it will not support One Beast to an Acre, and not more than Three or Four Sheep well, and is dangerous to put Sheep there; but when Farmers have a large Stock and no where else to keep them, they are glad to put them there: — That he judged by those Parts, which are at present dry, it would be worth Twenty-live Shillings an Acre when drained.

— Being asked, What the said Moor would be worth an Acre, if only drained ? he said. About Twenty Shillings — That he' has traversed the Moor at different Times, and believes in a very dry Summer the Moor would not sustain Eighteen thousand Cattle the whole Summer, except the last, which was the dried he had known these Ten Years. — Being asked. What Proportion the present Part, which is worth Twenty-five Shillings an Acre, bears to the rest of the Moor? he said,

Plain, which is about Three hundred Acres, is worth Twenty-five Shillings an Acre, and there are about Six hundred Acres more, nearly as good; and the Remainder is worth about Eighteen Pence.

That he was not interrupted in taking the Levels of the Moor, but had not surveyed it accurately, being prevented, and was told if he proceeded, he should receive Damage, and was threatened with his Life; and they went so far as to dig his Grave: That there were an Hundred or two met him; and a Reward of a Hogshead of Cyder offered to any one that would catch him.

Mr. Sylvanus Lake, a Farmer and Grazier, being examined, said. That he has lived in the Neighbourhood of Sedgmoor Common Seven Years, and has exercised a

Right of Common thereon Six Years; that the said Common is, in wet Summers, overflowed the whole Year, but in dry temperate Seasons, is fit for Cattle about Twenty Weeks, and in some Summers not Two Months, but upon an Average of Seven Years, it may be fit Three Months: — That his Cattle has frequently suffered from the Witness of the Moor, and has known Objections made at Fairs and Markets on account of their coming from Sedgmoor, the Nature of the Grass being such, as changes the Colour of the Hair of the Cattle, which is a Sign they are not healthy; that Sheep frequently cooth, and Cattle scour.

That the said Moor is Eleven or Twelve Miles in Length, and Two or Three broad, and he has experienced Inconveniences from the Extent of it by Plough Cattle getting Five or Six Miles from Home; and that he once loft a Horse Twelve Months, and found him on the Common at last; and thinks if the said Moor was divided into separate Commons, it would be advantageous to every Tenant and Occupier of Lands: — That there are frequent Trespasses thereon, which are not easily to be prevented in its present State; and he apprehends it is practicable of being drained by a certain Number of Drains, and which he thinks would operate to drain the Moor; and that any Division of the same would tend to increase the Value.

Being crol's examined, he said, That the Cattle which were objected to at Fairs were lean, the Moor being chiefly used for breeding, and not fatting: — That Cattle are generally poorer which come from Commons, but this is the wettest in the Country: — That there is a great Quantity of rich Land for fatting Cattle in jetshire, and it is generally agreed that Somersetjiire is not adapted so well for breeding as Devonshire. — Being

asked, If there is a Proportion of breeding, to fatting, King'* Land in Somersetshire ? he said. There is a great deal Sedgmoor

called fatting Land not fit for the Purpose, but is ap- "He* plied to it. — Being asked. If there were not great Numbers of Cattle bred on the Moor ? he said, They were brought there, but rarely fall there, being an improper Place, though it sometimes happens: — That Sheep are folded from the Moor upon the Arable Lands near. —

Being asked. If it was not the usual Course of Husbandry, for Farmers to do this ? he said, In certain Years they do, otherwise they decline it, for he had baned his Flock by it: — That Farmers usually turn out their Plough Cattle on the Moor, and then close up their Meadows for railing of Hay: — That the Difficulty of preventing Trespasses arises from the Gates leading to the Moor, which by Accident fall down, and by being left open, so that the neighbouring Farmers Cattle get in, and does not know they have any Right, for on Driving the Common, Cattle have been found which have had no Owners.

That the said Moor might be divided by multiplying the Ditches, and would not be dangerous to Cattle, as some Farms have no other Fence, though such Ditches would.waste some Land, but would increase the Value; that it is difficult to ascertain the Value of the Land, for" in some Years it is worth nothing, some Seven Shillings an Acre, others Four Shillings, and believes if it was only drained, it would be worth from Sixteen Shillings to near Twenty Shillings an Acre; but a Division would be advantageous to every Person who has Right of Common, and greatly so to Cottagers, as it.would improve the Land, and Persons would give more for such Right to enjoy as they now do, and be in less Danger of losing their Cattle.

That the Right of feeding on the Moor is in the Lords of Manors, but the actual Enjoyment is in the Tenants: — That Hundreds enjoy this Right, but could not say Thousands, and always understood the Tenants put on all their Cattle without Stint: — That if it was divided into Parish Commons, it might be an Improvement, perhaps to the Amount of Seven Shillings and Six Pence an Acre; and if it was made dry, it would not be prudent to convert it into Arable; and the inclosing it would be an Advantage to the Poor, as they would be employed in trenching, fencing, and' Hay-making, and thinks there would be additional Employment, by frequently cleansing of Ditches; that their present Employment is in Tillage, but there is none on the Moor.

That he cannot say what Number of Sheep are folded from the Moor, but there are not more than Eight hundred or One thousand Acres of it, upon which People will suffer their Sheep to go; and it would be more advantageous if the Moor could be made capable of fatting, than breeding. Cattle: — That People put on their Stock in the Moor which they cannot maintain in the Winter, and has heard it argued as to the Right, but they have always turned in at all Times of the Year at Discretion:

— That he cannot lay what Number of Geese are fed on the Moor, but believes Ten or Twenty thousand, and the greatest Number is at Michaelmas.

That if the Moor was drained, the Graft would be as good as if it was inclosed, but would be more advantageous if divided into separate Commons, and the Right more beneficial to the Commoners, as Cattle do much better in small Herds than in large; and the Poor would be greatly benefited, as the Cottagers frequently let their Right of Common (few having Stock of their own) for about a Guinea, but never heard for more; and that there may be an Hundred or Two of such, and are let to Persons out of Dorsetshire and , some

of whom have brought Forty or Fifty Head of Black Cattle.

Being asked. Whether a greater Extent of Grazing Right upon the Common of Sedg, is of less Value than a iinaller Extent divided off? he said, Yes, because Persons would with more Ease survey their Cattle,
