To prove the Allegations of the Second mentioned Petition.

Mr. Richard Hayes, being examined, said. That he is Sixty-six Years old, and has lived at on the Borders of Sedgmoor, Fifty Years, and knows every Part of the Moor: That there may be One thousand Acres of Land near , which are in

their present State, one with another, worth Thirty Shillings an Acre: — That the Lands near Somerton, Compton Dundon, Grienton,

linch, Sutton, Stowell, Bazvdrand are of

different Values; those lying near the Parishes may be worth, on an Average, Thirty Shillings an Acre, and there areThree or Four thousand Acres of that Value; but the'best Land lies near Sutton Mallet, Dumvare, and Weston Zoyland, which are worth from Thirty-five to Forty Shillings an Acre: — That in the other Parts of the Moor there may be Three or Four thousand Acres worth Fifteen or Sixteen Shillings an Acre, and some not Sixpence, according to the Time of the Year; and thinks the whole Eighteen thousand Acres, on an Average, may be worth Fourteen Shillings an Acre in its present State, and will maintain Two Bullocks and Two Sheep on each Acre during the Summer; that young Cattle, Cows, and Plough Oxen, are generally put on in or May, and are kept there till near Michaelmas, according to the Season; and young Cattle are kept there all the Winter.

That large Flocks of Sheep are depastured, and a great Part are kept all the Year there, which are folded on the Arable Land, and put on the Moor in the Day to feed: — That a great Nnmber of Mares foal thereon, which, with the Mares, remain all the Year together, with many young Bullocks, but cannot tell the Number of Bullocks, being sometimes great and others small, it depending on the Season; and believes they are seldom baned there, as he never knew of any; and that the Moor is not moire liable to bane Sheep than the Inclosures: — That some Welsh Cattle are made fat on the Moor, and fit for the Butcher.

That Trespasses may be easily prevented if looked after; and has known several detected this Year, and also in Years pad: — That the said Moor has always been open, and the Right of Common is in those who have Estates of their own, and those who rent them in the several Villages mentioned in the Petition, except Charlton Mackarel and Charlton Adam, and the Tenements of Four or Five Pounds a Year have as much Right as a Farm of One hundred Pounds a Year: — That the Tenements called Auftre Tenements, which are Parts of old Houses or the Scites thereof, have as unlimited a Right of Common as a Man of the greatest Estate; and that all the Commoners have a Right, and been accustomed to departure all their Cattle on the Moor at all Times of the Year without Stint.

That if a Drain was to be opened the Length of the Moor, from Somerton to Crandon Bridge, the Lands about Weston, Chedzoy. Dunware, Bower, Haufey, and Places adjacent, would be subject to be overflowed.

That there are many Tenements, from Five to Fifty Pounds a Year, which are occupied by the Owners, who maintain themselves by their Produce and the Right

of Common, and would be greatly injured by the Inclosure, and for Want of the Produce of the Moor, and the Expence of inclosing, would oblige the Owners of such Tenements to fell them, and some would be dif-treffed, though not obliged to fell: — That the poor Cottagers get their Subsistence entirely from the Moor, of whitfi there are Twenty or Thirty in the Parish of Weston, though some have less, who have all a Right of Common, and the rest of the Parishes have the same Number, one with another, who have a Right from old Auftres; and there are from Ninety to One hundred Rights of Common in the Parish of Weston, including Three or Fourscore Farms.

That the breeding of Cattle would be diminished by inclosing, as there would be less Grass, by reason of the Drains and Ditches, and should not be able to keep the Number of Cattle, for at present they have the Run of the whole Herbage, but would then be confined, but if only drained, Cattle would have the same Run as at present: — That Agriculture of the high Grounds would be diminished by inclosing the Moor, as the feeding would be less and not so good, and Danger to the Cattle falling into the Ditches necessary for dividing the fame: — That Roads cannot be made but at a great Expence, there being no Stone or Materials nearer than Five or Six Miles, and Stones would fink, the Soil being so soft; and the general Sense of the Country is against inclosing: — That when the Moor hath received the utmost Improvement by draining, there will be a great Difference in Value of some Parts to others, and the greater Part will not receive Improvement, and it is not possible to judge to Exadtnels of Five or Six Shillings an Acre, what Improvement it will receive by such draining; and if it could, without subjecting the Lands to be overflowed by the necessary Drains, it would be no Advantage, because there would be no Water in the Summer; but if properly drained it would be an Improvement, and thinks dividing it would not, as the Roads to the different Divisions would be impassable, and there can be no Division for the several Parishes to come without Roads, except from the Parish of Weston, and that it is impossible, if the Moor was divided into Thirty-five Commons, to make Roads that every Parish could enjoy their Right of Common in their respective Allotments, as there are several Parishes far from the Moor, and cannot be made without coming to some Part of the low Grounds, and they could not get to all the Divisions without them; and that it is impossible to make Roads over the fame, a great Part being a Morass, and no Bottom to be found at Thirty Feet deep.

That there are several poor People in his and the Parishes adjacent, permitted by the Commoners to keep some small Stock on the Moor, who have no Right, in order to prevent their becoming chargeable to their Parishes, and if divided would be a Means of making them so; that there are Five or Six such Poor in his Parish, and may be One hundred, or more, in the other Parishes: — That there is a great Scarcity of Labourers in the Summer Time in the said Parishes, and if turned out of their Habitations, it would be more so, thele Cottages being a Nursery for them.

That there are many young Bullocks bred on the Moor, and fatted by the Help of a little After-grass near it, which would not be if inclosed: — That the Graziers in Somersetshire are obliged to go into other Counties to buy lean Cattle, to the Amount of many Hundreds, and bring the re to be fatted, and would be more so if the Moor was inclosed: — That it is usual to fella great Number of Calves fallen in Somersetshire to Farmers in Devonshire, which when grown up are brought again into Someijetshire to be fatted; and Cattle for the

Plough are kept on the Moor in Summer, and the inclosed Pastureand Meadow Ground is thereby relie*^^ to furnish Hay and Grass for their Winter’s SuirjjftenCe. That it is very difficult and expensive to get other Manure, than by folding Sheep on the hjlly and high

Being cross examined, he said, He meant Trespasses might be prevented by driving the Prey, which had been done this Year, and Twenty, Thirty, or Forty, Cattle detected, or perhaps more, and Sixteen of them from one Person, and were found on the Moor near Weston: — That the People of and Chedxoy joined

Edward Conduit, being examined, said. That he is Fifty-eight Years old, has lived at Chedxoy between Forty and Fifty Years, and knows the Nature and Soil of all Parts of King's Sedgmoor, which is open and uninclosed; that the Land is of different Qualities, and that which adjoins to the Parishes and Hamlets of Bridge-water, Dunware, Weston Zoyland,

Compton Dundon, Pedwell, Greinton, Sutton,

Stow ell, Bawdrip, and Chedxoy, which all border on the Moor, is very good Land, and is worth Thirty Shillings an Acre or upwards, and there is between Three and Four thousand Acres of that Value; that the best Land lies near Weston, Dunware, Chedxoy, and Sutton, and thinks the whole Moor one Acre with another, and one Year with another, is worth Sixteen Shillings an Acre, in its present State: — That it will maintain Two Bullocks and Two Sheep an Acre the Year round, except when flooded, and Four Bullocks for Four Months, from the Beginning of May; and from the Beginning of September, to the Beginning of January, Two; and from that Time to May, Two Bullocks and Two Sheep.

— The Dairy Cows and Plough Oxen are put on the Beginning of May, and continue so till near and great Quantities of Sheep are depastured there all the Year, which are generally folded on the inclosed Arable Lands in the Neighbourhood, to manure and improve the fame; other Manure being not to be got but at a great Expence: — That many Calves and Foals are fallen on the Moor, and the Mares and other Horses for the Plough, and many Colts and young Bullocks are kept there all the Year; and he never knew a Bullock baned there in his Life, and is not apt to bane Sheep more than other Places; a great Part of the inclosed Lands will bane them as loon or sooner than the Moor, and that a great many young Bullocks are bred and fatted thereon, with the Help of a little After-grass in the inclosed Grounds near it: That he never exercised the Right of Common himself more than Two Years.

That the Right of Common is in those who have Estates of their own, or rent them, and those who have small Cottages — Being asked, What an old Auftre is? he said. An old House, or the Scite thereof, the Occupier of which has as much a Right as a Man of One hundred

fetshire, to Farmers in Devonshire, which when grown up, are brought again into to be fatted. —

That Agriculture and Tillage of the high and dry Grounds, would be lessened by inclosing the Moor, for that Cattle for the Plough, Dairy Cows, and other Cattle, are kept thereon in the Summer; and the inclosed Meadow and Pasture Ground is thereby relieved to furnish Hay and Grass for their Winter Subsistence. — That the high and hilly Ground surrounding the Moor, is of a very poor and barren Nature, a great deal of it not being worth above Two Shillings and Sixpence, and some Seven Shillings and Sixpence an Acre, which, if the Moor was inclosed, would be of no Value.

That Cattle are frequently drowned in the Ditches and Rhines in the present State of the Moor, which if increased, the Danger of losing Cattle would also be increased in proportion thereto: — That the Soil in many Parts of the Moor is very soft and rotten, and in some Parts no Bottom to be found, and there may be near Two thousand Acres of such Land in different Parts; and it is impossible to make Roads without a great Expence, Stones and Materials being at a great Distance; and the Sentiments of People interested in the Moor, and also the Proprietors of Lands in general, are against inclosing the fame; and that it would be difficult, and could not be done, on Account of the different Natures of the Soil, to make a just Division thereof into separate Commons, and apprehends, would

occasion Disputes and Quarrels; and many of the Commoners would be deprived of digging Turves, and cutting Sedge and Rushes thereon; and that if a Common was to be inclosed to each Parish, it would not be the Advantage it is at present.

would not be any further Improvement, because Cattle are at present frequently mired there, and as then there must be more Ditches, the Flies would drive them more into them; and it cannot be divided by Hedges, the Soil being so bad, and if it could be done would be prejudicial, because the more Liberty the Cattle have on the Ground the better it is, by their having different Sorts of Grass, and there is no Inconvenience from the great Number grazing together as they now do. — That Cattle frequently range from one End of the Moor to the other, but not generally, which is no Inconvenience, as they easily find them; though he once loft a Beast for Forty Weeks, and has known it happen to others, but very rare, and this was the only Instance which happened to him in Thirty Years; that the Moor being lurrounded by Hills, there arc frequent Breezes from different Quarters, and Cattle now grazing at large go to those Points for the Benefit of those Breezes, and Cattle confined on inclosed Commons, where there is no Shade, could not be kept so well, as when they have the Liberty of the whole Moor; that the inclosing the same would be the Ruin of several poor Families, who now keep a Bullock or a Horse thereon, and have a Right to get Firing, which they would not then have. — That Firing is not to be bad on all Parts of the Moor. — That Turves are to be had about Midlezoy, which is the only Part he knows; and does not know, that any other poor People cut them except those of that Place; but it is understood, the Poor have a Right to cut Turves all over the Moor, as well as to graze. — That the Commoners have a Right to cut Sedge on all Parts of the Moor, but there are only Two Places where it grows, which may be about One hundred and Fifty Acres, but is sure not Two hundred.

Being asked. Whether a Right of Common is better over One hundred Acres worth Five Shillings an Acre, or Five hundred Acres worth only One Shilling? he said, He would rather have a Right over the Hundred Acres.

That there are between Fifty and Sixty Tenements in Midlezoy, called Old Auftres, which he explained to be an old House, or Spot of Ground where a House flood, which have Right of Common; and about Six who claim a Right from such Spots of Ground; and that there is no other Right, and believes there may be about Half a Score of such Tenements occupied by the Owners.

That each of the several Parishes and Places mentioned in the Petition, except Charlton Mackerel and Charlton Adam, have a drift Way to the Moor; and the Owners of such Old Auftre Tenements have a Right to put on all their Cattle without Stint, and hath heard ancient People, who are since dead, say the fame; and has known One Commoner, who may have rented Forty Pounds a Years, put on Forty Head of Cattle, and many poor Persons in the different Parishes are permitted to keep some Stock thereon, to prevent their becoming chargeable to such Parishes,

That Roads cannot be made on the Moor without great Expence, there being no Stones or proper Materials but at a great DistanccThat the People in-.terested therein are much against inclosing the fame; and it would be difficult on Account of the different Natures of the Soil to make a just Division thereof, and that many Disputes and Quarrels would happen therefrom.

Being cross examined, he was asked, What he meant by Treipassers being well looked after ? he said. They might be prevented by the Lord’s Bailiffs going out once in a Fortnight or Three Weeks, though not to drive the Prey; but does not know what Power they have, or what Authority to make Trespassers pay without driving; that the Prey were driven Twice last Year by the Parishes of Chedzoyand , but never knew the Geele driven, or what Rules or Orders there are to

Vol. 33.

prevent Trespassers; and that Cattle do not very often - (tray a great Way on the Moor.

That there is some Marsh Land about and &c. ’

IVi*ston, divided into small Inclosures by Ditches and Hedges, and Cattle are drove into those Ditches very often; that those Inclosures join together in some Parts, and there may be One hundred Acres about Midlezoy, but can’t say how many in Weston, or how many in a Plot, some Plots having One, others Two, Three, and Four, and are divided, some by Ditches and some by Hedges. — Being asked. Whether it would be better for the Proprietors of those inclosed Meadows at Midlezoy if the Ditches were filled up, and the Meadows laid Open in Common, for the Use of the Proprietors ? he said. He did not know: — That the Grass on the Moor is of different Sorts, some rough and some fine, and the Cattle will go where they can have the best, but would be better if it was all good. — Being asked. Whether if the Moor was all his own it would be better to have it divided than in its present State ? he said. No, he had rather have it all abroad. — Being asked. Whether if the Parish of Midlezoy had a Right given them to divide off in One Common, Seven hundred Acres from an; Part of the Moor, the Right of Common to that Parish would be better or worse, having then no Right of Common upon any other Part of the Moor ? he said. It would be worse, even if taken from the best Part; and if it was so, the rest of the Parishes would be uneasy.

That it is above Twenty Years since he heard of Old Auftre Tenements in Chedzoy, and that they always went by that Name.

That every Person who has a Right of Common does the Rhine Work before his own Ground. — Being asked.

If a Cottager does as much as an Occupier of Land of Fifty Pounds a Year ? he said, Some do, and some do not — And that all the Parishes have not different Drifts to the Moor, several going the same Way.

Mr. Robert Bryant, being examined, said, That the Occupiers of Old Auftre Tenements in the several Places mentioned in the Petition, except the Parishes of Charlton Adam and Charlton Mackerel, have a Right of Common on Sedgmoor, and does not understand there is any other Right; and that the Moor is extra-parochial, except such Part as lies in the Limits of Dunware, which is in the Parish of Bridgwater.

That he apprehends Auftre to be an Old Norman French Word, and to mean Hearth or Chimney; and in Law Proceedings, particularly in Leases and Copy-hold Grants, technically used, to mean a Dwelling House; and an Old Auftre Tenement signifiesa Tenement having an ancient Dwelling House upon it, or the Toft or Scite of such Dwelling House, and that they are called Old Auftre Tenements in Contradistinction to Tenements which have no such Old Dwelling House,

Toft or Scite thereof, — Being asked. Whether the Right of Common belongs to the Scite of the Old Auftre alone, without Reference to any other Land? he laid. It belongs to the whole Tenement; that these Tenements originally had Land belonging to them, which might have been fevered from them, and the Right re^'j^s to the House or the Scite thereof; and that the Right of Common is unlimited, and is equal to a small Tenement as a large one: — That he does not know whether the Lords of Manors ever exercised any Rights or Ownership over the Soil of the Moor, nor does he know to whom Estrays belong, and thinks the Right of the Soil is in the Crown, or its Grantees but is

very doubtful.

Sir Joseph Mawbey reported from the Committee, Bastard who were appointed to enquire into the State of Settle- ren*

ments gained by Bastard Children, born in Lying-in Hospitals, and other Houses of Public Charity; That the Committee had enquired accordingly*an^ COIPe to several Resolutions; which they had dire<sted him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Settlement of Bastard Children born Lying-in Hospitals, and other Houses appropriated for the Reception of pregnant Women, is, by the Law, as it now (lands, in the Parishes wherein such Children are born.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That, by falle Informations, several unmarried Women have been admitted into Lying-in Hospitals, instituted for the Reception of married Women only, and wherein, by the Rules of Admission, an Oath has usually been required.

66o

3° — 6® Aprilis. A. 177

quirec’, to certify the Marriages of Persons therein admitted.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Charge of maintaining Bastard Children born in Lying-in Hospitals, and in other Houses appropriated for the R< cq tion of pregnant Women, is extremely burthenleme to the particular Parishes wherein they happen t,) be situated; and, if not put under some better Regulation, are likely to increase the Charge to ap Extent th; t such Parishes will not be able to bear.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the fixing . the Settlement of Bastard Children, born in Lying-in Hospitals, and in other Houses appropriated for the Reception of pregnant Women, to the Parishes to which the Mothers of such Children belong (as is enacted by the Seventeenth of George the Second, in the same of Women wandering and begging) would be an effectual Relief to Parishes burthened by such Bastard Children.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, for Leave to bring in a Bill for regulating the Settlements of Bastard Children, born in Lying-in Hospitals, and in other Houses appropriated for the Reception of pregnant Women; and allb for the better Regulation of such Hospitals and Houses.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said First mentioned Petition, is as follows:

Your Committee being informed, That several Reports or Certificates, had been laid before the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty; relating to Doctor Irving's Method of rendering Salt Water fresh; and also, in relation to a Discovery of a similar Nature, by Mr. John Hoffman, in the Year 1765, thought proper to order all such Certificates and Reports to be laid before them, to enable them to form a Judgment of the Utility of Doctor Irving's Discovery; and also of the comparative Merit of the Two Discoveries.

It appeared, by a Report from the Commissioners for victualling His Majesty’s Navy, to the Commissioners of the Admiralty, dated the Third of April 1765; a Copy whereof is hereunto annexed, N° I. "That Mr. Hoffman " had made an Experiment of his Invention, and that " from One hundred Ninety-four Gallons of Sea Water,

" from the Time of lighting the Fire under the Still, to " the End of the Process, which was Nine Hours and " 24 Minutes, he drew off from the said Sea Water " Eighty-one Gallons, Two Quarts, and Half a Pint of " fresh Water; and that the Quantity of Fuel expended " in drawing off the fame, was One Pound of Wood,

" and 139 Pounds of Coals. That the said Water was fresh, and, to Appearance, good, although somewhat " disagreeable to the Taste; and that the Tread of the " Still, with it’s Frame, and Worm Tub, was Seven " Feet Four Inches and a Half in Length, and Four Feet Five Inches in Breadth; and that the " of the Still Head from the Floor, was Six Feet Seven " Inches."

And it further appeared, by a Letter from the Commissioners for victualling His Majesty’s Navy, a Copy whereof is annexed, N° 2. That the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty had ordered the Sum of £.500 to be paid to the said Mr. Hofftnan, as a Reward for

Then a Report of an Experiment of Mr. Irvings Method of rendering Sea Water fresh, tried on board His Majesty’s Ship Arrogant, was read to your Committee; and is as follows:

" Pursuant to the Desire of Rear Admiral Buckle, we whole Names are hereunto fubforibed, have " carefully examined Mr. Irving's Method of ren-" dering Sea Water fresh, by Distillation; and do certify. That Eighty Gallons of Sea Water did* " in Twenty-five Minutes after being put into the "Arrogant’s Copper, and a Fire made* distil in the

Proportion of Twelve Gallons per Hour, into fresh " Water, perfectly well tailed, and of less specific Gra-" vity than the bell Spring Water in this Neighbour-

hood. — It completely dissolves Soap, and affords no " Precipitation, by adding a Solution of Silver in " Aquafortis.

" Mr. Irving's Apparatus coBlifts of a single Tube, u between Seven and Eight Feet long, which may be

ealily made on board the Ship, of Tin, or thin Iron " Plates, and the Distillation carried on without Inconvenience to the Business of the Ship.

"We further declare, to the bell of our Judgment, " That this Method is founded upon a Principle in " Distillation new, and hitherto not practised; and which we believe will afford great Advantages to that " Art in general, as well as fully answer the End proposed, of supplying Ships with a sufficient Quantity of sweet and wholesome Water, and not to be " distinguished from the best Spring Water, after being " a short Time exposed to the Air.

" Mr. Irving has also communicated to us the whole " of his Process, which appears to depend on such " simple and evident Principles, that we apprehend " the moil ordinary Capacity sufficient to carry it " into Execution, on board any Ship or Vessel whatsoever.

" Every Ship’s Boiler or Copper, though deemed as " Two, is in fact but One large Vessel, with a Partition a nearly in the Middle, and although only one Part or " Boiler is in Ufc at the Time when Pease or Oatmeal " are dressing, yet Water must be kept in the other, to " preserve it’s Bottom: This latter Circumstance Mr. " Irving takes the Advantage of, and has actually drawnoff Sixty Gallons of fresh Water during the boiling " of either of the above mentioned Provisions; and by " a strict Examination of the Cook and his Assistants, " no additional Fuel was uled.

" But in Cafes of great Sickness, or where there is " an absolute Necessity of a greater Expence of Water " than usual, Mr. Irving can, by employing both Coppers, distil Five hundred Gallons of Water in the Space of Twenty-four Hours; and that with the " same Quantity of Fuel, in proportion to the Time as " is required in the ordinary Business of the Ship; and we are clearly of Opinion, that by an inconsiderable " Alteration of setting the Navy Coppers, at a very small Expence, according to a Plan ftiewn us by Mr. " Irving, there will be a considerable Saving of Fuel, " without any Inconvenience whatever.

David Ramsay Karr, Surgeon of the' Yard at motitk, being examined, said. That he was present at the Experiment on board the A, and had signed the Certificate relating the reto: That the Contents thereof are ft rift ly true, but that the Apparatus was not then complete, and he is convinced (from other Experiments, which he has l'een since) that 16 or 18 Gallons of Water may be produced in an Hour while the Pease are boiling on board a Ship; and added, That the Steam is better collected by Doctor Irving's Process than by any former Method.

Mr. Simon Browne, Surgeon of the Arrogant, informed

your Committee, That he was present at the said Experiment, and signed the Certificate, and also the Certificate, dated on board the Northumberland: That the Contents of both the Certificates are strictly true; but that the Quantity of Water was computed under, rather than over. -

That the Water was measured as it was drawn off, which was at the Rate of One Gallon in Three Minutes and an Half; and he thinks any Ship’s Company may be supplied with fresh Water at that Rate.

He added, That when the Experiment was made, the Sea was lo rough, that Boats could scarcely get on board, and that the Ship was pitching.

Captain Richard Edwards, of His Majesty’s Navy, confirmed this Evidence in- regard to the Experiment on board the Centaur; and said. That he had seen a new Apparatus of Doctor Innng's, which distilled at the Rate

of Sixteen Gallons an Hour, from a small Model, much smaller than a Ship’s Copper.

Captain John Stott, of His Majesty’s Ship Juno, being examined, said. That on his Voyage to Falkland Island, in the Year 1771, he used Doctor Irving's Method of distilling Sea Water all the Time: That the Process is quite easy, and done while the Beef or any thing is boiling, is no Incumbrance or Inconvenience on board the Ship, nor attended with any additional Consumption of Fuel.

That he distilled about Three Hours every Day, and produced in general from Nine to Ten Gallons of Water an Hour, without uling more than One of the Ship’s Coppers j and he observed, that when he overlooked the Process, more Water was distilled than at other Times.

That the Water procured by this Process is more pure than any other Water, and mixes better with Grogg: — That the Officers and all the Crew preferred it to any other Water; and that they used it Five Months without any bad Effect:

That he thinks he could have produced Two Quarts of Water per Man every Day by this Means, though his Complement was quite complete, and that double this Quantity might be distilled, if both the Coppers were used, but thinks the Coppers would not stand this for any long Time, as it would require their working Twelve Hours each Day.

That no Ingredient is used with the Sea Water: That he thinks a Butt of Coals would produce Four or Five Butts of Water; and that the Apparatus is fixed as easily as you can put the Cover on the Copper:

That he so distilled ftom Water in which Beef, Pease, Oatmeal, and Pork were boiiing, and always found the Water fresh and good, though it partook of the Tasteof the Thing boiling.

He added, that he never found any Verdigreafe collect on the Coppers from this Distillation.

The Secretary to the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty informed your Committee, that their Lordships were lb well satisfied of the Utility of this Invention, that they had ordered the Apparatus to be put on board all the Ships lately lent to the E>jl Indies.

And another Member present informed your Committee, that all His Majesty’s Ships that have been sent out lately have had it.

A Letter was then read from the last mentioned Member, when he commanded His Majesty’^ Fleet at Vot. 55.

Portsmouth, to the Secretary of the Admiralty,- dated 27th May 1771, wherein he fays, " That he holds Doctor " Irving's Discovery in great Estimation, begs Leave " to recomradnd the same to the Lords of the Admiralty."

Copy of a Letter from the Commissioners for victuallingHis Majesty’s Navy, to,

Esquire, Secretary of the Admiralty; dated 3d of April 1765.

In Return to your Letter of the 7th February last, acquainting us, that Mr. Hoffman had represented to the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, that he had invented a Method of rendering Sea Water sweet and wholesome, by Means of a Still of a new Construction, and a certain Chymical Preparation; and that the Water would not only be better than has been hitherto produced from Sea Water, but that a larger Quantity would be obtained in leis Time, and with a smaller Quantity of Fuel than has been hitherto done by any other Process; and the said Invention would be of the greatest Utility to the Seamen of the Royal Navy, and to all Seamen in general, and signifying the Directions of their Lordships, as they understood the Apparatus was fixed in this Office, for making Trial of the said Invention; and the Sea Water arrived that was ordered to be sent us from the Nore, that we should cause Experiment to be made thereof, and circumstantial Minutes taken of the Quantity of Water rendered sweet from a certain Quantity of Sea Water, in what Time performed, with what Quantity of Fuel, the Goodness thereof when done; and, in short, of every particular necessary to enable their Lordships to form a true Judgment of the said Invention j and to transmit you the said Minutes, together with our Opinion upon the Whole, for their Lordships Information.

We pray Leave to acquaint you, that Mr. Hoffman having attended at this Office, and made an Experiment of his said Invention, we herewith inclose Minutes of the Process, by which their Lordships will be pleased to fee, that from a Still charged with One hundred and Ninety-four Gallons of Sea Water, Mr. Hoffman, from the Time of lighting the Fire under the Still, to the End of the Process (being Nine Hours and Twenty-five Minutes) drew off from the said Sea Water, Eighty-one Gallons, Two Quarts, and Half a Pint of fresh Water; and that the Quantity of Fuel expended in drawing off the fame, consisted of One Pound of Wood, and of One hundred and Thirty-nine Pounds of Coals. Eleven Quart Bottles of the said distilled Water were delivered to the Right honourable Lord Viscount Howe, One to Mr. Hoffman, and Eleven more to us, of which we have sent Six by the Bearer hereof, and the other

With regard to the Quality of the said Water, we beg leave to represent, that it is fresh, and, to Appearance, good, although lbmething disagreeable to the Taste, but whethelr rt be Wholesome, or fit for Men to drink, or better than any other which has 'been hitherto drawn from Sea Water, we are not enabled to say, these being Points, that upon Mr. Hoffmans disclosing the Nature of the Chythical Ingredients, which ke tirade use of in his Process, we humbly apprehend Will come most properly under the Confederation of the College of Physicians, who, in the same of the late Mr. Appleby's Experiment, mentioned in our Letter to.Mr. of

the 8th January 1752, were of Opinion, that the fresh Water distilled from Sea Water by his Method, as appears by their Lordships Order to' us of the 10th May1753> was sufficiently cleared of the noxious Contents of Sea Water, and that no noxious Particles contained in the said Mr. Appleby's Process of Distillation were in his said distilled Water, and that the feme might be tried with Safety; and their Lordships, by their said Order, were pleased to signify; that the said Invention, so experimented and approved, appeared to be of Public Utility, as tending greatly to the Preservation of-Seamens Health and Lives in long Voyages, and deserving of Public Encouragement; and therefore directed us to pay Mr. Appleby Two hundred Pounds as a Reward for his Invention. r-

As to that Part of Mr. Hoffman's Postion, which fays, that a larger Quantity of fresh Water could be produced by his Method, and in less Time, and with less Fuel than has been hitherto done by any other. We have already observed that by his Experiment, Eighty-one Gallons, Two Quarts, and Half a Pint of fresh Water, were produced from One hundred and Ninety-four Gallons of Sea Water, in Nine Hours and Twenty-five Minutes, at the Expence of One Pound of Wood, and One hundred and Thirty-nine Pounds of Coals: And by our aforesaid Report of the 8th of January 1752, it appears, that Mr. Appleby, upon his Experiment, produced Thirteen Gallons and Two Quarts of fresh Water from Sixteen Gallons of Sea Water, in the Space of Three Hours and an Half, and at the Expence of Half a Bushel of Coals; and that he (Mr. Appleby) represented, that a Still of a much larger Size than what he made use of (which held only Twenty Gallons) might be worked with the same Quantity of Fire. From these Circumstances, we humbly apprehend that noconclusive Comparison can be formed at present, how far Mr. Hoffman's Experiment has the Advantage of Mr. by' s, in Point of Fuel.

We beg Leave to add, that by the particular Construction of the Still made Use of by Mr. Hoffman, we do not apprehend that he could have drawn off more fresh Water from once charging the feme, than about the Quantity produced from his Experiment before mentioned, without burning the Still; and that the Tread of the said Still, with it’s Frame and Worm Tub, was Seven Feet Four Inches and an Half in Length, and Four Feet Five Inches in Breadth; and that the Height of the Still Head, from the Floor, was Six Feet Seven Inches.

Being.ilktd, Whether he could distinguish from whence the Cry came ?

He laid. It came from the Officers; and that they treated the Members as they did the Mob.

Being asked, If there was any Rudeness in putting out the Members?

He said, it did appear rude and precipitate, because, as being then under Orders, thought the Members ought to have Time given them to go out, without being incommoded by the Crowd.

Being asked, Whether they knew he was a Member ?

He laid, No; but 'thinks Mr. Howard did immediately turn round to the.UIher.of the Black Rod, and told him, the first Time he saw him in the House of Commons he would use him in the same Manner; and that the Black Rod was one who laid. You mull withdraw, you mull go o.ut.

Being asked. Whether at the Time the Officers treated him in the Manner he had- mentioned, he did not fee a Mix lure of Mob and Members?

Jrle said, There always is; that he never was there without; that there is always more Mob than Members, some of whom are let in before the Members come; and that most of the Mob were gone out, and not many Members left, when he, with other Members, were turned out.

Being asked. Whether he recollected at any other Time the same Rudeness to Members as at that Time ?

He hid, He never remembers any Thing of the Kind before the lait Regulation of the House of Lords, (the Regulation for excluding Members.)

Being asked, If he apprehended the Officers knew he was a Member ?

JHfe laid. He did not know; but thinks Mr. spoke to the Ulher of the Black Rod, so as to make him understand he was a Member.

Being asked. Whether, before the last excluding Regulation took place, he was not usually for many Years admitted as a known Member of the House of Commons ?

He said. He always was j that he was very near the Speaker on going in; and that he saw many Strangers there before the Speaker came.

Being asked. If he had communicated to the Speaker the rude Treatment he and the other Members received in the TToufeof Lords?

He laid. He never mentioned it to anybody.

A Petition of George Prescott, Esquire, was presented Milbom to the House, and read; Setting forth. That at the P.p?lt last Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for e on"

the Borough of Milbom Port, in the County of -

set, the Petitioner and Richard Combe, Esquire, were Candidates, and Thomas Noake and William Hyde were returning Officers; and that, during the whole Course of the Poll, the said Thomas Noake and William Hyde, behaved with the utmost Partiality, in Favour of the Odd'Richard Combe, by admitting several Persons to vote for him who had no Colour of Right, and by refilling several Persons who offered to vote for the Petitioner, and who had an undoubted Right to vote; and that the said Thomas Noake and William Hyde did, by their Conduct both before and during the Time of the said Election, shew a determined Resolution to return the said Richard Combe as duly elected, in all Events, by which, and several other illegal and unwarrantable Proceedings both before and during the Time of Election, a pretended Majority hath been procured in Favour of the Sitting Member, to the manifest Prejudice of the Petitioner, who had a clear Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been elected and returned for the said Borough: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioner such Relief as shall seem just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Wednesday the 6th Day of May next, at One of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Mr. Bacon, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the present State of the Corn Trade, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Importation of Wheat and Wheat Flour, into this Kingdom, be admitted, for a limited Time, free of Duty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Importation of Rice, from any of His Majesty’s Colonies in America, into Great Britain, be admitted, for a limited Time, free of Duty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, if the Importation and Exportation of Corn were properly regulated by some permanent Law, it would afford Encouragement to the Farmer, be the Means of increasing- the Growth of that necessary Commodity, of-affording a cheaper and more constant Supply to the Poor, and of preventing Abuses in that Article of Trade.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of {his Committee, That the Duties now payable upon Wheat and Wheat Flour imported into this Kingdom, when the Price of Wheat is at or above 48 s. per Quarter, shall, cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

County of Durham, in Behalf of therrtselves, and several

other Persons who claim Right of Common for and in respect of their ancient Messuages or Burgages, in and upon the said several Moors and Parcels of Ground, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending, for dividing and inclosing the said Moors, Commons, and Parcels of Ground, and for other Pun-poles therein mentioned; and that the said Bill hath been promoted and brought into the House without the Consent of the Petitioners, and of many others interested in the said Division; and that the Petitioners are Owners of several large and valuable Messuages or Burgages* for which, as the Bill now stands, they will not, upon the Subdivision of the said Commons, have greater Allotments than the Owners of Messuages or Burgages of the smallest Value -, and though several Persons may have signed the said Bill, who have large Houses, yet such Houses arc composed of -several Burgages laid :to»-gether, for every one of which they expect to have separate Alldtments; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that these is no Reason why, in the First Division, the Lands should have Allotments in proportion to the Whole, and the Houses only to Half, of their Rental, the Houses being subject to the Payment of greater Taxes, and more Repairs than Lands are liable to; and that the Petitioners are advised, that the Claims of Right of Common, in respect of Intercommon Lands, are not clearly provided for in the present Bill, nor -any Rule therein let down, to direct the Judgment of the Commissioners, in setting out any Part of the Lands proposed to be divided to the Freemen of the City of Durham, in case they should appear to have a Right; and that several other Matters are so doubtfully expressed in the said Bill, as it now stands, that, if it should pass into a Law, the Petitioners are advised, it could not be carried into Execution: And.'therefore praying.

That the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Petition; or have such further and other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Innkeepers of the Town of Maid- Innkeepers stone, in the County of Kent, was presented to the House, (Maidstone) and read; Complaining of the Hardships, which, the droops"* Petitioners alledge, they labour under, from the present Mode of quartering Soldiers and Horses; and Setting forth. That the Petitioners apprehend, if it was left to the Option of each Innkeeper, to provide Hay and Straw for the Horse to be quartered on him, at the present;

Price of Six Pence each Night, or only to provide the Troops with convenient Stables and Necessaries for the Horse gratis, as the Innkeepers shall find most convenient in future Times (this Alteration not to extend to Troops on a March, or employed on the Recruiting Service) the same would remedy the Grievance complained of: And therefore praying the House, to take the Complaints of the Petitioners into Consideration, and grant them the Relief thus proposed, or such other Alterations in the Laws for quartering Soldiers as to the House shall be found most proper for His Majesty’s Service, and the Ease of His Subjects.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Gunpowder. Sir George Savile reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Edmund Hill, Owner of divers Gunpowder Mills upon Heath, was referred;

That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fad contained in the said Petition; a State whereof they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed:; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fad contained in the said Petition, is as followeth:

Mr. Hill produced an Estimate of the Expence of building Two Setts of Gunpowder Stone Mills, amounting to j£*. 7*7, from which Calculation it appears that VOL. 33.

and conceives that a Mill with Two Pair of Stones could not be perfeded with all the necessary Apparatus for less than £. 800, or a Mill with One Pair of Stones for less than £.500: That the Seven Pestle Mills, as they now stand, and prohibited from working Gunpowder* are not really worth, for any Purpose they can be applied to, so much as £. 200; but if allowed to work, are worth £. 1,400.

Mr. John Brokehouse, a Millwright, being examined, said. That what is left of the Two Mills lately blown up, is not now worth more than £. 5; but if restored to Pestle Mills, would be worth £. 50, 60, or 70.

That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, until the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, against the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the present Mode of Watching, and Pay of the Watchmen, within the City and Liberty of Westminster, is very irregular and various, and ought to be put under proper Regulations.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it would tend to the Safety of the Inhabitants of the said City and Liberty, if a regular and uniform Watch, with Patroles, was established, under proper Regulations.

Cl. Dom. Com.

Thomas Brad/haw, Esquire, having this Day presented his Petition, complaining, That at the last Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the Borough of , in the County of Cornwall, John Williams, Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; that Mr. John Hill, the Returning Officer of the said Borough, behaved with the utmost Partiality in favour of the said John Williams, and admitted several Persons to vote for him who had no Right so to do, and rejected One Person who offered to poll for the Petitioner; by which, and other unwarrantable Proceedings, a pretended Majority hath been procured in favour of the said John Williams, contrary to Law and Justice and in manifest Wrong of the Petitioner, who had a fair and clear Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned for the said Borough accordingly; and the House having appointed this Day Three Weeks, the 5th Day of June next, at One of the Clock in the Afternoon, to take the said Petition into Confederation, you are therefore to take Notice, That the House will, at that Time, take the same Petition into Consideration.

Given under my Hand, the Fifteenth Day of May, One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-two.

Fl" Norton, Speaker.

To Thomas Bradjliaw, Esquire.

The like Notice to John Williams, Esquire.

the County of Bucks, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to explain and amend an Act, made in the Seventh Year of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act for altering the Stamp Duties upon Policies of Assurance; and for reducing the Allowance to be made in respect of the prompt Payment of the Stamp Duties on Licences for retailing Beer, Ale, and other exciseable Liquors; and for explaining and amending several Acts of Parliament relating to Hackney Coaches and Chairs, lo far as the same relates to Hackney Coaches; and Setting forth, That, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioners will be prevented for the future from going to London on the Outside of Stage Coaches, which has been the usual Way of the Petitioners travelling; and that the Inside Carriage will be, by Means thereof, greatly increased; and that the Petitioners will not be able, on account of the Expence, to carry on their Trade in the Manner they have been used to do, to the great Injury, it not total Ruin, of many of the Petitioners and their Families: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration; and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

The House being informed, by several Members in J*uW,c their Places, that they had, during the last Recess of ccot *' Parliament, examined (together with Mr. Speaker) the State of the Public Records of this Kingdom, and the Repositories in which the same are now kept; and had found one of the said Repositories, viz. The Rolls Chapel, very much out of Repair, and the Records therein in bad Condition, and decaying daily:

And that the rest of the Records were in tolerable good' Preservation, but not disposed and arranged in a Manner to be so useful to the Public as they might be.

And the same being confirmed by Mr. Speaker;

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to examine the present Condition of the Records of this Kingdom, the Repositories wherein, and the Manner in which, they are now kept; and that they do forthwith consider of some proper Method, to be immediately taken, to prevent the further Decay of the Records at The Rolls; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House.

And a Committee was appointed of Sir John Mr. Fuller, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

lankeepers A Petition of the Innkeepers of the Town of Market (Market Harborough, in the County of Leicester, was presented to House, and read; Complaining of the Hardships Troop*, which the Petitioners alledge they labour under from the present Mode of quartering Soldiers and Horses; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend, if it was left to the Option of each Innkeeper to provide Hay and Straw for the Horses to be quartered on him at the present Price of Six Pence each Night, or only to provide the Troops with convenient Stables and Necessaries for the Horses gratis, as the Innkeepers shall find most convenient in future Times (this Alteration not to extend to Troops on a March, or employed on the Recruiting Service) the same would remedy the Grievance complained of: And therefore praying the House to take the Complaints of the Petitioners into Confederation, and grant them the Relief proposed, or such other Alterations in the Laws for quartering Soldiers, as to the House shall be found most proper for His Majesty’s Service, and the Ease of His Subjects.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Public Sir John Turner reported from the Committee, who Records, were appointed to examine the present Condition of the Records of this Kingdom, the Repositories wherein, and the Manner in which, they are now kept; and to consider of some proper Method to be immediately taken, to prevent the further Decay of the Records at The; and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, (rom Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had examined the State of the Records at the Chapel; and had directed him to report the fame, together with their Opinion thereupon to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Upon viewing the Records at the Rolls, the Committee find, that very many of those in the Body of the Chapel are much decayed, and partly obliterated, and the rest in Danger of Destruction, by being placed close to the Walls, the Damps from which have penetrated Vol. 33.

through the Backs of the Presses wherein they are piaced: and that those in the Room, or Garret, over the said Chapel, are continually receiving Injuries, either from the Rain, which often penetrates through the Covering, or by the intense Heat in the Summer Season; and the Weakness of the Floor is such, as scarce to be able to' support the Weight of the Records there: And your Committee were informed, as w.ell by several of the Members present, who tnfpected the same Records last Summer, as by the Testimony of Mr. Rooke, who is Clerk of the Chapel, and as such has the Care of the said Records, that many of them are very considerably impaired since that Time;

And your Committee ‘hiving been informed by the Master of the Rolls, That it has been usual, for the Purpose of trinferibing the said Records, for the Master of the Rolls, for the Time being, to allow them to be carried out of the said Chapel to the Clerks Chambers, which are always at some Distance from the said Chapel, (there being no convenient Place in the said Chapel for that Purpose) by which the said Records are exposed to the Danger of being loft or injured; and that there is a Dwelling House very convenient fof that Purpose in Chancery Lane, late in the Occupation of William Ambler, Esquire, from which a Door might be made into the Yard in which the said Chapel (lands, which House might be hired for a small Rent; and the Master of the Rolls being asked. If he would consent that the Rolls Chapel, or such Part thereof as shall be found necessary, may be fitted up, in such Manner as to prevent the Records receiving further Damage, till a more proper Re-pository can be provided for them, he readily gave his Consent thereto; at the same Time expressing his Willies,-that the Chapel might be so fitted up as to leave Room sufficient for the Celebration of Divine Sendee therein: — Upon which your Committee came to the following Resolutions j viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Body of the said Chapel, or such Part thereof as may be found necessary, be forthwith fitted up for receiving the said Records, so as to prevent further Damage to the fame, leaving a sufficient Space for the Celebration of Divine Service; and that, when the same shall be so fitted up, the said Records be accordingly placed and kept therein, until a more proper Repository be provided for them.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House in Chancery Lane, late in the Occupation of William Ambler, Esquire, be lured as a propel Place, wherein the said Records may, for the future, be transcribed.

The First Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Second Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto,' by inferring after the Word " hired" the Words " and " prepared." ,

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Then the said Resolution, so amended, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That the House in Chancery Lane, late in the Occupation of William Ambler, Esquire, be hired apd prepared, as a proper PJjice wherein the said Records may for the future be transcribed,

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to give such Direct ions as His Majesty shall think proper, for the better Preservation of the Records in the Rolls Chapel-, and to assure His Majesty, that whatever extraordinary Expence shall be incurred for that Purpose, this House will make good the fame.

Eats India' Colonel Burgoyne reported from the Committee, who ^fcitis. were appointed to enquire into the Nature, State, and Condition, of the East India Company, and of the tijhAffairs in the East Indies; That the Committee had made some Progress in the Matters to them referred; and had directed him to make a Report thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the tame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Committee have found it impossible, with their

3

utmost Diligence to go through the Multiplicity of Matter, which the Order of the House comprehends; and they, besides, have thought themselves obliged to depart from the regular Course of their Enquiry, in order to make a distinct and separate Report, upon the Petition of Gregore Cojamaul, late of Bengal, in the East , on Behalf of himself and others, which the House referred to them by a subsequent Order.

notwithstanding the Business of your Committee has been by this Circumstance, and by the insufficiency of the Time, left incomplete; yet as the Session, as they apprehend, is drawing to a Conclusion, and as every Parc of their Enquiry is full of important Matter, they thought it right to report the Progress they have hitherto been enabled to make.

Your Committee beg Leave to premise, that, for the Regularity of their Enquiry, and in order to give the: cleared State of it to the House, they thought it expedient to arrange their Proceedings under the following Heads:

i ft.The several Charters granted to the East India Company, with the Acts of Parliament respecting the fame: and allb, the Grants and Treaties which have fub-fifted between the Company and the Powers in India, from their first EstablHhment to the present Time.

idly, The Commissions, and other Instruments, by which the Company authorized and impowered their Servants to carry on their Affairs in India,

2,dly. To pursue, by' historical Deduction, the State of Affairs in India, the Manner in which the present Pof-sessions in that Country were acquired, and the different Tran factions attending, those Acquisitions; beginning with the Transactions of Bengal, and dividing them into Three Periods; viz.from the Establishment of the present Company to the Completion of the Resolution, in the Year 1757; from thence to the affirming the Dew-anny in the Year 1765; and from thence to the present Time; and in each Period respectively to slate the Situation of the Company’s Affairs, and the material Parts of the Conduct of the Company’s Servants, with respect to the Powers intruded with them by the Company, in the Civil and Military Departments; in the Administration of Justice; in the accepting of Presents; in the Management of Trade; and in the Revenues and Coinage.

4 thly.The various Disputes with Foreign Companies since the Year 1765.

thly. The Conduct of the Directors at Home, during all the Periods comprehended in this Enquiry, respectively, to the different Powers exercised at any Time by them; to the Manner of keeping and checking Public Accounts at Home and Abroad; to the Controul of their Servants; and to the Abuses to which the Whole, or any Part of the East India Affairs is liable, from Defects in the Constitution of the Company, when applied to their present Situation at Home and Abroad.

Pursuant to the above Plan, your Committee proceeded to read such Charters and Acts of Parliament as are applicable to their Enquiry; all of which are in the Toffeflion of the House, and a Schedule of them is annexed, in the Appendix, N° 1. p,826.

The Copies of Commissions and Instruments from the Company to their Servants are included in the above Number of the Appendix.

Your Committee would not presume to state to the House the Constitution of the East India Company, without the moll critical and minute Examination of each Charter and Act of Parliament i and they could not in the Space of Time allotted them, enter upon so great a Work, which may be taken up hereafter and Hated from the Materials referred to in the Appendix.

Being asked, Whether the Answer to the Nabob’s Letter was communicated to the Council, or whether it was sent as Mr. Drake's, private Letter ? the Witness said, The Purport of both the Letter and the Answer itself were communicated; he does not recoiled who the Answer was sent by, nor how long it might be after the Receipt of the Letter, but believes, it might be the same Day or the Day following, and did not recoiled the whole Contents of the Letter.

Being asked, If it was the usual Practice, when a Messenger brought a Letter from the Nabob, to order him to leave the Town without any Answer sent with him ? he said, It was not, nor could he alflgn any Reason for l'o doing, for the Receipt of the Letter was not public, nor was the Treatment of the Messenger so.

In regard to the Measures the Fadory took to pacify the Nabob, after they were informed of his hostile Intentions, the Witness said, Mr. Drake was repeatedly desired to write to the Nabob, to know the Cause of his Resentment, and that he had no Doubt but he did so, but believed, he received no Answer; among other Methods, Coja IVaffield, a Merchant of considerable Rank and Substance, and likewise a Tenant of several considerable Farms, was requested by Letters to apply to the Nabob, to know the Reason of his Resentment, and was deftred to act as a Mediator upon the Occasion; it was also tried to be informed by Means of this Coja Wafjecd, whether Money was the only Object in view, and, in general, he was requested to interest himself as well as he could to appease the Nabob; his Answer was. That it was not in his Power to be of any Use upon the Occasion, and that the Payment of a Sum of Money was not the Object; the Reason of applying to Coja IVaffield, was, that he was supposed to be a Man

of some Weight, and in Favour with the Nabob, from the Circdmftance of his having entertained him at his House, when he was Chuta Nabob.

The Witness being asked, Whether he had any Reason to believe, that any Sum of Money or Present was given to Mr. Drake, or any other Person by Kiffindafs ? he said, He did not know, nor had any Reason to believe that any were given to Mr. Drake, or any other Person.

Being again questioned. Whether he was sure, that Kiffindafs was not received in Calcutta, before the Death of Alii Verdi Cawn f he said. He was not sure — And

whether the Contents of the Letter from Mr. Watts, were not to permit Kiffindafs to remain Two Months in the Town, and that there was a particular Recommendation of Kiffindafs's Family, as being particularly

lcrviceable to the Enghffit he said, He could not recoiled the particular Purport of the Letter; that in general it was a warm Recommendation of Kiffindafs, as the Son of Rajah Bullub, a Man of Power and Interest at the Durbar, and who might be of Service to the Affairs of the India Company at the Durbar.

Your Committee next called Richard Beecher, Esquire, who was desired to relate what he knew of the Origin of the Troubles in Bengal:And he informed the Committee, That about the End of the Year 1755, he was appointed Chief of the Subordinate Fadory at;

that from that Time he did not attend at any of the Councils that were held at Calcutta, and of course

could only speak of Transudions that passed there, by Report from others; that at the Time the Letter of the 10th of July 1756, was wrote from Dacca, himself and the other Gentlemen that signed it, were Prisoners to the Nabob, and by his Permission allowed to reside in the French Fadory; that, for some Time before the Taking of Calcutta, they had no Correspondence with the Gentlemen of Fort William, but for Intelligence' were obliged to trust to the Natives of the Country, or what the French received from their Settlement at Chandernagore; that he thought it his Duty at

that Time to forward to the Court of Directors, and to the Governor and Council at Madrajs, l'uch Intelligence as he was able by those Means to procure; that he has since had the greatest Reason to believe, the Accounts transmitted to the Governor and Council at Madrass, then obtained from the French, were greatly exaggerated, and very fallacious in many Particulars; that the Report of Kiffindafs's being received and pro-teded in Calcutta, being a Cause assigned by Serajah Dowla for his Displeasure against the he heard

from Numbers of People where he then was, both French and Natives, and he gave Credit to it, and therefore assigned it to the Court of Directors as the principal Reason.

In relation to the Affair of Kiffindafs, the Witness said. That he recollected to have heard Kiffindafs was received in Calcutta about the latter End of March 1756, and remained there till the Place was taken by Serajah Dowla, on the aoth of June; he and were both Prisoners in the Fadory, by Order of the Governor, as he believed: And the Witness further said. That in the Situation the India Company then were, as Merchants living under the Protection of the Country Government, he then was, and still is, of Opinion, that neither Kiffindafs, nor any other Subject of the Nabob, should have been received and protected in the Company’s Settlement; and he still thinks, that this did give a Pretence to Serajah Dowla, to shew his Resentment against the English, but at the same Time he is now convinced, from the many Opportunities he hath since had of conversing with those who were at that Time principal Officers and in high Station about Serajah Dowla, at Muxadavad, that even if that Pretence had not been given, lie would have marched his Army down against Calcutta-, his Object was Money, Calcutta was reported to be very rich, and so were the other European Settlements of Chandernagore and Chin sura-, Serajah Dowla was a young Man, violent, passionate, of great Ambition, tindured with Avarice, and he expected both Wealth and Honour, by attacking the European Settlements, and by extorting Money from

them; that this appears from his Conduct in attacking Calcutta, and from the Suras he extorted from the French, Dutch, and Danes, after that Transaction.

The Witness being asked. Whether he ever heard of the Nabob’s demanding Kiffindafs after lie was received in Calcutta ? he said. He did not recoiled that he heard it before Calcutta was taken, though he may have done so, but he heard it soon after: That his Opinion at that Time was, that if Kiffindafs had been delivered up, and a Sum of Money offered, the Nabob would not have proceeded to the Lengths he did in attacking Calcutta; and he grounded this Opinion in great Measure upon what had been the former Custom of the Nabobs and Princes of that Country, when they were displealed with the English: That Alii Ver di Cazvn, who was a wile Prince, had upon different Occasions shewn his Dif-pleasure, and taken Money from them, but appeared always to be so sensible of the Benefits accruing to his Country, by the Trade carried on by the English, that he never proceeded further than to put a Stop to the Trade of the Company, and to place Forces round their Factories, by which Means he always brought them to the Terms lie pleased<

Several Letters and Messages passed between the President and Coja Wazeed, in which the latter was desired to use his Influence with the Nabob in our Favour, and authorized to accommodate Matters by giving a Sum of Money, which it was imagined was what the Subah aimed at, according to the Custom of his Predecessor, who had frequently squeezed large Sums from the Europeans under various Pretences; but we were disappointed in our Judgment of Serajah Dowla'% Views, and we quickly found he was too much exasperated to be appealed by the ordinary Method of a Present.

Orders were accordingly given for a Suspension of Hostilities on our Part; but in left than Half an Hour Intelligence was brought to Mr. Holwell, that the Enemy were crouding in great Numbers under the Walls of the Fort, to the Eastward and Southward, whereupon he hastened up himself to the South East Bastion to view their Motions, directing every one to be at their Quarters: By this Time the Besiegers had been suffered to advance dole up to the Foot of the Walls, without a single Musket being fired upon them; and Mr. Holwell (still imagining every thing would be compromised) forbid all Acts of Hcftiiity, notwithstanding the Enemy pressed in such Multitudes upon us: By way of Capitulation or Conference he waved a Flag of Truce, which not being understood by the Moors, no Regard was paid to it; and while this was transacted to the Eastward, a Body of the Enemy sealed the North West Bastion, as did another Party to the Southward (where the Wall was low) and drove our People from their Stations there. — As soon as this was known, a Dutchman of the Artillery Company broke open the Back Door of the Fadlory, and with many others attempted to make their Escape that Way. — The Besiegers now poured in great Numbers from all Parts; and Mr. Holwell, finding how Things were circumstanced, and how impracticable it would be to drive the Enemy out of the Fort, now that so many had penetrated within the Walls, with the West Gate of it open, and considering that further Opposition would not only be fruitless, but might be attended with bad Con-'sequences to the Garrison, he and Captain Buchanan delivered

That at that Time, there were no Covenants existing; the Company’s Servants were at Liberty to receive Presents; they always had received Presents; and his Idea of Pre- fents is as follows: When Presents are received as the Price of Services to the Nation, to the Company, and to that Prince who bestowed those Presents; when they are not exacted from him by Compulsion; when he is in a State of Independance, and can do with his Money what he pleases, and when they are not received to the Disadvantage of the Company; he holds Presents so received not dishonourable: But when they are received from a dependant Prince; when they are received for no Services whatever; and when they are received not voluntarily; he holds the Receipt of such Presents dishonourable. — He never made the least Secret of the Presents he had received; he acquainted the Court of Directors with it; and they, who are his Masters, and were the only Persons who had a Right to object to his receiving those Presents, approved of it.

-Every Thing being agreed on between Meer Jaffier and the Secret Committee, we marched the Army to meet the Nabob, whom we entirely defeated: — His Death followed soon after, and Meer jaffier was in a few ' "ays ii> JPossession of the Government, and of a Revenue of TTiree Millions and a Half Sterling per Annum. — The On e-half of the Secret Committee being then present sat the Capital, and a Report made by the Nabob’s N/Xinifter of the State of the Treasury, it was settled that Half the Sum stipulated by Treat y should be paid in Three Months, and the other Half in Three Years; all conditionally, that we supported him in the Go 'vernment. — The Nabob then, agreeable to the known and usual Custom of Eastern Princes, made Prelvnts, both to those of his own Court, and to such of the -Eng/i/hwho by their Rank and Abilities hail

been in strumental in the happy Success of so hazardous tvn Lnt. terprize, suitable to the Rank and Dignity of a greaefc Prince. — I was one amongst the many who be-nenUeci by his Favour; I never fought to conceal it; but declared publicly, in my Letters to the Secret (Committee of the India Directors, that the Nabob’s Generality had made my Fortune caly, and that, the Company’s Welfare was now my only Motive for Raying in India. What Injustice Was this to the Company; They could expect no more than what was stipulated in the Treaty: Or what Injunction was I under to refute a Present from him, who had the Power to make me one, as the Reward of honourable Services ? I know of none; I had surely myself a particular, Claim, by having devoted my left to the Company’s Military Service, and neglected all commercial Advantages. What Real on.can. then be given, or what Pretence could the Company have to expect, that I, after having rilked my Life so often in their Service, flibuld deny myself the only honourable Opportunity that ever offered, of acquiring a Fortune without Prejudice to them, who, it is evident would not have had more for my having had less ? When the Company had acquired a Million and a Half Sterling, and a Revenue of near £. 100,000 per Annum, from the Success of their Forces under my Command; when ample Restoration had been made to those whose Fortunes suffered by the Calamity of Calcutta; and when Vol. 33.

Individuals had, in consequence of that Success, ac- East India quired large Estates; what would the World have said, Affair:-had I come Home, and rested upon the Generality of the present Court of Directors ? — It is well known to every Gentleman in Bengal, that the Honour of my Country, and the Interest of the Company, were the Principles that governed all my Actions; and that, had I only taken the advantageous Opportunities that prfe-fented themselves, by my being Commander in Chief; and at the Head of a victorious Army, and what by the Custom of that Country 1 was.intitled to, the Jag-hire itleif, great as it is, would have been an Object. scarce worth my Consideration.

The City of Muxadavad is as extensive, populous, and rich, as the City of London; with this Difference, that there are Individuals in the first, posselfing infinitely greater Proper!}' than any in the last City: These, as well as every other Man of Property, made me the greatest Offers (which nevertheless are usual upon such Occasions, and what they expected would have been required) and had I accepted these Offers, I might have been in Post’eflion of Millions, which the present Court of Directors could not have dispoflell’ed me of:

But preferring the Reputation of the Euglijlt Nation, the Interest of the Nabob, and the Advantage of the Company, to all pecuniary Considerations, I refused all Offers that were made me, not only then, but to the last Hour of my Continuance in the Company’s Service in Bengal; and do challenge Friend or Enemy to bring one lingle Instance of my being influenced by interested Motives to the Company’s Disadvantage; or to do any Act that could reflect Dishonour to my Country, or the Company, in any one Action of my Administration, either as Governor or Commanding Officer. — I little expected ever to have had my Conduct: impeached, or. to have received such Treatment from the Court of Directors, especially after the many public and honourable Testimonies of Approbation I had received.

Copy of Company’s Letter to Colonel Clive, March 8,

1758-

SIR,

Our Sentiments of Gratitude, for the many great Services you have rendered to this Company, together with the Thanks of the General Court, have been hitherto conveyed through the Channel of our General Letters; but the late extraordinary and unexpected Resolution in Bengal, in which you had so great a Share

of Action, both in the Cabinet and the Field, merits our more particular Regard; and we do accordingly embrace this Opportunity of returning you our most sincere and hearty Thanks for the Zeal, good Conduct, and Intrepidity, which you' have so eminently exerted on this glorious Occasion, as well as for the great and solid Advantages resulting therefrom to the East India Company: We earnefty wish your Health may permit

your Continuance in India, for such further Term as will give you an Opportunity of securing the Foundation you have laid; as likewise to give your Assistance in putting the Company’s Mercantile and Civil Affairs on a proper and advantageous Footing, upon the Plans how transmitted. For this Purpose, as well as in Consideration of your eminent Services, we have appointed you Governor and President of Fort IVII/iaM in Bernal, and its Dependencies, in the Manner mentioned in the General Letter, by this Conveyance; to which we have annexed an additional Allowance of

£. 1,000 a Year, as a Testimony of our great Regard for you.
