Mr. Sutton, Mr. Vane, Mr. Straches, Mr. Curzon, Mr. Fuller,

Mr. Otigley, Mr. Hot ham, Mr. Pitt,

Mr. Cornwall, Mr. Ellis.

Read, the Petition of Gregore Cojamaul \ as follows: To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain, in " Parliament assembled.

The humble Petition of Grejore Cojamaul, late of Bengal in the East Indies, on Behalf of himself. and " others:

" Sheweth,

" That your Petitioner, who is an Armenian Christian, and Native of Ifphahan in Perfta, has for many Years resided in India as a Merchant, particularly in the Provinces of Bengal and its Dependencies, where those of his Nation have ever been allowed to carry on Trade, according to the ancient Usages of those Countries, and even were indulged with certain Privileges in that Relpetft.

" That your Petitioner, who has ever strictly conformed himself to the Usages of those respective Countries, has, with many others of his Nation, of late, been greatly impeded in their Business as Merchants, by the most cruel, destrutftive, and injurious Regulations, and grievously oppressed by long and cruel Imprisonments, and otherwise, by the nominal Nabobs, and other Servants of the English East India Company in Bengal, notwithstanding your Petitioner never in any Degree injured the said Company, nor was ever guilty of any Breach of the Laws, either of India or this Nation; to the known Justice of which last, he has already applied for Satisfaction for the great Lodes and Injuries he has sustained.

" That, when your Petitioner, and others, have been injured and oppressed by such Imprisonments, within the Districts to which His Majesty’s most gracious Charter of Justice, granted to the said Company, is not allowed to extend, they have applied to the said nominal Nabobs of Bengal for Justice, who have referred them and your Petitioner to the President or Secret Committees of Calcutta in Bengal, alledging such Imprisonments to have been effected by their Orders; and when, on the Part of your Petitioner and such other Persons, Application has been made for Justice at Calcutta to the said Company’s Governor and President of the Secret Committees, they have been referred back to the said Nabobs; and in this grievous Situation, without ever being able to know of what Crime he was accused, your Petitioner, by such Evasions, has been ruined, and left without any other Remedy than the precarious Redress which lie

T'Mie Petitioner, Gregore Cojamaul, was then called upo n to give an Account of the Circumstances of his beir-xg taken up and confined, to the Time of his Re! caiement and Embarkation for England; which he did in the following Words:

On the 14th March 1768, Rajah Bulwantjing's Officer feiz.ed me at Bara Fort, and told me it was in con-fec|\ience of an Order that the Rajah had received from the Calcutta Governor, Mr. Then I was taken

to different Forts under Forty Men, who guarded me. On the 17th they put me in a Boat, where was another pril'oner, an Armenian Gentleman, called Melcomb Phillip. We were carried to Chowfah, where I received from the Rajah and his Ministers, Letters of Condolance on my Imprisonment, and Approbation of my Conduct. After some Days we were carried to Fatna, where we arrived the 30th March, and we were carried before the Company’s Collector named Shitabroy, who confined us in his Cutcherry till the 6th April. He then sent away Rajah Bulwantjing's Guards, and put English Sepoys over us. As loon as the Guard was changed, they carried us into a Boat in such a hasty Manner, that we could not know what we were accused of: One Day we heard there was an Order of Mr. Vereljl, the Governor of Calcutta, that we should be carried to before

Mahomed Reza Khawn. We arrived at Murjhedabad on the 26th April 1768, and we were carried before Mahomed Reza Khazvn, who was the Superior of the Vol. 33.

English ColleClots. He drdered its to be carried to a E*ft iodU Place called Ferrakbag. On the 27th April, the First *

Sepoys Guard was sent away, and other were put in their Place, under the Command of* Major Christian Fife her. — While we were Prifofters, our Relations and Friends applied to the Nabob to release us, who told them he had wrote to Calcutta for Orders. At Calcutta our Relations presented a Petition to the Governor and Council, which was presented to Mr. Vereljl himself, who told them to go and apply to the Nabob at the City of Murjhadaba On the 23d May we were released. We went to Calcutta, where we arrived the 8 th June. On the 10th we Waited on Mr. Vereljl, to know his Pleasure, He infilled we had not been Prisoners. I told Mr. Verelft that I had transacted Business for some English Gentlemen, under a Purwannah, sealed with the Company’s Seal j he said.

If this is the Cafe, then you are blameless: Bring the Purwannah and Ibew it me — I did not bring my Purwannah to shew him, being advised not to do it* because the other Gentleman, Melcomb Phillip, told mo that he had carried his, and that Mr. Vereljl had detained it. Afterwards I was diffrefied, from an Ordef that no Armenian or Portuguese should go out of thtf English Dominions, lb I remained without having- my Goods, or being able to collect my Money, which determined me to come to this Country to seek for*

Q. To what Value do you suppose the Goods and Debts you left behind you amounted to ?

A. In all £.5,000.

Q. Was that belonging to yourself ?

A. Yes.

Q. Did you leave no Goods or Debts with which you was intruded by other People ?

A. I did.

Q. Whose Goods ?

A. Mr. Bolt's and Mr. Hare's. I guess about, 10 Of £. 12,000 worth.

Q. In what Part of the Country were those Goods and Debts ?

A. In Bulwantjing's Dominions,

Q. Since that Time have you received no Account of your own Debts, or those belonging to Mr. Bolts or Mr.

Hare f

A. I have had no Account — 1 have been in England since August 1769.

Q. Did you never hear that the Company’s Servants were forbid to trade in Bulwantjing's Country ?

A. No — -I think the Company’s Servants were allowed to trade in that Country, because I have often seen Goods there belonging to the English, and have seen English Gomaflahs in that Country.

Q. Do you think your Goods and Debts, together with those of Mr. Bolts and Mr. Hare, are loft, so that you shall never receive them ?

A. I don’t expect a Farthing.

Q. Of the £.5,000 you left, what Part was in Goods* and what in Debts ?

A. Rather more in Debts than Goods.

Q. When you left that Country, did you look upon your Debts as good ?

A.At that Time every one was good.

Q. W hat Part of Mr. Bolt's and Mr. Hare's Property left behind, was in Goods, and what in Debts I

A. As I guess, rather more in Goods than in Debts.

Q. Did you apprehend that their Debts were good when you left that Country ?

A. They were good.

Q. Do you know of any Goods of English Manufac* tory being fold in Bulwantjing's Countty ?

A. No.

Q. Do you know of any English Broad Cloth and Copper, or other English Commodities, being fold in Bulwantjing's or Sujahal Dowla's Country ?

A. 1 never saw it, but have heard of it.

Mr. Cojamaul was then asked, Had you ever any Warning or Notice either from the Servants of the English Company or Bulwantfing, or any of his Officers, that you was conducing yourself improperly, before you was seized and imprisoned ?

A. I never had any Notice.

Q. Did you think that Purwannah gave you Authority to trade for Mr. Bolts ?

A. No.

Q. Had you any Purwannah to trade for Mr. Bolts ?

A. No.

Q. Had you a Right to trade for the English without Purwannah ?

A. I had, being a Merchant settled in that Country.

Q. If you had a Right to trade without a Purwannah, what Use was there in having one ?

A. I was ad vi fed if I did any Business for English Gentlemen to get one — 1 had Liberty and Permission from the Rajah Bukvantjing to do Business in that Country, and never was molested the Rajah and the People were satisfied.

Q. Was Ghazipore Part of Bulwantfing's Country ?

A. It was.

When you came to this Kingdom, did you apply to the East India Company ?

A. I arrived in London the 18 August 1769 — I presented a Petition to the Court of Directors on the 12 September, and I never had any Answer — In October the Secretary sent me a Letter that he would be glad to speak with me any Morning. I employed Mr. Bolts, because I could not talk English myferf.

Q. Did Mr. Verelfi ever desire you to give him a List of your Goods, and say he would assist you in recovering them ?

A. No.

Q. When you carried on Trade in Bulwantfing's Country, did you ever make use of the English Name ?

A. I did not, 1 had no Occasion, because I was a Merchant — I traded for English Gentlemen, but did not call myself an English Gomaftah, nor laid I traded by English Authority.

Q- Who pays Shitabroy his Salary ?

A. He is paid out of the Revenues, the same as other Officers employed in the Collection of them.

Q. Who is it that pays him, the Nabob or the Company ?

A. Certainly the Nabob; he receives it out of the Revenues, and makes up his Accounts every Year to the Nabob, at Murjhedabad.

Q. Was it paid out of the Gross Revenue, or out of the particular Revenue assigned to the Nabob by Treaty ?

A. Out of the Gross Revenue.

Q. About what Time were these Purwannahs first issued?

Q. Were any Purwannahs ordered by Lord Clive ?

A. I don’t recollect.

Q. Were Purwannahs of the same Effect as those produced, issued in Bengal, Bahar, and Orifta ?

A. There were, to the Company’s Servants, mentioning the Name of the Gomaftahs employed by them.

Q. Could a Gomaftah, acting under such a Purwannah, fend Goods free of Duties without a Duf-tuck ?

A. Certainly not — The Duftuck passes the Goods by the different Custom Houses, which are called Chokies; but there is a Duty upon almost every Species of Goods that is paid to the Farmer where those Goods are manufactured, which the Duftuck has nothing to do with, and which all the Countrjr Merchants are subject to, but which the Purwannah given to our Merchants exempts them from, as I have always understood. I am not lure, whether the Duty is paid by the Purchaser or Manufacturer, but whichever it is, the Purwannah ex* empts him — I have traded in Shujah Dowla'% Country, in Ophium and some little Saltpetre.

Q. Do they pay Duties in Shujah Dowla'% Country ?

A. I always traded as a Servant of the Company, and consequently my Agents were furnished with Pur-wannahs and Duftucks, and therefore I cannot speak positively to the Duties — When those Orders came to me, every Gomaftah of mine was recalled.

A. I never heard any thing in particular about them.

Q. Had you ever any Complaint from any of the Princes of the Country, while you was Chief at , against Mr. Bolts ?

A. No; not to my Recollect ion.

Letter to Mr. Gentil.

" Dear Sir,

" It is a long Time since I heard from you, which " has made me a little uneasy. I have long intended " to come from hence to have the Pleasure of seeing you*

" as also to pay my Respects to the Nabob, but my " Affairs have not as yet permitted me; nevertheless, it ,c is what I hope to be able to do in a short Time.

" In regard to the Saltpetre, I hope the Disputes on " that Subject are ended, but it is not possible forme to " abandon my Right for the Advantage of other Gentlemen, who have no other Pretensions than what " are founded on Injustice, and who would take the " Advantage of my Absence for to deprive me of the " Advantage of my Contrafts, which haveexisted a long " Time, and which were drawn out with all Propriety " and Justice, conformable to the Customs of Merchants. If that -had been for the Nabob, it would " have been another thing. But before I give up the " Point to Gentlemen who are not in anyway my " Superiors, I allure you, I will follow the Affair to the *c last Court of Justice, where I can have llecourse. " Next Year I will give over all further Commerce, " but in the mean time, I hope you will help me with " your Assistance. My Gomaftah Goaidafs writes me " you had informed him, that Colonel Barker had wrote " Letters to stop all my Business, and to drive away my " People; I shall be obliged to you for your Information " on that Subje ft, for that Gentleman is not authorized " to act in such a Manner.

" I have taken the Liberty to fend you a Letter for " Cogee Rafael; I beg you will deliver it to him and " fend me his Answer. I am surprised the Nabob has " not as yet paid (as they write me) the Amount of the " Broad Cloth which my People fold him; if that is " true, be so good as to represent the same to him. " Melcomb writes me, that he also has sent some Cloth " from Dacca to the Nabob’s Camp: I do not doubt " of your favourable Assistance for the Sale. I shall be " very glad when you give me an Opportunity of " rendering you any Service here, in Return for the " Trouble I have given you. I shall never be convinced of your Friend ship, unless you give me some " Opportunity or other of testifying mine; but you, " who are Naib Subah, and immerged in Business, are " perhaps above these Trifles. Let it be as it will; I " allure you, my dear Sir, that nobody wi(hes you " better than I dp.

" I have wrote a Letter to the Nabob, to whom I " beg you will give my humble Respects. There is " arrived an Eng/ish Europe Ship, and another French one.

" The Affairs of our Company are in great Agitation, and " are laid before the King and Parliament of England, " and according to the Letters I have received, there is " a great Likelihood that my Associate Mr. Johnstone " will come out Governor from the King. I shall be " be glad from Time to Time to hear from you, who " am, with a most perfect Esteem,

" Dear Sir,

" Calcutta, u Your most humble Servant,

" the 19 June 1767. William Bolts.

" P. S. I need not recommend Mahomed Ashrujf " Cawn to your Notice."

" I will engage to find ver}r responsible Merchants who will undertake to execute such a Plan, and en-! gage to deliver, on the Company’s Account at , " for the first Year 25,000 Maunds of refined Petre, " which fiin.ll be near Three Times finer than that they " have generally received from Patna, at a Price to be " hereafter stipulated; upon which the Company might " be lure of gaining at least Fifteen thoul'and Pounds <c Sterling per Annum clear, if they were even to fell it " again in Bengal.

" Other Advantages, which would likewise accrue " from such a Plan, are obvious; the Foreign Companies might be supplied with their Allowances from " this Petre, and our Company be thereby freed from " those large Drawbacks on that Branch of their " Trade. And it would also prevent the French or " Dutc/i from manufacturing it themselves in those " Parts, which they will certainly attempt whenever " the English Gomaftahs are totally recalled. At the same Time it must be remembered, that though the " Gomaftahs of private Gentlemen be all recalled; " yet while, our Armies continue in those Parts, there is a great Risque, that, however strict the Orders " of the Board be, some or other Gentlemen of In-«c lluence with the Army, will find Means to evadethem, and to engross the whole of this Article in confe-« quence of their Influence over, and the Ignorance " and Fears of, the Country Princes. So that it does " not appear possible so advantageously to obviate the Evils apprehended by any other than this Plan, which I have submitted to your Consideration.

" I am. Sir,

" Yqur most obedient Servant, (Sighed)

Whereas Repre-" fentation hath been made to us by Sir Josiah Child\ " Baronet* our Deputy Governor, that upon long Con-xi ferences by him had with Coja Panous Calendar, an Armeniaii Merchant of Eminency, and an Inhabitant of 4t Ifpahan in Persia; as also with Sir John Chardin, of London, Knight, they had on Behalf of the Armenian Nation " proposed to him several Particulars for carrying on a " great Part of the Armenian Trade to India and Persia, and from thence to Europe, by way of England; which u will redound greatly to His Majesty’s Advantage in " His Customs, and to the Encrease of the Englishi Navi-u gation, if the Armenian Nation might obtain such Licence from this Company, as will give them Encou-k* ragement lo to alter and invert the ancient Course of " their Trade to and from Europe: And we being always " willing to encrease and encourage the public Trade and " Navigation of this Kingdom, after a serious Debate of " all the Propositions relating to this Affair, have " thought fit to agree and resolve as follows; viz.

" First, That the Armenian Nation shall now, and at all Times hereafter, have equal Share and Benefit of " all Indulgencies this Company have, or shall at any " Time hereafter grant to any of their own Adventurers " or other English Merchants whatsoever.

" Secondly, That they shall have free Liberty at all " Times hereafter to pals and repass to and from India, " on any of the Company’s Ships, on as advantageous " Terms as any Freeman whatsoever.

" Thirdly, That they shall have Liberty to live in any " of the Company’s Cities, Garrisons, or Towns, in India, " and to buy, fell, and purchase Land or Houses, and be " capable of all civil Offices and Preferments, in the " same Manper as if they were Englishmen born, and shall " always have the free and undilturbed Liberty of the " Exercise of their own Religion. And we hereby declare, that we will not continue any Governor in our " Service, that shall in any kind disturb or discountenance " them in the full Enjoyment of all the Privileges hereby granted to them; neither shall they pay any other " or greater Duty in India, than the Company’s Fa<flors. Mr. Verelfl was then called, and asked,

- Q. What do you know with respect to the imprison-Tnent of the Armenians, the Cause of it, and by whole Authority they were confined ?

A. I should be very glad to give any Account in my Power to the Committee of those Transactions; but as the Petitioner Cojamaul, and Rafael, another Armenian, have commenced Suits against me, both in Chancery and the Court of Common Pleas, to which I have a Defence, and don’t doubt a full Justification; and as those Suits are now depending, 1 am adviled by my Counsel not to answer before this Committee, Matters which are the Subjects of those Suits; I therefore with to decline answering the Question.

Mr. Bolts.

Q. What Time did you resign the Company’s Service ?

A. I believe in November 1766.

<2. When was it first notified to you, by the Governor And Council, that you should return to England ?

A* A few Months after I resigned the Service, but while I was a Magistrate of the Mayor’s Court.

Mr. Cojamaul.

Q. Did you never hear that one Reason of your being lent away, was, your evading signing the new Covenants, Relative to receiving of Presents?

A. I never heard of any such Reason.

Q. Did you sign. the new Covenants?

A. I did not sign them myself, but I did by my Deputy, which was equally as valid, and which I always acknowledged ,to be so.

Q. Why did you hot sign them yourself?

A. Because it was my rleafure.

Q. Oid you 'ever give any- other Reason for not ’fcgning yourself ?

A. if I have it will appear upon the public Records. — I believe I did;

Q. Did y6u enter into any new Contrafts or Concerns in Trade after you had resigned the Service ?

A. I did, because I had a Right to do it.

Q. Do you know any Instance of any other Person, who had resigned the Service of the Company, forced out of the Country in the Manner you was ?

A. I know of none in the civil Service of the Com* pany, but I know of several Gentlemen, who had been in the Military' Service, being seized and ordered for England} but I know of none that were seized so suddenfy, and with so much Violence as I was.

Q. Is it not usual for Civil Servants to go when they receive Notice?

A. I never knew of any such Custom-among any of the Civil Servants, though I have known many Instances *of such arbitrary Orders.

Q. Have those Orders been obeyed ?

A. Sometimes they have, and sometimes not.

Q. What is done with the Civil Servants when they do not obey ?

A. I have not known of any Civil Servants sent away by Force. — Sometimes their residing was dispensed with; but I suppose they would have been lent away if they had not gone voluntarily. ’

Q. Do you know of any Civil Servants going away when they were ordered ?

A. Yes.

Q. When did that Custom begin of ordering People to be seized and sent Home by Force ?

A. I never knew of any Instance before 1765 or 1766. Q. Did you ever know of any Civil Servants refilling to go when the Orders were not dispensed with ?

A. I don’t remember any of the Civil covenanted Servants of the Company refilling to go; but I know of several British Subjects being forced, upon such Orders, tofeek that Protection in the foreign Settlements that they could not enjoy in their own.

Q. Did you ever know of any British Subjects, covenanted or not covenanted, who continued to reside in Calcutta after ordered to quit, and that Order not difi penfed with ?

A. None in my Time; but have heard of others in former Times.

Q.What Instances have you heard of in former Times ?

A. There was a Gentleman named Cooke, and several others, whole Names I don’t recollect. — Mr. Cooke was in the Company’s Civil Service at Dacca, and, as I heard, dismissed for Embezzlement, and ordered Home by the Directors, but refilled to go, and remained in the Country; — the Governor and Council, at that Period, did not think themselves safe to execute such Orders.

" The Nabob represented to me the great Inconveni- ences which arise from the Gomaftahs and Dependants of English Gentlemen residing in his Dominions, " particularly at Garrackpoor, and in the

A. The Representation that I made to the Council upon the 3d January 1768, is very strong, and very pointed to that Purpose — 1 thought it absolutely ne-celfary to rcca! them.

Q. Was Capt" Harper one of those among whom you said you distributed your Profits of Trade i

A. Capt" Harper had served me as an Aid de Camp and Secretary for Two Years, and he was one of those to whom the Distribution was made.

The Board drew up the following general Opinion.

" Every Method has been tried fer carrying on the " Inland Trade upon such a Footing as to prevent " Disputes between our Agents and the Country Government, or between one Agent and another; and " for deciding, in a just and reasonable Manner, such VOL. 33.

f‘ as might unavoidably happen. Having experienced East India " the Obstructions to which that Trade would be liable A " if the Officers of the Country Government were admitted to any Authority over the Agents, it

was refblved in Consultation the 5th March 1763,.

" that the Chief of the nearest English Factory should kt finally determine all such Disputes, and as the Rungpore, Dinagepore, and adjacent Districts, where a very " considerable Part of this Inland Trade centers, appeared to be too far removed from any of our Fasto-.

" ries to admit of such Enquiry being made in a satis-.,

" fadlory and accurate Manner; for this Reason,

" principally, it was agreed, that a Senior Servant " should be appointed to reside at Rungpore, who " should have Power to hear and determine all Disputes.

" No sooner is this Resolution carried into Practice,

" than some of the En%lish Agents complain as loudly " of Injuries suffered from the Authority of the English)

Resident, as they did before of the Nabob’s Government.

" Shall there then be no Government, no Restraint " upon those Excesses, which either Ignorance, Passion,

" or Self-interest, may lead an English Agent to com- '

" mit in the Country ? This is really the same at present; and although it is very certain that some of the Gentlemen employed are of unexceptionable Character, and whose good Behaviour might be depended " on, yet many there are of a contrary Disposition,

" but there need not many Arguments to prove, that " both the good and the bad should be under foine " Law; yet if We examine the same of the English Agents " up the Country, we shall find they are under none.

" Our Charter does not authorize our Courts to take " Cognizance of any Crimes they might commit in *e these Parts; and it has been laid down as a fundamental Principle, that the Country Government shall " have no Power of them.

" We need not look further for the Root of that " Licentioufhefs which has produced such innumerable " Complaints from the Country Government, and the " Inhabitants in those Parts where European Agents " have been sent: It can now no longer be doubted,

" that many of those Complaints have been wellgrounded, particularly in the Article of felling " Goods by Force for more than the current Market " Price: A Practice called in this Country Barja, or " Guchavut.

" All the Power we can give the Chiefs of our " Factories over these Agents will be very insufficient " to remedy this Disorder, since we have in Reality " none ourselves; and therefore, disagreeable as it is to " deprive so many of our Nation of the Benefits they

now receive, by being employed as Agents in the " Country, yet it seems an unavoidable Necessity, and " for the fake of the public Tranquillity and Welfare " must be adopted, and the Trade carried on for the " future by Black. Gomaftahs, who may be tried and " punished by our Court of Zemindary, if they commit anyExcelfes or A&soflnjustice; and that Power " delegated, as far as shall appear necessary, to the " Chiefs of the Subordinate Factories.

" It will be objected by those concerned in the Inland " Trade, that Gomaftahs will be liable to be oppressed " by the Country Government, who have taken, and " will take, every Opportunity of restraining us from " that Trade which they regard as an Innovation; this " Objection we believe is very just, and we shall expect that many Difficulties will be found in the Beginning in carrying on this Trade by Gomaftahs, but " these we think may be lurmounted by proper Application to the Nabob and his Officers; and, upon the " Whole.are of Opinion, that all private Inconveniences " must be submitted to, even the Rilque ot being errtircly deprived of the Trade, rather than suffer the 11 G " Inhabitant

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Justices should hold their Special Sessions, for aPpointing Surveyors, in the Week next after Michaelmas Sessions in every Year; and every Surveyor continue in Office till a new one should be appointed.

Rest/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Proportion of the Surveyor’s Salary, which should be allotted by the Justices to be paid, by any Parish, Township, ot Place, should be paid out of the Morvey toarife from Compositions, Penalties, or Levies, to fc»e raised within the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Surveyor of every such District should, at the Time of his Appointment, give Bond to some proper Person, in every such Parish, Township, or Place, to be nominated by the Justices, with sufficient Sureties, to account for the Money which should come to his Hands as Surveyor, in such Penalty as the Justices should think fit 5 and that every’ Surveyor should make up separate Accounts, to each Parish, Township, or Place, according to the Directions of the Ad; and produce them at the V eftry, or General Meeting of the Inhabitants, to be held within the same, at least Three Days before the Meeting of the Justices for the appointing new Surveyors, and should pass such Accounts before the Justices, at such Meeting, on Oath; and if such Surveyor should die, or become incapable of doing his Duty, Two Justices should have Power to appoint another for the Remainder of the Year.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, instead of allowing Two separate Rates or Assessments, not exceeding Six Pence in the Pound for each Rate, according to the present Act; videlicet, One of them for the Purposes of buying Materials, erecting Guide Posts, and making Satisfaction for Damages done to Lands by the making of new Ditches, or Drains, and the other for the Purposes of repairing the Highways, causewavs, and Bridges, where the Statute Duty shall be insufficient, it would be more convenient and effectual to have Power given to Two Justices, acting for the District where the Roads lie, to make an Order, at some Special Sessions, to authorize an Assessment to be made, within any Parish, Township, or Place, to raise Money for those Purposes; anil all'o for the paying the said Proportion of the Surveyor’s Vol. 33.

Salary, in case the Compositions and Penalties should Highway* not be sufficient for the same; but no more than One and such Assessment to be made in the same Year, and not TnfnpiktJ. to exceed Six Pence in the Pound for all those Purposes; and the Money raised thereby to be expended within such Parish, Township, or Place; and Notice to be given of such intended AsselTment, in the Church or Chapel of the Parish or Place requiring the fame, on some Sunday within a Month before such Application shall be made, specifying the Intention of applying for such Assessment, and the Day and Place of Meeting of the Justices to whom such Application is intended to be made; and if such Place be extraparochial, the Surveyor should give Information to the Inhabitants thereof, by fixing a Notice in Writing, to the Eff'ed before-mentioned, upon some conspicuous Place there, a Week before such Meeting of the Justices; and that the Person or Persons applying for an Order for such Assessment should be at Liberty, either to apply to the Justices at their Special Sessions, or to the General Quarter Sessions, as he or they should think fit; but if the Order be made at the Special Sessions, any Person liable to contribute to such Assessment, who should think himself aggrieved thereby, ought to have an Appeal to the next General Quarter Sessions of the Peace against such Order, on giving Notice of such Appeal within Seven Days after such Order should be made.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, in order to make the Statute Duty more effectual, and to obviate Doubts which have arisen in the Construdtkm of the said Act, every Person who shall keep a Waggon, Cart, Wain, or Tumbrel, and Three or more Horses or Beasts of Draught used to draw therein, should be deemed to keep a Team, Draught, or Plough, within the Meaning of the said Act, and be liable to perform Statute Duty with the fame; and every Person, who shall not keep a Team, Draught, or Plough, but shall keep One or more Cart or Carts, and One or Two Horses or Beasts of Draught only, used to draw in each of such Carts upon the Highways, should be obliged to perform his Statute Duty with such Cart or Carts, and Horse or Horses, or Beasts of Draught, and One Labourer to attend each Cart, or to pay, according to the Directions of the Act, for the Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, which he shall occupy, at the Option of the Surveyor; but if the Surveyor should make his Election to have the Duty performed in Kind, the Person liable to perform the same should have Liberty to compound, by paying for each Day’s Duty One Shilling and Six Pence for a Cart and One Horse or Beast of Draught, and Two Shillings and Six Pence for a Cart and Two Horses or Beasts of Draught; and every Person, who shall keep a Coach, Post Chaise, Chair, or other Wheel Carriage, and not keep a Team, Draught, or Plough, nor occupy Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, of the annual Value of Fifty Pounds, should be liable to pay One Shilling, in respect of every Day’s Statute Duty, for every Horse which he shall draw in such Carriage, or pay according to the Value of the Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, which he shall occupy, as the said Act directs, at the Option of the Surveyor.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Statute Duty ought to be performed, or compounded for, in the Parish or Place where the Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, lit, in respect whereof such Duty is required; and if any Person, who shall keep a Team, Draught, or Plough, and not occupy Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, of the yearly Value of Fifty Pounds, in the Parish or Place where he relides, and shall occupy Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, in any other Parish or Place, such Person ought to perform his Statute Duty in the following Manner; viz.One Day’s Duty in the Parish or

(i 1 Place

Highways

and

Turnpikes.

950

Place where he so refutes, and One other Day’s Duty for every Ten Pounds per Annum which he shall occupy in such Pari Hi or Place, and One Day’s Duty for every Ten Pounds pei Annum which he shall occupy in any other Parish or Place, provided the same should be sufficient to take his full Six Days Duty, if not, the Remainder to be performed in the Parish or Place where he shall so reside; and if he shall occupy Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, in Two or more Parishes or Places besides that wherein he shall reside, which shall in the Whole amount to more than Fifty Pounds per Annum, then such Team Duty ought to be performed in such of them as lie nearest to the Parish or Place wherein he shall so reside.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Notice, required by the Act for compounding Statute Duty, ought to be given on the First or Second Sunday in November, instead of January; and that no Composition ought to be permitted, if not made, and the Money paid, on the Day fixed by such Notice; and that Power should be given to the Justices, at their Special Sessions for appointing Surveyors, to order the Team Duty to be performed in Kind, within any Parish or Place, when it shall appear, from the Complaint of the Surveyor thereof, that he has Difficulties in hiring Teams at reasonable Rates, for the Repair of the Roads within the same, occasioned by the Compositions made for such Teams.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Hedges on each Side the Highway, ought to be so cut and pruned every Year, within the Time limited by the Act, that no Part of them, when cut, should be more than Four Feet above the Ditch Bank, where there shall be a Ditch, nor more than Five Feet above the Ground where there shall be no Ditch; and that Surveyors ought to be restrained from cutting down, or lopping, any Timber Tree, or Trees, used for Timber, in the Country where the Road lies, except Pollards, until the same shall have been viewed by Two Justices of the Peace, and certified to be proper to be pruned or fallen.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Surveyor ought to be permitted to go into private Lands or Grounds, to dig Materials, without the Permission of the Owner or Occupier thereof in Writing, until an Order shall be made for that Purpose, by Two Justices of the Peace, at a Special Sessions, after having received Evidence, upon Oath, that Materials could not be found on the Wastes, Rivers, or Brooks (where they are allowed to be got by the Act) convenient for the Purposes for which they are wanted.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Number of Horses allowed to draw upon all Highways, not Turnpike, ought to be as follows: To every Waggon, having the Fellies of the Wheels of the Breadth of Nine Inches, Eight Horses; to every Cart, having the Fellies of the Wheels of the same Breadth, Five Horses; to every Waggon, having the Fellies of the Wheels of the Breadth of Six Inches, and rolling on each Side a Surface of Nine Inches, Seven Horses; to the like Waggons, rolling a Surface of Six Inches only, Six Horses; to every Cart, having the Fellies of the Wheels of the Breadth of Six Inches, Four Horses; to every Waggon, having the Fellies of the Wheels of lets Breadth than Six Inches, Five Horses; to every Cart, with the like Fellies, Three Horses; and that Two Oxen ought, in all Carriages, to be considered as One Horle.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Provision in the General Turnpike Act, allowing additional Horses in deep Snow or Ice, ought to be extended to the Highways in general.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That where the Turnpike Road or Roads, leading

Refo/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Carriages ought to be restrained to the following Weights; viz. Waggons having the Fellies of the Wheels of the Breadth of Nine Inches to Five Tons Ten Hundred, between the 5th Day of April and the 10th Day of October, and to Five Tons between the 10th Day of October and the 5th Day of; Carts having the like Wheels to Three Tons, between the 5*h of April and the 10th of October, and to Two Tons Fifteen Hundred, between the 10th of October and the 5H1 of April; Waggons having the Fellies of the Wheels of the Breadth of Six Inches, and rolling on each Side a Surface of Nine Inches, to Four Tons Fifteen Hundred, between the 5th of April and the 10th of October, an.ci to Four Tons Eight Hundred, between the 10th of October and the cth of April-, Waggons having the Fellies of the Wheels of the Breadth of Six Inches, constructed in the common Manner, to Four Tons Five Hundred, between the 5th of April and the 10th of October, and to Three Tons Fifteen Hundred, between the 10th of October and the 5th of April; Carts having the Fellies of the like Breadth to Two Tons Twelve Hundred, between the 5 th of April and the 10th of October, and to Two Tons Seven Hundred, between the 10th of October and the 5th of April; Waggons having the Fellies of less Breadth than Six Inches to Three Tons, between the 5th of April and the 10th of October, and to Two Tons Ten Hundred, between the icth of October and the 5th of April; Carts having the Wheels of the like Breadth to One Ton Ten Hundred, between the 5th of April and the 10th of October, and to One Ton Five Hundred, between the xoth of October and the 5th of April, in every Year; each Carriage to be"included in the above Weights, and every Hundred to consist of Five Score and Twelve Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Waggons and Carts, having the Fellies of the Wheels of the Breadth of Six Inches, or upwards, ought to have the Privilege of Exemptions and Compositions which are allowed by the particular Turnpike Acts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Carriages, having the Fellies of the Wheels of the Breadth of Six Inches, or upwards, ought to pay no higher Tolls than those fixed by the particular Turnpike Acts; but that all Waggons and Carts, having the Fellies of the Wheels of Ids Breadth than Six Inches, ought to pay the Tolls allowed by those particular Acts,. and One Half more, and to be excluded from all the Privileges of Compositions and Exemptions; and that

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, rop That the Tolls upon Turnpike Roads would be much increased, if the Trustees were to farm them out to the best Bidders, on a Day and Place to be appointed, for any Term not exceeding Three Years, with Liberty for either Party to vacate such Con trad at the End of each Year, upon giving Three Months Notice; proper Advertisements for that Purpose being first fixed upon the several Toll Gates, upon the Market Crosses in the neighbouring Market Towns, and inserted in some Journal or Newspaper circulated in that Part of the Country where such Roads respectively lie, specifying the Sum which such Tolls amounted to in the preceding Year, and that no less was to be offered; and if every Bidder' was to make his Proposal by a Ticket sealed up-and delivered to the Clerk in the Presence of the Trustees, and the best Bidder was to give Security for the Performance of his Contract; and that Power should be given to all Trustees to farm out the Tolls, who are not authorized to do it by the particular Turnpike Acts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That much Trouble would be saved to the Trustees, much Expence to the Public, and many Frauds prevented, if every Turnpike Road was to be made and kept in Repair by Contract, instead of Wages; for which Purpose, it should be divided into convenient Districts, specifying each Part of the Road so intended to be made or kept in Repair, by separate Allotments, and notified in Writing in Manner aforesaid; and, to prevent Impositions in such Contracts, the Road in each Allotment should be previously viewed, and each intended Contract estimated by a skilful Surveyor; and the Undertakers should be allowed to call in such Statute Duty from the adjacent Places, as should be agreed upon, to be employed in performing such Contract.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, when any Turnpike Road shall be indicted or presented, the Expence attending the fame, and also the Fine to be set by the Court for the repairing of such Road, should be proportioned between the Persons liable to repair the same and the Treasurer of such Turnpike Road, in such Manner and Proportions as the Court, in which such Indictment or Presentment shall be preferred, shall order; and that the Treasurer should pay the Sum so ordered, out of the First Money which shall come to his Hands, and be allowed the same in his Accounts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, where any ancient Road shall be turned, by Virtue of any Turnpike Ad, and the old Road shall be (hut up, the Parish, Township, or Place, which was liable to repair such old Road, should be and continue, in like Manner, liable to repair the new Road, after the same shall have been put in sufficient Repair by the Trustees of such Turnpike Ad, and be so certified by Two Justices of the Peace, so that the same do not exceed the Length of the old Road; if it Fhould, then so much as lies nearest to such Parish or Place, equal in Length to such old Road; and that no old Road ought to be (hut up, till such new Road shall be so repaired and certified.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That no Bill, for making any new Turnpike Road, ought to be presented to the House, until an Estimate of the Expence of making the same shall have been made, and proved to the Committee to whom the Petition for such Bill shall have been referred, and Three-fourths of the Money contained in such Estimate subscribed; and that no Toll Gate ought to be erected, nor any of the Laws relating to Turnpike Roads enforced, upon any Part of such Turnpike Road, until Two-thirds, at least, of the Money so subscribed, shall have been expended in the Repairs thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Carriage, liable to be weighed, should pass upon any Turnpike Road, or public Highway, un-leis the same shall be made and constructed in such Manner, that no Pair of Wheels shall be wider than Four Feet Six Inches from Inside to Inside, to be measured on the Ground; and that the Distance from the Centre of the Fore Wheels to the Centre of the Hind Wheels of all such Waggons, or Four-wheeled Carriages (^not being used for the Carriage of Timber only) shall not be more than Nine Feet, to be mea-l'ured from the Centre of the Axle-trees at the Ends thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, after the intended Act shall be patted into a Law, there ought to be a Standing Order of the House, that no Turnpike Bill should pass without a Clause in it, that nothing therein contained should extend, or be construed to extend, to vary or alter any Regulations contained in that Act.

THE Hour, appointed for taking into Confederation the Petition of Thomas Esquire,

complaining of an -undue Election and Return for the Borough of Saltash, in the County of Cornwall, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Election and Return, according to the Directions of Two several Acts of Parliament, palfed in the 10th and nth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the regulating the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returt\s of Members to serve in Parliament.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members, on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned -,

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and hi Members being found to be present;

The Petitioner, his Counsel and Agents, and the Counsel and Agents for the Sitting Member, who attended at the Door, were called in to the Bar — The Clerk of the Select Committees of Elections attending also at the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Box, containing the Names of all the Members of the House, and sealed with Mr. Speaker’s Seal, was placed upon the Table, and the Seals being inspected by Mr. Speaker, the Attestation annexed to the Outside of the Box, ligned by Mr. Speaker, purporting, " That " the said Box was, on the 3d Day of June 1772, made " up in his Presence, in the Manner directed by an Ad, made in the 10th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament," was read.

And the Seals being broken, and the Box opened, the Attelfation inclosed therein, and signed by the Clerk, purporting, " That the Names of all the Members " were by him, in the Presence of the Sjteaker, put " into the said Box, on the 3d Day of June 1772," was read.

And the said Names, written on diflind Pieces of Paper, being all as near as might be, of an equal Size, and rolled up in the same Manner, were by the Clerk taken out of the said Box, and put in equal Numbers, into Six Uhdfes, placed on the Table for that Purpose, and were there shaken together; and then the Clerk publicly drew out of the said Six Glafl'es, alternately, the said Pieces of Paper, and delivered them to Mr.

Speaker, who read the same to the House.

And the Names of Eight other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of John Cleveland, Esquire, being drawn, he informed the House that he had given his Vote at the Election complained of by the Petition now taken into Consideration; and his Name was thereupon set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House.

And the Names of Two other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of James Wallace, Esquire, being drawn, the Counsel for the Petitioner declared, that the said Mr. Wallace was intended to be nominated by the said Petitioner; and the said Mr. Wallace having in his Place contented to such Nomination, and no Objection being made to his serving on the said Select: Committee as such Nominee, his Name was set aside.

And the Name of the Lord Clare being drawn, he required to be excused from serving on the said Select Committee, on Account of his being 6b Years of Age, or upwards; and having at the Table verified the Cause of such Requisition upon Oath, he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Nine other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Robert Harley, Esquire, being drawn, he required to be excused from serving on the said Select Committee, on Account of his being 60 Years of Age, or upwards; and having at the T'able verified the Cause of such Requisition upon Oath, he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Three other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of the Right honourable Themes Harley being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for rnot serving on the said Select Committee, that he was one of the Aldermen of the City of London, now on the Rota, attending the Session of general Ga d Delivery at the Old Bailey, and that his Absence from that Duty would be. attended with great Inconvenience in carrying on the Business of fthe said Session; and the Substance of what was so alledged by him being taken down by the Clerk, in Manner before mentioned, and the said Member having at the Table verified the same upon Gath — the Opinion of the House was taken therein, Mr. Speaker putting the Question to the House, That the said Member (in respect of what he has now so alledged and verified) be excused from serving on the said Select Committee — Which being agreed to by the House, he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Three other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Sir Harry Burrard, Baronet, being drawn, he required to be exculed from serving on the said Select Committee, on Account of his being 60 Years of Age, or upwards; ^nd having at the Table verified the Cause of such Requisition upon Oath, he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Eight other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

After which, His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as followed!; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I cannot put an End to this Session of Parliament* without expressing the Satisfaction I have felt in ob-» serving the Temper and the Prudence, which have governed all your Deliberations, during the Course of it; and Without returning you My particular Thanks for the fresh Proof you have given of your affectionate Attachment to Me, in the additional Security you have provided for the Welfare and Honour of My Family.

I can, with great Pleasure, acquaint you. That the of the Powers of Europe give Me the

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty; where His Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills following; viz.

An Act for granting to His Majesty a certain Sum of Money, out of the Sinking Fund; and for applying certain Monies, therein mentioned, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-two; and for further appropriating the Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament; and for making forth Duplicates of Exchequer Bills, Lottery Tickets, Certificates, Receipts, Annuity Orders, and other Orders, loft, burnt, or destroyed:

An Act for rendering the Payment of the Creditors of Insolvent Debtors more equal and expeditious; and for regulating the Diligence of the Law' by Arrestment and Poinding; and for extending the Privilege of Bills to Promissory Notes; and for limiting Actions upon VuL. 33.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I thank you heartily for the Supplies, which you have granted with so much Chearfulness and Dispatch; and for the ample Provision you have made for every Branch of the Public Service: And I fee, with Pleasure and Approbation, that you have, at the same Time, been able, by a proper Disposition of the Public Money, to make a further Progress in reducing the National Debt.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I make no Doubt but that you will carry, into your respective Counties, the same Principles, and the same Zeal, for the Public Good which 1 have experienced from you in Parliament; and that you will continue to exert your best Endeavours, to cultivate and improve a Spirit of Harmony, and Confidence, amongst all Ranks of my faithful Subjects. Let it be your conllant Care to convince them. That, without a due Reverence for the Laws, and a chearful Obedience to just Authority, neither their Civil nor Religious Rights, and Liberties, I1 L can

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, laid.

It is His Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued to Titefday the Eleventh Day of August next, to be then here held; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday y the Eleventh Day of August next.
